publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Chronic diseases are a major global public health concern and place a substantial burden on individuals, healthcare systems, and society. Their prevention and management depend not only on effective medical treatment but also on sustained engagement in health-promoting behaviors. These behaviors include regular physical activity, healthy dietary practices, medication adherence, self-monitoring, smoking cessation, and other disease-related self-management activities. However, initiating and maintaining such behaviors can be challenging, particularly because individuals differ in their health conditions, risk profiles, knowledge, motivation, behavioral readiness, and support needs. Therefore, accessible, personalized, and continuous interventions are needed to support health behavior change in both individuals at increased risk of chronic diseases and those already living with chronic conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents have emerged as promising tools for supporting health behavior change. Through natural language interaction and other interactive functions, these agents may provide personalized health information, motivational support, goal setting, action planning, self-monitoring, feedback, reminders, and ongoing behavioral guidance. Advances in natural language processing, machine learning, and large language models have further expanded the potential capabilities of AI agents, enabling more flexible, context-sensitive, and personalized interactions. Nevertheless, the application of AI agents in chronic disease prevention and management is developing rapidly, and the available evidence remains diverse in terms of target populations, technological approaches, intervention strategies, theoretical foundations, and evaluated outcomes. A comprehensive mapping of this evidence is needed to understand the current state of the field and identify priorities for future research and development. This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on the application of AI agents for health behavior change in chronic disease prevention and management. Specifically, it will examine the characteristics of the populations and chronic diseases addressed, the types and technological features of AI agents, the health behaviors targeted, the design and delivery of interventions, the behavioral theories and behavior change techniques employed, and the outcomes reported. Particular attention will be paid to how AI agents support behavior change through interactive communication, personalization, behavioral monitoring, feedback, motivational strategies, and other intervention components. The review will be guided by the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. The population will include individuals living with chronic diseases and those at increased risk of developing chronic diseases. The concept will focus on AI agents that provide interactive communication and behavioral support, including AI-powered chatbots, large language model-based agents, virtual health assistants, virtual coaches, dialogue systems, and other relevant interactive AI systems. The context will encompass chronic disease prevention and management across healthcare, community, home-based, and digital health settings. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in nine electronic databases: China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data Knowledge Service Platform, China Science and Technology Journal Database (VIP), Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (SinoMed), PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, ProQuest, and Embase. The search strategy will combine terms related to artificial intelligence agents, chronic diseases, and health behavior change. Studies published in English or Chinese will be considered, with no restrictions on publication year. Reference lists of included studies and relevant review articles will also be screened to identify additional eligible publications. Eligible studies will include original empirical research investigating AI agents designed to promote, improve, or maintain health behaviors relevant to chronic disease prevention or management. A broad range of study designs will be considered, including randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, observational studies, qualitative studies, mixed-methods studies, pilot studies, and feasibility studies. Studies focusing exclusively on disease diagnosis, risk prediction, clinical decision support, or static health information provision without an identifiable behavioral intervention component will be excluded. Study selection will be conducted independently by two reviewers through title, abstract, and full-text screening, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Data will be charted using a standardized extraction form covering study characteristics, population and disease characteristics, technological features of AI agents, health behavior targets, intervention characteristics, theoretical foundations, behavior change techniques, outcomes, feasibility, acceptability, safety, and implementation challenges. Behavioral theories and techniques explicitly reported by study authors will be distinguished from those identified through secondary coding by the reviewers. The findings will be synthesized using descriptive numerical summaries and narrative analysis. The review will characterize the distribution of studies across publication years, countries, disease categories, AI agent types, and behavioral targets. It will also examine the relationships between AI agent capabilities, intervention strategies, and reported health behavior outcomes. Particular attention will be given to the extent to which existing interventions incorporate established behavioral theories and evidence-based behavior change techniques, as well as the reported effectiveness, feasibility, acceptability, and safety of these systems. items.title: Exploring multimodal AI--XR interactions for software development: From expert perspectives to semantic code outlines

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

items.abstract_text: This dataset comes from a nonequivalent control group pretest–posttest quasi-experiment conducted in a primary school in City S, Henan Province, China. It examines the effects of a GenAI-based interdisciplinary project-based learning (IPBL) agent—developed to match the cognitive characteristics of primary school students—on students' learning motivation and interdisciplinary problem-solving competence, both when used alone and when combined with teacher scaffolding. Participants were 136 fourth-grade students (aged 9–11 years; 66 boys, 70 girls) from three intact parallel classes, assigned to conventional IPBL (n = 45), GenAI-supported IPBL (IPBL-GenAI, n = 47), or IPBL co-supported by the GenAI tool and teacher scaffolding (IPBL-GenAI-TS, n = 44). The study comprised five sessions: a uniform pre-test (Session 1), platform-orientation training (Session 2), the core intervention (Sessions 3–4, with the same instructor, the same project topic, and differentiated treatment across groups), and a parallel post-test after project completion (Session 5).The dataset contains three sheets: (1) learning motivation data (adapted from the elementary-school MUSIC Inventory; 12 items, 4-point scale, 4 dimensions: empowerment, usefulness, success, interest); (2) interdisciplinary problem-solving competence data (self-developed with reference to Tan et al.'s problem-solving assessment dimensions; 17 items, 5-point Likert scale, 3 dimensions: problem inquiry, problem representation, strategy execution with process regulation); and (3) a codebook with variable definitions and coding. Reliability and validity were satisfactory (learning motivation: total-scale α = .894, KMO = .872; problem-solving: α = .917, KMO = .903; post-test α = .96 for both instruments).All data have been de-identified: student IDs are anonymous codes (A01–A44, B01–B47, C01–C45) assigned solely for data pairing and cannot be linked to any personally identifiable information; no names, class rosters, or school identifiers are included. The study was approved by the Science and Technology Ethics Committee of Northeast Forestry University (Approval No. 2026176), and written informed consent was obtained from the legal guardians of all participants. The dataset supports the manuscript entitled "Synergistic Effects of Generative AI Tools and Teacher Scaffolding on Interdisciplinary Project-Based Learning in Primary Education: An Empirical Study."

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and digital transformation are reshaping occupational tasks and challenging conventional models of career and technical education (CTE). This conceptual article argues that CTE should be reconceptualized from an educational pathway to workforce infrastructure that continuously connects education, industry, technology, policy, and lifelong learning. Drawing on the contrasting institutional contexts of the United States and China, the article examines how decentralization, systemic coordination, industry-education integration, apprenticeship, technological transformation, and continuing skill development shape national workforce capacity. It proposes a conceptual model of CTE as workforce infrastructure organized around five interconnected functions and four outcomes: occupational competence, human agency, workforce adaptability, and economic and social mobility. Five propositions explain relationships among institutional articulation, AI augmentation, transferable human capabilities, lifelong learning, and equitable access. The article concludes that AI increases CTE's strategic importance by requiring integrated systems capable of continuously developing human expertise, judgment, adaptability, and opportunity.

items.abstract_text: AI‐enabled carbon management is reshaping the hospitality industry, but its promise depends on a workforce that can combine digital fluency with critical ESG judgment. To address this need, this study develops and tests a framework linking ESG‐oriented mindful technology engagement (EMTE) and generative AI capability to five dimensions of digital carbon technology literacy and perceived sustainable carbon achievement (PSCA). We analyzed survey data from 174 hospitality undergraduates in Taiwan using a two‐stage higher‐order PLS‐SEM approach. EMTE and generative AI capability were positively associated with all five dimensions. However, generative AI capability selectively attenuated the EMTE–evaluation relationship, while the other four interactions were not supported. In the direct‐path model, design, ethics, and vision were positively associated with PSCA. By conceptualizing EMTE as a mindfulness‐informed technology‐engagement composite and digital carbon literacy as a multidimensional capability, the study advances a contingent view of human–AI collaboration and highlights verifying AI‐assisted work as a priority for pre‐entry ESG human capital development.

items.title: Can GenAI numeracy tutors support self-regulated learning?

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been the focus of much attention in the higher education sector, both for its potential to support personalised and adaptive learning, but also due to the risk that students may outsource learning to it, leading to gaps in their professional or discipline competencies. This risk of cognitive offloading applies equally to learning how to learn, a skill set explored through studies of self-regulated learning (SRL). Two GenAI numeracy tutors were piloted at a regional Australian university as one component of a newly launched mathematics and statistics support centre, one focusing on medication calculations for Nursing students (NiNA), and the other on threshold numeracy skills for Education students (EdNA). Detailed analysis of students’ conversations with these agents using Zimmerman and Moylan’s 2009 SRL framework revealed extensive evidence of some elements of SRL such as strategic planning, task-specific strategies, and adaptive competence; trace evidence of other elements including self-efficacy and self-evaluation; and no evidence of the remaining elements. This study contributes an underrepresented qualitative perspective to the body of research into the crossover of GenAI and SRL and foreshadows avenues for further research and refinements in the design of GenAI numeracy tutors.

items.title: Beyond Transhumanist Perfectionism: A Prohumanist Framework for AI, Digital Health, and Dignified Longevity

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: AI-enabled medicine does not express a single anthropology, and digital health is not intrinsically transhumanist. Some platformised health arrangements nevertheless stabilise optimisation drift: a transition in which bounded aims of support, prevention, or capability preservation are progressively recoded as an open-ended duty of measurable correction. The drift becomes structurally closer to transhumanist perfectionism than to bounded enhancement when three properties converge: principled stopping rules lose practical force, embodiment is governed as an indefinitely corrigible substrate, and selective interventions escalate into a recursively expanding package of optimisation. Platform incentives, preventive rationalisation, and organisational pressures explain the emergence and diffusion of this pattern more directly than transhumanist doctrine; structural affinity identifies the normative grammar enacted once those properties converge. A reconstructive prohumanist framework evaluates that grammar through dignified longevity, understood as technologically supported continuation of life that preserves embodied agency, plural goods, recognition, justice, and meaningful exit. Four constraints follow: proportionality, contestability, non-totalisation, and epistemic autonomy. Applied to remote patient monitoring and episodic diagnostic AI, they distinguish bounded support from optimisation-by-default across design, deployment, review, and withdrawal.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: This study compares how mediators and potential clients perceive and accept the use of AI in mediation, drawing on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). Using data from 109 mediators and 152 potential clients, this study found that clients are more receptive to AI than mediators, as indicated by significantly higher performance expectancy on 8 tasks and behavioral intentions across all tasks. To map these similarities and differences, this study proposes the Dual Concern Task Model, a theoretical framework mapping AI acceptance in mediation between mediators and clients. This study also found that professional acceptability—mediators' overall judgment that AI is acceptable for use in mediation practice—plays an important role in shaping mediators' performance expectancy, which in turn influences their behavioral intention. This suggests that mediators' evaluations of AI may be grounded in professional accountability and their obligations to clients. This study offers a focused extension of UTAUT by introducing professional acceptability as a construct influencing performance expectancy in mediation. This study also provides practical insights for mediators, training programs, and governing agencies to make informed decisions about AI in mediation, grounded in empirical findings.

items.abstract_text: We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and engagement of three digital formats for dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) mindfulness skills training. In a 30-day randomized pilot study, 45 university students were assigned to GenAI-DBT, a general-purpose large language model chatbot (Chatbot), or a static web resource (Web). Forty-two completed the study, and nine completed follow-up interviews. Usability scores were within acceptable ranges across conditions, with no significant between-group differences. GenAI-DBT showed the highest observed participant-week adherence (71.4%, vs. 53.3% for Web and 42.3% for Chatbot), a descriptive difference. Mindful Attention Awareness Scale and Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale scores showed no significant time-by-group interactions, and session-level self-reported mood changes did not differ significantly across conditions. GenAI-DBT showed a larger positive change in linguistic valence than Chatbot (4.28 vs. 1.59, P = .02, Cohen's d = 0.99). Interviewees valued contextualized, scenario-based practice and identified response latency, repetition, and limited personalization as areas for improvement. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of DBT-informed conversational AI for skills practice and motivate further evaluation in larger, more clinically relevant samples. Clinical efficacy remains to be established.

items.abstract_text: International students’ psychological adjustment is shaped by challenges involving everyday agency, social connection, and separation from familiar support networks. This study examined short-term changes in psychological wellbeing, social self-efficacy, and homesickness following a 12-day generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted daily activity programme among Pakistani international students in China. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, the programme combined activities intended to support autonomy, competence, and relatedness with GenAI-assisted planning, reflection, and conversational rehearsal. Twenty-eight participants completed self-report assessments immediately before and after the programme in a single-group pre-test–post-test design. Outcomes were assessed using Ryff’s Psychological Well-Being Scale, a social self-efficacy measure, and the homesickness subscale of the Acculturative Stress Scale for International Students. Reported Wilcoxon signed-rank analyses indicated an increase in overall psychological wellbeing from 86.38 to 98.14 (p = .004) and a decrease in homesickness from 10.90 to 7.52 (p = .002). Social self-efficacy increased from 96.38 to 107.34, although this change was not statistically significant (p = .092). These findings provide preliminary evidence of favourable changes in selected psychosocial outcomes during participation in a structured GenAI-assisted activity programme. However, the absence of a comparison group, the small purposively recruited sample, and the lack of follow-up prevent attribution of these changes to GenAI or conclusions about their durability. The study offers an initial application of need-supportive programme design in a South–South educational mobility context and provides a basis for subsequent controlled evaluation.

items.abstract_text: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.

items.abstract_text: The study uses a Christian-anthropological approach to evaluate the educational application of generative artificial intelligence. Its central question is: what gives the teacher a human, irreplaceable essence, and which tasks can be delegated to artificial intelligence in ways that preserve the goals of Christian education while making learning more effective? The argument connects theological anthropology, personalist thinking, and educational research. As a conceptual-normative synthesis rather than an empirical intervention, it draws on the doctrine of Imago Dei, Buber’s I–Thou relation, and Simone Weil’s notion of attention to mark the ontological difference between the person and machine simulation. The article argues that artificial intelligence can significantly strengthen technical and informational pedagogical work, but it cannot replace the relational, moral, spiritual, and vocational dimensions of education. Functional similarity, on this reading, does not amount to substantial identity: a language model has no conscious self that could answer for its outputs. Learning understood as formatio also demands effort, waiting, and uncertainty, which the promise of frictionless learning tends to erase. Five dimensions of the teaching role – presence, moral responsibility, authority, vocational guidance, and community – are shown to resist automation. The study proposes a three-zone delegation matrix: delegable tasks, co-pilot tasks under teacher supervision, and non-delegable, person-specific pedagogical moments. Each zone is paired with its main risk and a pedagogical condition: factual error calls for teacher control and source criticism, deskilling for the teacher’s final decision, and depersonalization for a personal, accountable human judgment. The article concludes that the role of artificial intelligence in Christian education lies in multiplying human capabilities rather than replacing the human teacher.

items.abstract_text: Background Although scoping reviews of the ethical challenges of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in medical education already exist, these studies are primarily grounded in Western educational contexts. Objectives With electronic searches covering November 2022 to August 2026. This scoping review aimed to systematically examine the current status, scenario-specific patterns, and evolving trends of ethics-related concerns among Chinese students in health-science majors when using AI within the country's distinctive clinical/non-clinical dual-track education system. Methods “Ethics-related concerns” was adopted as the operational umbrella construct, and the 35 studies that finally met the inclusion criteria were stratified accordingly: the main narrative synthesis covered the 25 studies centered on affective reactions (worry, anxiety, fear, and guilt), while cognitive and behavioral ethical constructs (awareness, attitudes, and literacy) were described as supplementary evidence from the remaining 10 studies. Given the heterogeneity of measurement instruments and construct definitions, only a narrative synthesis and associational analysis were conducted, without pooling of effect estimates. Results The evidence revealed clear scenario-associated patterns: concerns in research settings concentrated mainly on academic integrity, whereas clinical settings were highly focused on accountability (attribution of responsibility) and patient privacy, and the influence of demographic variables such as gender on ethics-related concerns was mixed and inconsistent across studies. Conclusions These observed patterns and associations suggest that a moderate level of ethics-related concern reflects students’ preserved moral defenses and prudent awareness. Rather than blindly eliminating such concerns, medical educators should strengthen AI ethics education and systematically enhance students’ knowledge and practical capabilities regarding academic integrity, accountability, and privacy protection, so as to promote responsible AI use.

items.abstract_text: The focus of the study is on the impact of the EU AI Act on AI-based cybersecurity solutions in healthcare. Adopting AI in healthcare cybersecurity is expected to enhance threat identification, bolster operational stability, and safeguard against increasingly complex cyber threats. The European Union's AI Act mandates new regulatory requirements for AI systems utilised in high-risk settings, particularly in healthcare. This study investigates the EU AI Act's influence on the creation and implementation of AI-driven cybersecurity solutions, focusing on representative AI-based cybersecurity solutions used in healthcare environments. Qualitative research methods were employed via a literature review and policy analysis of the EU AI Act, healthcare cybersecurity regulations, and global AI governance systems. The research contrasts the EU's AI regulation with the NIST AI risk management framework and the OECD AI principles and evaluates how AI-enabled cybersecurity functions align with key regulatory criteria such as risk assessment, disclosure, human supervision, and system stability. The findings indicate that AI-driven cybersecurity tools can assist in regulatory adherence and enhance healthcare stability, contingent upon organisations establishing robust governance frameworks, detailed practices, and human supervision mechanisms. Additional actions are required to achieve full alignment with the new transparency and accountability mandates, though existing systems demonstrate robust support for operational security and decision-making. The investigation finds that the EU AI regulation should be considered not just as a requirement to comply with but also as a chance to enhance the reliability, transparency, and enduring viability of AI-driven healthcare security systems.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping English-language learning and digitally mediated work, yet research on AI-supported language development, psychological conditions, AI literacy, and graduate employability has largely developed in separate literatures. This focused narrative review integrates these domains to examine how AI-supported English learning may relate to graduate employability among university students and recent graduates, particularly in EFL and other non-native-English-speaking higher-education contexts. The final evidence base comprises 46 unique sources, including 19 published between 2018 and 2026 and 27 earlier foundational or contextual sources, drawn from empirical studies, reviews, theoretical literature, competence frameworks, and selected authoritative reports. The review examines how specific AI affordances support or constrain language-learning processes and differentiated English outcomes; how functional English communication relates to employability capabilities; how motivation, language anxiety, linguistic and digital self-efficacy, and career confidence operate as distinct antecedents, conditioning factors, or outcomes; and how critical AI literacy intersects with language and professional competence. Its distinctive contribution is a mechanism-based framework linking AI affordances, language-learning processes, English communicative outcomes, employability capabilities, perceived employability, opportunity access, and labor-market outcomes while explicitly distinguishing comparatively well-supported proximal relationships from tentative downstream transitions. The synthesis indicates that AI-supported learning can support feedback uptake, revision, repeated practice, interaction, and selected linguistic and psychological outcomes, but evidence for durable independent proficiency is more heterogeneous and direct evidence for employment, earnings, retention, or career progression remains limited. Benefits are conditional on pedagogical design, independent practice, human interaction, equitable access, and responsible AI use. Accordingly, the framework should be interpreted as a set of mechanism-based propositions rather than a validated causal model linking AI use directly to employability or employment. Because source identification and selection were purposive rather than exhaustive, the conclusions remain subject to selection and publication bias, geographical imbalance, methodological heterogeneity, reviewer judgment, and the rapid evolution of AI technologies. Of the 46 sources, 15 are classified as primary empirical publications, and four provide RQ1-specific direct evidence on AI-supported English-language learning. Two primary empirical publications examine graduate employability-related competencies or perceptions; one additional publication synthesizes earlier empirical assessments. Although some evidence concerns graduates’ employment experiences, no included study directly tests the effect of AI-supported English learning on job attainment or other labor-market outcomes.

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of large language models (LLMs) into intellectual activities requires a reconsideration of prompt engineering as more than the technical optimization of instructions. Although conventional prompting techniques primarily seek to improve the relevance, accuracy, and structure of artificial intelligence outputs, they often provide insufficient attention to the cognitive processes through which users formulate requests, evaluate generated information, regulate reliance on automation, and maintain independent judgment. This paper introduces Metacognitive Prompt Engineering (MPE) as a proposed human-centered framework for designing, monitoring, and regulating interactions with generative artificial intelligence. Drawing on theories of metacognition, self-regulated learning, cognitive monitoring, automation reliance, and human–AI collaboration, MPE conceptualizes prompting as an iterative process involving goal clarification, cognitive task allocation, epistemic monitoring, evidence-based verification, and adaptive strategy regulation. The paper distinguishes metacognitive prompt engineering from conventional prompt optimization and model-centered metacognitive prompting. It proposes a five-phase regulatory framework, identifies practical design principles, introduces reusable prompting protocols, and develops a research agenda for evaluating the framework's potential effects on cognitive autonomy, confidence calibration, decision quality, and independent learning. Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between model-generated expressions of uncertainty and independently justified confidence, as well as the limitations of self-correction without external feedback. The central argument is that effective human–AI interaction should be assessed not exclusively through the quality of generated outputs but also through the quality of the cognitive regulation exercised by the human user. MPE is presented as a theoretical and methodological proposal rather than an empirically validated intervention. Its effectiveness, boundary conditions, and possible unintended consequences require systematic investigation

items.abstract_text: Nearly a century of focused behavioral sciences research has attempted to tackle widespread behavioral challenges, including insufficient levels of physical activity, poor quality eating patterns, poor adherence to medical regimens, and more. Behavioral scientists are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI)-based technologies to advance the study of behavioral sciences, extend the precision and reach of their programs, and improve their ability to intervene at key moments. At this early stage, it is critical that experts from diverse and relevant fields provide their perspectives on opportunities and challenges in the implementation of AI for guiding behavior change in older adults. To this end, the National Institute on Aging Research Centers Collaborative Network hosted a workshop, where a various body of scientific and clinical experts discussed opportunities and challenges regarding the use of AI in behavior change interventions for older adults. We summarize this discussion, highlighting both opportunities and challenges, and present several key areas for future research.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in educational practice, transforming lesson planning, instructional delivery, assessment, learning analytics, and teacher professional development. Although research on AI in education has expanded rapidly, the psychological consequences of AI adoption for teachers remain theoretically fragmented. Existing studies have examined technology acceptance, AI literacy, technology self-efficacy, instructional confidence, and professional identity, yet these constructs have rarely been integrated into a coherent account of how AI reshapes teachers’ beliefs about their own professional capabilities. This narrative review synthesizes the emerging literature through a theory-building perspective grounded primarily in social cognitive theory and informed by technology acceptance, cognitive load, professional identity, social comparison, and human–AI interaction perspectives. We propose a framework of AI-Mediated Efficacy Reconstruction, conceptualizing AI not as a direct determinant of teacher self-efficacy but as a socio-technical factor that changes the availability, interpretation, and attribution of efficacy-relevant experiences. AI can facilitate mastery experiences, provide vicarious learning opportunities, offer timely feedback, reduce routine cognitive demands, and expand access to professional learning. However, the same technologies may generate cognitive overload, technical anxiety, professional comparison, identity threat, reduced autonomy, and technological dependence. We identify Efficacy Attribution as a potentially central mechanism determining whether AI-supported performance is internalized as evidence of teachers’ own professional capability or attributed primarily to the technological system. On this basis, we distinguish Augmented Efficacy, in which AI extends teachers’ capabilities while preserving professional agency, from Dependent Efficacy, in which perceived competence becomes increasingly contingent upon AI assistance. The framework further proposes that these processes are moderated by teacher characteristics, AI-system characteristics, teaching tasks, organizational context, and time. We conclude by outlining implications for measurement, teacher professional development, AI design, organizational policy, and future longitudinal and experimental research.

items.abstract_text: Purpose There is a close association between the fast acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the rise in the time spent on screens by Generation Z students on a daily basis. Previous studies have focused on AI literacy as a facilitator of AI adoption and utilization. This paper attempts to find out whether AI literacy, self-regulation, digital wellbeing literacy, academic productivity, and FoMO predict students’ willingness to reduce digital habits through mindful technology use, moderated by digital self-efficacy and peer influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained through survey from 556 Generation Z college students and analysed using PLS-SEM. The measurement model was examined in terms of reliability and validity, the structural model was tested for direct, mediation and moderation effect, while the predictive relevance was estimated via a blindfolding approach. The results were validated using ANN analysis and fsQCA. Findings All five antecedents were found to be significant predictors of mindful technology usage in the hypothesized direction, and mindful technology use was a significant predictor of digital wellness and hence acted as a partial mediator of the five relationships. AI literacy was uniquely significant as a predictor of digital wellness. Digital self-efficacy selectively moderated only AI literacy and self-regulation paths, whereas peer influence did not moderate the relationship between mindful technology usage and digital wellness. The results from ANN highlighted the non-linear significance of digital well-being awareness and AI literacy, while fsQCA identified three equifinal combinations that could predict high digital wellness. Practical implications Educational Institutions should combine their AI-literacy training with digital wellbeing programmes instead of conducting them independently, focus on instilling self-efficacy and self-regulation over peer norm messages, and treat AI-literacy training as a wellbeing intervention in addition to an academic skills intervention. Originality/value This paper shifts the focus of AI literacy from its association with digital usage to digital disengagement and presents a methodologically triangulated (PLS-SEM, ANN, fsQCA) explanation for how competency, awareness, and affect influence the Generation Z intention to engage less with harmful digital practices.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is entering psychotherapy at almost every point of clinical work: therapist training, screening and detection, risk prediction, diagnostic support and treatment planning, patient education, chatbot-delivered session content, between-session tracking, supervision, and documentation. Discussion of the associated dangers to this process has so far been overwhelmingly patient directed. This narrative review addresses these questions from a futures-oriented perspective: what AI may do to psychotherapists as professionals. We first map current and emerging applications across the phases of therapy. We then distinguish four forms of competence loss reported in the wider clinical literature, namely deskilling, never-skilling, mis-skilling, and moral deskilling, and use them to structure a function-by-function analysis of nine clinical tasks. The risks we identify, most of which rest on extrapolation from medicine and education and are therefore best read as hypotheses, extend beyond technical skill. Algorithmic flags may redistribute clinical attention, and accountability may shift from the quality of judgement to adherence to procedure. Case formulation may close prematurely, and theoretical pluralism may narrow toward the traditions best represented in training data. Findings that chatbots are rated as more empathic than clinicians may threaten professional identity, while supervision may lose its relational and formative functions. We then set out four possible trajectories for the field: AI as a support to professional judgement, gradual dependency, standardized AI-mediated practice, and systems designed explicitly to preserve and cultivate expertise, together with the drivers that may lead toward each. Implications are drawn for training, clinical governance, and professional ethics.

items.abstract_text: Disruptions in the supply chain (SC) are occurring more often and becoming more complex, posing significant challenges for engineering management and operational resilience. Current prediction methods do not adequately reflect the relationships and uncertainty among variables, as well as the causal factors of disruption events. In this study, we present a novel uncertainty-aware hybrid framework, namely, the University of Queensland Creative Arts/Creativity Network (UQ-CRGATNet), which introduces Dynamic Graph Attention Networks (DGAT), a tab transformer network for contextual feature learning, resilience-aware representation, Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, and an ensemble meta-learner of Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost). Moreover, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Non-combinatorial Optimization via Trace Exponential and Augmented lagRangian for Structure learning (NOTEARS) enable feature attribution and causal disruption analytics that are human-understandable and support trustworthy decisions. The proposed framework is a joint model that models graph-structured relationships, heterogeneous tabular information, predictive uncertainty, and resilience indicators within a unified learning architecture. The extensive experiments performed on a real-world supply chain dataset show that they significantly outperform conventional machine learning, ensemble learning, and transformer baselines. UQ-CRGATNet achieves excellent Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) and Precision-Recall characteristics, with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 99.87, 99.87, 99.89, 99.88, and 99.73%, respectively. The uncertainty-guided ensemble will increase prediction accuracy, while causal analytics will provide actionable managerial insights into the drivers of disruptions. The results show that the proposed framework provides a strong, interpretable, and scalable solution for proactively predicting supply chain disruptions and supporting resilient engineering management.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into diverse fields, including education, where it offers innovative approaches to enhance self-regulated learning (SRL). For many students in Chinese higher education, developing robust SRL skills remains a significant challenge. This review addresses the need for a clearer understanding of how AI tools influence these skills by synthesizing ten empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following the PRISMA framework, the literature was identified from prominent academic databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC. Drawing on Zimmerman’s SRL Three‑phase Model, this synthesis suggests that AI tools show potential to assist students with goal‑setting and foster motivation within the forethought phase. During the performance phase, such tools may support learning‑strategy deployment and progress monitoring via timely feedback. In the reflection phase, AI can facilitate outcome evaluation and subsequent strategy adjustment. However, the review also identifies potential risks, such as student over-reliance on AI, and notes a limited research focus on long-term SRL development and group regulation. Accordingly, future research should adopt longitudinal designs, investigate AI’s role in co-regulated learning, and integrate AI literacy and emotional support into SRL development frameworks. publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Marking is among the most time-consuming activities in education, and artificial intelligence (AI) is widely proposed as a remedy. Attention has centred on generative large language models, yet regulators raise concerns about their bias, consistency, and explainability. This paper contrasts generative grading with per-question classification models trained only on an educator’s own marking and deployed in a human-in-the-loop workflow. The architectures are compared against criteria drawn from regulatory guidance: transparency, construct-relevant features, determinism, and specifiable training data. A narrower role for generative models is also identified, in composing and restructuring marker-approved feedback rather than in marking. Deployment analytics from one platform are then reported, covering approximately 166,000 marked questions, 39,500 essays, and six institutions: 66.2% of questions were marked in under one minute, 77.6% to 89.5% of AI suggestions were accepted, and essay models reached a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.93 for high-confidence predictions. Questionnaire responses from earlier pilots (33 markers, 30 students) are also reported: markers described marking as faster and consistent feedback as easier to provide; most students rated feedback more consistent and higher in quality. Implications for institutions selecting or building such tools are discussed, alongside the limitations of vendor-collected data.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence can provide explanations and comments on circuit solutions, but its educational value depends on how students interpret and use those responses. This focused narrative review examines the use of generative AI to help students identify and correct errors in introductory circuit analysis. Published sources were identified through OpenAlex searches, publisher records, and reference checking, with full-text assessment informing selection and synthesis. Twelve reports were selected for their relevance to circuit reasoning, feedback, or learner verification; an electronics-course perception study provides an explicitly adjacent comparison. Foundational research on formative feedback and self-regulated learning informs the interpretation. The synthesis addresses circuit representation and diagnostic accuracy, students' use of feedback, and the interpretation of educational outcomes. Technical evaluations show that input representation, reference information, and computational support shape the conditions under which responses are assessed. Classroom and tutoring reports describe opportunities for explanation, comparison, revision, and instructor intervention. The selected reports provide more direct evidence of perceived usefulness than of independently retained understanding. Observational grade associations and a historical-cohort comparison offer additional perspectives, although their designs limit causal interpretation. The review proposes teaching considerations that preserve students' initial reasoning, check the represented circuit, focus guidance on a specific difficulty, and require students to justify corrections. These considerations are derived from the literature and have not been evaluated as a combined intervention. items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. Drawing comparative insights from the EU AI Act, it examines gaps in Bangladesh’s digital legislation and institutional practice and identifies best practices. It also compares practice in the neighbouring countries of India and Pakistan to assess Bangladesh’s position within South Asia’s regional AI governance framework. Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

items.abstract_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune condition associated with markedly elevated cardiovascular disease (CVD) morbidity and mortality. Both disproportionately affect women and racial and ethnic minority populations, highlighting the profound influence of social determinants of health (SDOH) on disease trajectories. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on socioeconomic determinants and lifestyle factors that contribute to CVD among individuals with SLE and evaluates emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in CVD risk prediction and management. A comprehensive search (PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science; 2012–2026) identified original research, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and guidelines reporting CVD-related outcomes in SLE. Evidence demonstrates strong associations between low socioeconomic status, limited healthcare access, and educational inequities with heightened CVD risk. Black, Hispanic, and Latin American individuals experience disproportionate CVD burden due to intersecting structural, social, and clinical barriers. Modifiable lifestyle factors, including physical inactivity, tobacco use, and suboptimal dietary patterns, further exacerbate risk. Emerging ML-based studies suggest improved individualized CVD risk stratification in SLE compared with traditional general-population risk calculators, highlighting the potential for precision-focused approaches. Equity-centered strategies integrating clinical care with SDOH are essential. AI-enabled tools offer promising avenues for personalized risk prediction and resource optimization; however, rigorous attention to algorithmic fairness, transparency, and health equity is essential to ensure responsible implementation. This is the first review to synthesize SDOH, lifestyle factors, and AI in an equity-centered SLE-CVD framework, given AI’s rapid expansion in rheumatology and the urgency of addressing cardiovascular health inequities in SLE.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a promising resource for supporting students with dyslexia. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature examines AI primarily as an assistive technology, with limited attention to the cognitive mechanisms through which it may enhance reading development. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework that integrates Baddeley’s multicomponent model of working memory with contemporary AI-supported educational tools. Through this cognitive alignment, AI has the potential to facilitate decoding, comprehension, learner engagement, and reading autonomy among students with dyslexia. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded perspective that connects cognitive theory with emerging educational technologies. Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of a specific intervention, the paper provides an integrative model to guide future empirical research, instructional design, and the development of AI-supported reading interventions for learners with dyslexia.

items.abstract_text: Digital devices support learning but can also divert students’ attention, and little is known about how students experience this in technology-rich classrooms in Bukidnon, Philippines. This qualitative study used a descriptive phenomenological design to explore the lived experiences of Grade 12 Humanities and Social Sciences students with digital distractions at Bocboc National High School during school year 2026–2027. Fifteen students were purposively selected and interviewed individually using a researcher-made, semi-structured interview guide. The interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed, and the transcripts were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged. In interrupted flow, learning was broken by digital pulls and followed by guilt, anxiety, and embarrassment. In a layered pull against focus, distraction arose from habit and platform design, peer pressure, fatigue, and home and school conditions such as shared devices, weak connectivity, and unclear device rules. In reclaiming control, students removed tempting sources, structured their time, set boundaries with others, and drew on personal motivation. In shared responsibility, students called on teachers, parents, peers, and the school for clear rules, engaging teaching, and support. Two accounts differed from the rest, attributing distraction to lesson quality and to limited access, respectively. Learning in a technology-rich environment therefore appeared as a continuous negotiation between digital temptation and academic purpose. The study addresses a gap in Philippine phenomenological research, which has centered on the Visayas and Davao, by describing student experiences in an inland province of Northern Mindanao. Supporting focused learning may require student self-management together with consistent device policies, purposeful instruction, and stable, equitable access to connectivity. Future studies may include other schools, compare urban and upland settings, and add teachers’ and parents’ perspectives.

items.abstract_text: Large language models can now outperform human persuaders in controlled settings, and they do so in whichever direction they are instructed to persuade. Regulatory and ethical responses to this development nevertheless remain anchored in what this article calls the deception paradigm: the assumption that communicative influence becomes wrongful when, and because, it involves false assertion. The article argues that this paradigm systematically fails to capture AI hyperpersuasion. Drawing on the philosophical literature on manipulation, it shows that hyperpersuasion characteristically operates through true but selectively curated content, adaptive framing, simulated intimacy, and the exploitation of individually diagnosed cognitive dispositions – techniques that bypass rather than deceive rational agency. It then examines Article 5(1)(a)–(b) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Although the prohibition is conceptually open to manipulation without deception, its operative test – material distortion, appreciable impairment of informed decision-making, counterfactual decision change, and significant harm – is inherited from unfair commercial practices law and reproduces the architecture of fraud, leaving paradigmatic cases of hyperpersuasion untouched. Extending the analysis from individual autonomy to democratic epistemology, the article contends that hyperpersuasion threatens democracy not primarily by aggregating individual harms but by degrading the epistemic conditions – independence of judgment formation, a shared space of reasons, and the contestability of public claims – on which collective self-government depends. Regulating hyperpersuasion therefore requires a shift from content-based tests of falsity and harm to process- and relationship-based criteria that target asymmetric epistemic power.

items.abstract_text: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into mental health support settings, understanding how individuals engage with AI‐based tools for psychological support is increasingly important. This study introduces the nine‐item AI‐Assisted Psychological Support Use Scale (AAPSU), a behavioural measure of how people use conversational or generative AI for emotional regulation, self‐reflection, well‐being‐related decision‐making and support‐seeking. The scale development process included item generation, expert review, pilot testing, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and reliability testing. EFA identified two theoretically coherent subscales: self‐regulatory and reflective use (six items) and substitutive use (three items). CFA provided internal confirmation of this structure, with satisfactory model fit and strong factor loadings. Internal consistency was high for self‐regulatory and reflective use (Cronbach's α = 0.903), substitutive use (Cronbach's α = 0.888) and the total scale ( α = 0.919). Convergent‐validity analyses showed meaningful associations with attachment to AI systems, attitudes towards AI in mental health contexts and AI mindset. These findings support the AAPSU as a brief, reliable and theoretically grounded measure of AI‐assisted psychological support use while indicating the need for replication in more diverse samples.

items.abstract_text: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

CONCLUSIONS: AI-driven approaches demonstrate a promising convergence of computational power and clinical expertise, with the potential to support more personalized, efficient, and informed management of MCS patients. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been the focus of much attention in the higher education sector, both for its potential to support personalised and adaptive learning, but also due to the risk that students may outsource learning to it, leading to gaps in their professional or discipline competencies. This risk of cognitive offloading applies equally to learning how to learn, a skill set explored through studies of self-regulated learning (SRL). Two GenAI numeracy tutors were piloted at a regional Australian university as one component of a newly launched mathematics and statistics support centre, one focusing on medication calculations for Nursing students (NiNA), and the other on threshold numeracy skills for Education students (EdNA). Detailed analysis of students’ conversations with these agents using Zimmerman and Moylan’s 2009 SRL framework revealed extensive evidence of some elements of SRL such as strategic planning, task-specific strategies, and adaptive competence; trace evidence of other elements including self-efficacy and self-evaluation; and no evidence of the remaining elements. This study contributes an underrepresented qualitative perspective to the body of research into the crossover of GenAI and SRL and foreshadows avenues for further research and refinements in the design of GenAI numeracy tutors.

items.abstract_text: This community engagement activity aimed to strengthen artificial intelligence (AI) literacy among high school students, particularly their ability to use generative AI as a learning aid without replacing independent thinking, source verification, and academic responsibility. The activity was designed as an educational socialization and workshop addressing the nature of AI and generative AI, appropriate and inappropriate uses in learning, risks of AI dependence, critical thinking, information verification, and ethical and responsible use. Thirty students participated in a pre-test and post-test consisting of ten multiple-choice items aligned with the learning objectives. Descriptive analysis was used to compare participants’ scores before and after the intervention. The mean pre-test score was 64.67, while the mean post-test score reached 84.67, representing an increase of 20 points or 30.93% relative to the pre-test mean. Before the activity, 2 students (6.67%) were categorized as very good, 14 (46.67%) as good, 13 (43.33%) as fair, and 1 (3.33%) as poor. After the activity, 11 students (36.67%) were categorized as very good and 19 (63.33%) as good, with no participants in the fair, poor, or very poor categories. The findings indicate an improvement in measured understanding of responsible AI use, including verification, independent reasoning, recognition of AI dependence, and positioning AI as a learning aid. The activity contributes a practical school-based model of AI literacy that combines conceptual explanation, ethical reflection, and scenario-based assessment. Because the evaluation used a single-group pre-test–post-test design, the results should be interpreted as evidence of improved measured understanding rather than definitive causal evidence of long-term behavioral change.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into human decision-making creates opportunities to extend analytical capabilities, explore alternatives, anticipate consequences, and improve the consistency of complex judgments. However, the availability of AI-generated recommendations does not necessarily produce better decisions. Effective collaboration requires an appropriate distribution of cognitive functions, calibrated reliance on AI outputs, independent human judgment, and explicit mechanisms for resolving disagreements. This conceptual paper introduces the Human–AI Joint Decision Architecture (HA-JDA), a proposed framework for organizing collaborative decision-making between humans and generative AI systems. The framework distinguishes eight interconnected stages: problem formulation, independent human assessment, evidence acquisition, alternative generation, scenario analysis, evaluative deliberation, decision authorization, and outcome monitoring. Each stage assigns different responsibilities to human and artificial intelligence according to their capabilities, limitations, and the normative requirements of the decision. The paper conceptualizes joint intelligence not as the replacement of human judgment or the mechanical aggregation of human and machine recommendations, but as a structured process of cognitive complementarity. Particular attention is given to epistemic independence, metacognitive regulation, uncertainty management, critical evaluation, and the preservation of human agency. An operational decision protocol, a functional responsibility matrix, and a preliminary research agenda are presented. The framework also addresses automation bias, algorithm aversion, erroneous forecasting, accountability diffusion, and the potential erosion of independent decision-making competence. The principal contribution is a testable architecture for integrating human judgment and AI-assisted analysis while maintaining human responsibility for value-sensitive decisions. The proposed approach aims to support more informed, transparent, adaptable, and accountable decisions without assuming that human–AI collaboration is inherently superior to independent human or machine performance

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies are transforming teaching and learning by offering new pedagogical opportunities while posing challenges. Despite their critical role in preparing future teachers, many teacher educators lack the necessary AI-related knowledge and pedagogical strategies for responsible GenAI integration. The current study first aimed to examine teacher educators’ perceptions, use, and needs regarding GenAI integration. For this, we interviewed teacher educators, transformed their collected experiences into case studies, and asked them to reflect on them. Our second aim was to explore the role of teacher educators’ self-reported AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK in these case reflections. To understand this knowledge, we used the Intelligent-TPACK and AI literacy frameworks. Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) revealed that higher self-reported AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK may be linked to critical, multi-layered reflections, while lower levels reflected practice-focused, classroom-level reasoning. Interviews further showed that teacher educators (a) perceived GenAI as useful for teaching tasks but emphasised critical evaluation, (b) mainly used it for academic writing correction and lesson planning, and (c) expressed a need for practical and ethical guidelines. This study contributes to teacher education by highlighting the potential of structured, case-based reflection to support AI-related knowledge and skills for pedagogical and ethical GenAI integration.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education presents additional challenges for international students, including dependence on technology, adaptation to another culture, and the need to be ethically prepared to learn a foreign language. This research explores the social and technological dilemma created using AI in Arabic language learning and how international students in Indonesia adapt to it. The research employed a qualitative approach using digital ethnography, i.e., digital observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis and verified through source triangulation, methodological triangulation, and member checking. Results suggest that the use of AI in Arabic language learning is contradictory. While AI offers increased access to materials, flexibility in learning, and academic efficiency, it also creates dilemmas in cognitive-academic, socio-cultural, and ethical-technological areas. Dependence on AI may reduce critical thinking and independent learning. It may also lead to fewer opportunities for cross-cultural social interactions and create greater ethical dilemmas due to limited digital literacy and/or a lack of established standards for AI use. To address these challenges, students developed adaptive strategies through selective use of AI, strengthening direct communication, and enhancing ethical awareness regarding digital technology.

items.abstract_text: Population spatialisation serves as a critical nexus transforming aggregated population counts into spatially explicit population distributions, providing an essential foundation for urban planning, disaster management, and public health assessment. However, the inherent complexity of human settlement patterns presents significant challenges for population spatialisation and fine-grained population disaggregation. With the convergence of geospatial big data and artificial intelligence (AI), population spatialisation has undergone rapid changes in data sources, spatial representations, and modelling approaches, yet its evolution has received limited systematic attention. To address this gap, this paper reviews the evolution of population spatialisation through a structured literature synthesis complemented by bibliometric analysis, tracing its development from traditional redistribution approaches to recent AI-enabled methods, with a particular focus on emerging geospatial foundation models. Furthermore, the synthesis reveals a methodological transition from rule-based redistribution towards data-driven, probabilistic, and representation-learning approaches, coupled with the progressive diversification of spatial representations and growing attention to temporally explicit and demographically differentiated population estimation. Based on these findings, future research should prioritise robustness across scales and contexts, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and the representation of demographic heterogeneity. Through this review, we aim to elucidate the key transitions in the evolution of population spatialisation, thereby facilitating the development and evaluation of more reliable and demographically informative spatial population products.

items.abstract_text: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

items.abstract_text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational processes is transforming not only how work is performed but also how teams are structured, coordinated, and led. As generative AI systems and increasingly autonomous agents assume analytical, creative, informational, and operational functions, leadership must evolve beyond the conventional management of exclusively human contributors. However, the introduction of AI does not automatically improve collective performance. Effective hybrid intelligence requires deliberate coordination of complementary capabilities, transparent allocation of decision rights, appropriate reliance, continuous evaluation, and the preservation of human professional autonomy. This conceptual paper examines Hybrid Intelligence Leadership (HIL) as an emerging approach to managing teams in which human professionals and AI systems perform interdependent functions toward shared organizational objectives. Drawing on theories of human–AI complementarity, distributed cognition, organizational learning, psychological safety, and sociotechnical systems, the paper introduces the Hybrid Intelligence Leadership Architecture (HILA). The proposed architecture comprises six interdependent leadership functions: strategic alignment, capability-based task allocation, collaborative coordination, epistemic and operational assurance, human capability development, and adaptive governance. The model emphasizes that leadership effectiveness depends not simply on technological sophistication but on how human and artificial contributions are organized, evaluated, and continuously reconfigured. Practical applications, implementation principles, organizational risks, and testable research propositions are presented. Particular attention is given to avoiding automation bias, preventing the erosion of human expertise, maintaining accountability, and ensuring that AI adoption strengthens rather than marginalizes human contributors. The paper argues that the central responsibility of hybrid intelligence leadership is to create organizational conditions in which human judgment and artificial capabilities generate sustainable collective value without compromising autonomy, responsibility, or professional development.
