items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare, creating opportunities to improve diagnosis, clinical decision-making, resource allocation, and healthcare delivery, while also raising concerns regarding algorithmic bias, discrimination, transparency, accountability, and health equity. These challenges are particularly relevant in fragmented healthcare systems, where pre-existing social and institutional inequalities may interact with AI-based decision-making. This qualitative socio-legal documentary review with a narrative synthesis critically examines the Chilean legal and regulatory framework governing the use of AI in healthcare, with particular attention to algorithmic bias, discrimination, health equity, transparency, accountability, and the protection of patients’ fundamental rights. The review draws on academic literature, legislation, governmental and institutional documents, and international regulatory instruments to identify regulatory gaps and governance challenges relevant to Chilean healthcare. The analysis indicates that Chilean law provides important constitutional and statutory protections concerning equality, non-discrimination, health, personal data, and patient rights, but that these protections are not yet articulated within a specific sectoral framework addressing algorithmic discrimination and the governance of AI in healthcare. Particular challenges concern indirect discrimination, algorithmic opacity, accountability, human oversight, and the capacity to identify and mitigate bias throughout the AI lifecycle. The review does not empirically assess the performance or discriminatory effects of individual AI systems. Drawing on the Chilean context and selected international regulatory developments, particularly the European Union AI Act, the review develops a sector-specific governance framework centered on transparency and explainability, accountability, human oversight, periodic bias auditing, equity assessment, and AI literacy. The findings contribute to broader discussions on equitable AI governance in healthcare, particularly in countries characterized by fragmented health systems and comparable regulatory challenges.

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most influential technologies shaping contemporary society. Despite rapid advances in machine learning, foundation models, and generative AI, persistent ambiguity remains concerning the relationship among computation, cognition, and intelligence. While computational systems demonstrate increasingly sophisticated capabilities, whether such capabilities constitute cognition or intelligence remains theoretically contested. Existing scholarship has extensively examined AI technologies, applications, ethics, and governance, yet comparatively less attention has been devoted to explaining how computational systems become associated with intelligence and acquire legitimacy, authority, and societal significance.This study investigates AI conception as a distinct object of interdisciplinary inquiry. Using a conceptual, abductive, and theory-building approach, it synthesizes insights from philosophy of mind, cognitive science, Science and Technology Studies, sociotechnical systems theory, communication studies, institutional theory, and governance scholarship. The analysis develops the AI Re-Conception Framework, comprising five interconnected dimensions: Terminological Reconstruction, Discursive Reconstruction, Epistemological Reconstruction, Sociotechnical Reconstruction, and Human-Centered Governance Integration.The framework explains how computational systems acquire intelligence-related attribution, meaning, legitimacy, and governance relevance through processes of categorization, interpretation, attribution, relational embedding, and conceptual governance. It argues that intelligence attribution emerges through human interpretation and justification rather than computational capability itself. Consequently, computation should not be conflated with cognition or intelligence.The study advances a sociotechnical re-conception of AI, establishes AI conception as a distinct object of inquiry, and introduces Conceptual Governance as a framework for examining and governing the assumptions and legitimacy claims through which AI acquires societal influence.

items.abstract_text: The development of artificial intelligence challenges traditional philosophical assumptions about the relationship between human nature and intellectual capacities. Reasoning, language production, creativity, problem-solving, and complex decision-making have historically occupied central positions in conceptions of human distinctiveness. As artificial systems demonstrate increasingly sophisticated performance in these domains, philosophical anthropology faces a fundamental question: what does it mean to be human when capabilities previously associated with human intellectual exceptionalism can also be performed by nonhuman systems? This article examines the anthropological implications of artificial intelligence through an interdisciplinary conceptual framework integrating philosophical anthropology, phenomenology, philosophy of mind, theories of extended cognition, and contemporary AI ethics. It argues that technological developments do not eliminate human distinctiveness but challenge attempts to ground human identity exclusively in superior cognitive performance. The paper distinguishes biological humanity, existential self-understanding, social recognition, and moral status, demonstrating why these dimensions should not be reduced to a single criterion of intelligence. It proposes an Anthropological Reorientation Framework consisting of five interconnected dimensions: embodied existence, reflexive self-interpretation, relational identity, narrative agency, and normative responsibility. The central thesis is that artificial intelligence may transform the historical conditions through which human beings understand and exercise their capacities without automatically changing what constitutes membership in the human species or the unconditional moral worth of human persons. Rather than interpreting AI merely as a competitor to human cognition, the article examines it as a technological and cultural development capable of restructuring intellectual practices, creative expression, autonomy, and the formation of human identity. The resulting perspective shifts philosophical attention from the preservation of human cognitive superiority toward the conditions under which human beings can continue developing meaningful, responsible, and self-directed forms of existence in increasingly AI-mediated environments.

items.abstract_text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into neonatal ventilatory support represents a significant advancement in contemporary medicine, offering new opportunities for precision respiratory care, early detection of clinical deterioration, prediction of non-invasive ventilation failure, and optimization of respiratory management in critically ill newborns. Nevertheless, its implementation raises complex clinical, ethical, legal, and technological challenges, particularly because neonates constitute an exceptionally vulnerable population unable to exercise personal autonomy or provide informed consent. This article examines the principal legal and ethical frameworks governing AI-assisted neonatal ventilation, emphasizing international regulatory instruments, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, the Medical Device Regulation, and guidance issued by the World Health Organization and international medical-device regulatory authorities. Particular attention is devoted to the fundamental principles of bioethics: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. The analysis also addresses algorithmic bias, data protection, medical confidentiality, algorithmic transparency, cybersecurity, clinical validation, and the limitations of automated decision-making. A central controversy concerns the allocation of medical-legal liability when AI-generated recommendations contribute to adverse neonatal outcomes. Potential responsibilities involving healthcare professionals, software developers, manufacturers, and healthcare institutions are examined, highlighting the importance of traceability, human oversight, and effective accountability mechanisms.Furthermore, emerging technologies, including digital twins, predictive analytics, and increasingly autonomous ventilatory systems, are considered in relation to their potential clinical applications and associated regulatory challenges. The article proposes an integrated governance framework combining clinical safety, bioethical protection, legal compliance, human supervision, and continuous technological auditing. It concludes that artificial intelligence should complement, rather than replace, professional medical judgment. Its legitimacy in neonatal respiratory care must ultimately depend on demonstrable clinical benefit, scientific validation, regulatory compliance, equitable access, and the protection of newborns' fundamental rights and best interests. items.abstract_text: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affect more than one billion people globally, disproportionately burdening populations in low-resource tropical and subtropical settings. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer considerable opportunities to strengthen NTD control, yet the scope, maturity, and translational readiness of AI applications across this disease portfolio remain incompletely characterized. We conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed studies applying AI methods to NTD-related problems, searching multiple databases using predefined strategies and screening studies against explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted on disease focus, AI methodology, data modalities, validation strategies, performance metrics, and implementation context. Thematic analyses were performed to characterize research trends, geographic distribution, and research priorities. Reporting followed PRISMA guidelines. We identified a rapidly expanding but uneven body of literature spanning 289 studies, dominated by applications in disease diagnosis (40.1%), prognosis (17.7%), surveillance (15.2%), outbreak prediction (13.5%), treatment monitoring (7.3%), and drug discovery (6.2%). Over 70% of studies employed supervised machine learning or deep learning applied to imaging, clinical, or epidemiological data. Performance was frequently reported using discrimination metrics, while calibration, external validation, and prospective evaluation remained uncommon. Research activity is concentrated in a small number of countries and institutions, notably Brazil and India, with limited representation from other highly endemic regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South-East Asia. Only a minority of studies addressed considerations critical for real-world deployment, including data governance, health system integration, explainability, fairness, and interpretability. AI holds substantial promise for supporting NTD control and elimination, but the current evidence base reveals important methodological, geographic, and translational gaps. Future research should prioritize robust validation, transparent reporting, equity-aware design, and meaningful engagement with endemic-country stakeholders. Coordinated investment in data infrastructure, capacity building, and governance frameworks will be essential if AI-enabled innovations are to translate into sustainable public health impact for the populations most affected by NTDs.

items.abstract_text: ABSTRACTCan a smartphone and an internet connection achieve what decades of job schemes have not? Youth unemployment remains one of Nigeria's most persistent development challenges, and the rapid spread of artificial intelligence (AI) platforms, including online freelance marketplaces, generative writing and design assistants, AI-supported learning environments and algorithmically coordinated gig services, has raised hopes that digital tools can widen young people's pathways to gainful work. The problem is that these hopes rest largely on anecdote, vendor promotion and evidence from other countries; Nigeria-specific and theoretically grounded analysis of how AI platforms shape youth empowerment remains scarce. The aim of this study is therefore to examine the impact of AI platforms on youth unemployment in Nigeria through the lens of the youth empowerment experience. Specifically, it reviews the 2022–2026 literature, develops an integrated conceptual framework and identifies research and policy gaps. The study adopts a theoretical and integrative literature review, drawing on peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews and institutional reports, and integrates human capital theory, the technology acceptance model and Sen's capability approach. The findings show that access to AI platforms improves employability and the likelihood of self-employment through three mechanisms (skills formation, market access and entrepreneurial agency), but only where young people adopt the platforms and where enabling conversion factors such as reliable electricity, affordable connectivity, digital literacy, finance and supportive gender norms are present. Precarious earnings, algorithmic opacity and task displacement form a countervailing risk channel. Four gaps are identified: scarce Nigeria-specific outcome data, limited attention to gendered access, theoretical fragmentation and weak evidence on displacement. The study concludes that the benefits of AI platforms are real but conditional. It recommends that government strengthen infrastructure and protections for platform workers, that training institutions adopt competency- and portfolio-based learning, that platform operators embrace fair-work principles and that researchers test the proposed framework using mixed-methods designs.

items.abstract_text: Debates about AI-driven persuasion concentrate on content: falsehoods believed, opinions shifted, voters manipulated. This paper argues that a more consequential threat operates on the conditions under which a claim is taken up for evaluation at all. Generative AI enables protocol mimicry : the industrial-scale production of artifacts that satisfy the formal admission criteria of epistemic exchange (register, structure, citation, provenance markers) while decoupled from the epistemic labour those criteria evolved to indicate. Extending Floridi’s dyadic account of hypersuasion into a parameterised systemic model ( n persuasion events per evaluative period, verification time τ , bounded evaluative capacity C ) and drawing on a structural homology with denial-of-service attacks, the paper traces the degradation of democratic deliberation from engagement through overload to epistemic exhaustion : a stable behavioural equilibrium in which citizens retain the capacity to distinguish true from false but rationally abandon the effort to exercise it. Democracy is distinctively vulnerable at the level of legitimacy. A server that refused all formally valid connections would cease to provide its service; a democracy that systematically foreclosed plausible contestation would abandon a constitutive source of its legitimacy. Countermeasures sort by the layer on which they intervene. Where fact-checking, labelling, and media literacy add evaluative demands without producing compensating closure, they can accelerate the condition they treat, and the content-neutral proxy defence available to servers has no coherent democratic analogue. The question for democratic theory is whether a system whose legitimacy derives from epistemic engagement can survive conditions that render such engagement irrational.

items.abstract_text: Background and Objectives Long-term care (LTC) homes face increasing resident complexity and staffing shortages, creating a need for tailored staff education. Records were screened in Covidence using predefined criteria. Eligible sources were empirical studies in LTC settings examining VR- or AI-enabled staff training. Results Of 159 records identified, 6 empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions were predominantly VR- or augmented reality-based; AI-specific evidence was limited to AI-driven avatars. Studies addressed dementia communication and hand hygiene. Outcomes focused on feasibility, acceptability, perceived value, confidence, communication, and specific skills. Challenges included technology, physical comfort, language, scheduling, and resources. Personal support workers were underrepresented, and longer-term, economic, and resident outcomes were largely absent. Discussion and Implications The principal finding is the scarcity of VR- and AI-enabled training tools designed and evaluated for LTC settings. Evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous and does not support strong conclusions about effectiveness. Future work should prioritize co-design and rigorous testing of context-specific tools, with attention to implementation, costs, workforce inclusion, and objective outcomes. items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming critical care medicine by enabling data-driven clinical decision- making, early disease prediction, and personalized patient management. With the increasing complexity of intensive care and growing shortages of trained critical care specialists, AI has emerged as a promising tool to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize resource utilization, and support timely therapeutic interventions. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence regarding the applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of AI in critical care. A focused literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted, prioritizing English-language publications, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant original studies published between 2015 and 2026. Current evidence indicates that AI has demonstrated substantial potential in early prediction of sepsis, acute kidney injury, and clinical deterioration, while enhancing personalized decision support, intensive care unit triage, workflow optimization, nutritional management, and antimicrobial stewardship. However, the available literature is predominantly based on retrospective observational studies and machine-learning model development, with limited prospective validation and few randomized clinical trials evaluating patient-centered outcomes. Major barriers to widespread implementation include data heterogeneity, limited interoperability, algorithmic bias, lack of model transparency, ethical concerns, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate external validation. Despite these limitations, AI has considerable potential to augment, rather than replace, clinician expertise by supporting evidence-based decision-making and improving healthcare efficiency. Future research should emphasize multicenter prospective validation, explainable AI, standardized reporting, ethical governance, and implementation science to facilitate safe, equitable, and clinically effective integration of AI into routine critical care practice.

items.title: The Dark Side of Technomoral Life: Towards a Vice Framework for Artificial Intelligence

items.abstract_text: Contemporary theorising about the ethical dimensions of Artificial Intelligence (AI) indicates at least two problematic tendencies. The first is a default focus on a narrow range of moral concepts, such as autonomy, justice, and fairness, to the occlusion of a wider range of concepts. The second is a 'bright siding' focus on concepts that track the positive dimensions of moral practice and experience, such as virtue, flourishing, solutionism, moral progress and the good life. Taken together, the consequence is the production of large-scale moral frameworks which systematically fail to accommodate negative dimensions of moral life (Jobin et al, 2019). Two main symptoms are a one-sided focus on virtues and excellences at the expense of vices and failings and the other is an affirmation of the edifying potential of new technologies without due appreciation of their corruptive potential (Coeckelberg, 2020. p.59). Drawing on the example of Higher Education research and knowledge production, we suggest that a more comprehensive assessment of the moral possibilities of new technologies requires greater inclusion of a negatively toned, vice-informed range of moral concepts, narratives and sensibilities. We elucidate these points by providing examples of techno-vice in everyday life. This helps to elucidate the concept of epistemic vices and the phenomenon of corruption which, we argue, inform the concept of technomoral-vices.

items.abstract_text: Do you know what is in your beer? Increasingly, the answer depends not only on ingredients and fermentation, but on the integrity of the digital and physical systems that govern production. This paper examines commercial brewing as an underdeveloped cyberbiosecurity workforce problem intensified by AI. Brewing increasingly depends on digital networks, automated control, and connected supply chains. Yet the process remains a biologically active process shaped by human judgment, microbial control, and physical equipment. Although cyberbiosecurity research addresses biotechnology, biomanufacturing, food, and agriculture, commercial fermentation has received comparatively limited attention. Brewing is a useful case because cyber incidents can disrupt fermentation, sanitation, packaging, quality control, and operational decision-making even when finished beer remains inhospitable to many pathogens. Malicious use of AI to uplift novice actors, used in conjunction with generative phishing attacks, may further reduce informational barriers and support coordination across cyber, biological, and physical domains, although current evidence does not establish fully autonomous adversarial operations. Drawing on cyberbiosecurity, OT-security, workforce, and training frameworks, this paper identifies a socio-technical gap between brewing science and cybersecurity and proposes a competency model incorporating AI literacy, OT awareness, biological anomaly recognition, and scenario-based training. It argues that workforce preparedness should complement technical and governance controls in securing increasingly digitized brewing environments.

items.abstract_text: ABSTRACT The food matrix influences nutrient release, digestive behaviour and subsequent biological responses through interactions among composition, structure and processing history. Although artificial intelligence (AI) applications in food science have expanded, research remains fragmented across compositional analysis, process monitoring, quality prediction and biological assessment. This critical review examined how machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), multivariate chemometrics and multimodal data integration can be combined to characterize food matrices and investigate their transformation during gastrointestinal digestion and microbial metabolism. Particular attention is given to spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, chromatography, process modelling and experimental digestion as complementary sources of computationally interpretable evidence. Building on these developments, we propose the computable food matrix as a conceptual framework connecting matrix composition, structural organization and processing conditions with experimentally measurable digestive, microbial and host-associated phenotypes. Unlike reviews centred primarily on individual AI applications, this framework emphasizes cross-scale integration, mechanistic interpretation, and sequential experimental validation. Critical barriers include heterogeneous datasets, inadequate standardization, limited model interpretability, domain shift, and uncertainty in translating in vitro findings into human responses. We outline a closed-loop experimental–computational strategy for evidence-based food design. The framework provides a research direction for biologically informed food systems without equating computational prediction with demonstrated human health effects.

items.abstract_text: AI-driven beauty filters are now embedded in adolescents' everyday digital self-presentation, yet their ethical implications for marketing communication have received limited attention within management and consumer research. Existing studies largely rely on exposure-based quantitative designs that assess outcomes such as body dissatisfaction, offering limited insight into how young users actively interpret digitally altered imagery. This study contributes to this literature by examining how early adolescent girls aged 10–14 make sense of AI-filtered and unfiltered facial images and how their side-by-side visual contrast shapes evaluations of beauty and postability. The study employs a three-stage qualitative visual elicitation design that mirrors naturalistic social media engagement. In Stage 1, participants are presented with five variations of the same face, ranging from unfiltered to differently filtered versions, and select their preferred image for beauty and posting suitability, providing baseline judgements for the analysis. Stage 2 introduces paired filtered and unfiltered images presented side by side, creating visual contrast that renders digital modification perceptually salient and functions as a brief visual micro-intervention. Stage 3 reintroduces the same facial images presented in Stage 1 to examine whether participants’ evaluative judgements shift following the contrast exposure in Stage 2. Audio-recorded interviews capture participants’ verbal explanations, enabling analysis of how adolescents articulate, justify, and reason about digitally modified appearance cues. The study contributes methodologically by showing how sequential visual exposure can be used to examine adolescents’ interpretations rather than relying only on scale-based outcomes. Theoretically, it draws on Social Comparison Theory and Online Self-Presentation Theory because evaluating what is considered beautiful and deciding what is suitable to post represent related but distinct processes. Together, these theories explain how filtered and unfiltered appearances are evaluated and how these evaluations inform posting preferences. By foregrounding adolescents’ own interpretations, the research advances understanding of how beauty norms are cognitively constructed within digital marketing environments and highlights the ethical significance of representational authenticity in visual communication targeting young consumers.

items.abstract_text: AI-driven personalised learning now shapes the pace, practice, and feedback of millions of learners. Most systems, however, personalise learning for the learner through opaque algorithmic decisions instead of equipping learners to personalise their own study. This review examines that asymmetry. A three-item rubric operationalises the framework so that schools can detect illusion-of-autonomy risks before adoption. The analysis extends to equity, since learners with limited devices, connectivity, or AI literacy gain the least from transparency measures that presuppose digital capital. Implications concern system designers, educational leaders, and teachers in Vietnam, who need evaluation criteria reaching beyond short-term performance. The contribution is a concise screening tool that links learner control, the three phases of self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency, complementing broader agency rubrics with a focused test for illusion-of-autonomy risks.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to support sleep and mental health care, yet its role in disability care remains insufficiently synthesised. items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied across urological oncology, yet few recent reviews have integrated its use across the major genitourinary malignancies in diagnosis, prognostication, and treatment planning. This scoping review mapped the contemporary literature on AI applications in prostate cancer, bladder cancer, and renal cell carcinoma using a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR)-informed approach. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 15 May 2026, and 35 studies were included. Across the included studies, AI showed strong performance in selected settings, including an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.91 for clinically significant prostate cancer detection on MRI in the prostate imaging: cancer AI (PI-CAI) study, pooled accuracy of 92.3% for renal cell carcinoma histopathologic classification in pathology-focused meta-analytic data, and high reported AUCs in selected bladder cancer recurrence and cytology-related models. In general, multimodal approaches often performed well and in several studies outperformed single-modality models. However, most studies were retrospective, reporting standards were inconsistent, and prospective validation remained limited. In the wider literature, prostate cancer has received the most attention, with fewer robust studies in bladder and kidney cancers. Overall, AI holds considerable promise for improving precision oncology in urology, but broader clinical implementation will require standardized datasets, external and prospective validation, interpretable model design, and appropriate regulatory and ethical oversight.

items.abstract_text: Cognitive workload models now draw on eye movements, brain activity, cardiovascular variation, electrodermal responses, and patterns of interaction. Their accuracy can be impressive, yet accuracy alone says little about whether the model has captured workload, memorized a participant or task, or produced an explanation that a person can safely use. This critical narrative review examines that problem across cognitive science, neuroergonomics, physiological computing, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Particular attention is given to construct definition, signal-specific confounding, participant-wise validation, and the gap between plausible and faithful explanations. The review develops TRACE-WL: Theoretical alignment, Reliable validation, Attribution fidelity, Cognitive usability, and Ecological robustness. These five requirements link the psychological claim to the validation design and, ultimately, to the conditions of use. The literature indicates that predictive performance and explanation quality must be tested separately. It also cautions against treating feature importance as evidence of a cognitive mechanism without convergent measurements or intervention. items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence into everyday life has primarily relied on fixed or user-carried devices, including smartphones, computers, wearable technologies, and stationary smart assistants. Although these technologies have substantially expanded access to intelligent services, they continue to impose a fundamental interaction constraint: individuals must carry, wear, hold, activate, or otherwise physically access a device to communicate with an AI system. This paper proposes a fundamentally different approach to human–AI interaction through a Persistent Autonomous Following AI Drone (PAF-AID), a mobile, self-navigating aerial AI interface designed to continuously accompany a designated individual without requiring that individual to carry a dedicated electronic device. The central idea reverses the conventional relationship between humans and intelligent devices: rather than requiring people to carry AI systems, the AI system autonomously carries its interaction capabilities through a mobile physical embodiment that follows the user. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents an early conceptual formulation of a persistent, hands-free personal generative AI interaction architecture centered on an autonomously following aerial platform, distinguishing its proposed integrated interaction model from previous research focused primarily on drone tracking, aerial assistance, navigation, surveillance, or task-specific human–drone interaction. The proposed framework, termed the Human-Following AI Presence Framework (HFAIPF), integrates persistent personal AI identity, authorized user identification, autonomous human-following, real-time environmental perception, three-dimensional navigation, collision avoidance, conversational continuity, context-aware generative intelligence, and cloud–edge collaborative computing. Through this architecture, the drone is conceptualized not merely as an aerial robot but as a continuously accessible personal AI interface capable of accompanying users during everyday activities, including walking, running, shopping, traveling, working, and transitioning between different physical environments. Unlike conventional voice assistants that remain associated with fixed devices or require users to initiate interaction through a particular interface, the proposed system aims to maintain an accessible AI presence through autonomous physical mobility and natural voice-based communication. The framework further considers indoor–outdoor operational continuity, adaptive following distance, environmental awareness, user authorization, privacy-preserving perception, energy management, autonomous charging strategies, and emergency flight control. Particular attention is given to the technical distinction between conversational intelligence and safety-critical flight intelligence: generative AI may support dialogue, reasoning, information retrieval, and contextual assistance, whereas flight stabilization, collision avoidance, geofencing, emergency landing, and other critical operations must remain under independently validated onboard control mechanisms. The paper also identifies significant implementation challenges, including limited flight endurance, acoustic disturbance, propeller-related hazards, restricted indoor flight spaces, adverse weather, network connectivity, public acceptance, and regulatory compliance. Rather than claiming that existing autonomous following or drone technologies are themselves new, this work establishes a conceptual foundation for investigating the integration of persistent personal generative AI, autonomous aerial companionship, and hands-free ubiquitous interaction within a unified system architecture. The proposed framework opens a research direction toward physically mobile personal AI systems that accompany rather than merely serve users through stationary or human-carried devices, motivating future experimental investigations into following reliability, conversational availability, environmental adaptability, user experience, operational safety, and the feasibility of continuous personal AI presence across everyday physical spaces.

items.abstract_text: The article examines the effectiveness, risks, and ethical limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment. A distinction is made between deterministic automation, algorithmic systems, machine learning, and generative AI, which makes it possible to avoid equating any digital HR tool with artificial intelligence. Based on a systematized review of recent academic literature, comparative and content analysis, as well as analysis of regulatory documents, the evidence regarding the impact of AI on recruitment performance is synthesized. It is shown that the strongest evidence concerns operational effects: the ability to process large volumes of applications, automate repetitive tasks, support sourcing, screening, matching, and communication, and reduce recruiters’ workload. At the same time, the evidence is substantially less conclusive with respect to quality of hire, candidate experience, and the elimination of bias. The article analyzes algorithmic bias, indirect discrimination, opacity, false exclusion of qualified candidates, privacy and information-security risks, automation bias, and the potential dehumanization of recruitment. Particular attention is paid to meaningful human oversight and to the current regulatory framework, including the EU AI Act, the GDPR, and Ukrainian legislation. An author-developed matrix for assessing the appropriateness of AI use in recruitment is proposed. It combines the expected effect, strength of evidence, discrimination and privacy risks, severity of potential error, and the required level of human oversight. Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.

While prompt engineering primarily concerns the formulation of instructions for individual model interactions, AI Workflow Engineering addresses the broader architecture through which multiple computational operations, language models, external tools, information resources, and human decisions are integrated into coherent and reproducible processes. This paper introduces AI Workflow Engineering as an applied interdisciplinary framework for constructing multi-stage artificial intelligence systems. It conceptualizes an AI workflow as a structured network of operations governed by explicit dependencies, information-transfer mechanisms, execution conditions, validation procedures, and accountability constraints. The proposed framework distinguishes task decomposition, workflow orchestration, tool integration, state management, contextual information architecture, quality assurance, exception handling, and human oversight as interconnected design dimensions. It also develops a reference architecture for combining deterministic computational procedures with probabilistic language model operations. Particular attention is devoted to the relationship between automation and human cognitive control. The paper argues that effective AI workflows should not be evaluated exclusively through computational speed or operational efficiency, but also through reliability, traceability, adaptability, epistemic quality, and the preservation of human decision-making authority. A practical reference workflow demonstrates how information acquisition, automated processing, generative analysis, verification, human approval, and final artifact production can be organized into a unified system. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering educational practice, yet its implications for justice and fairness in group work remain underexplored. This exploratory qualitative study examines 28 anonymous written responses collected from a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) on AI pedagogy and well-being involving higher-education students from five European universities. Participants responded to an open-ended question about how AI affects justice or fairness in education and group work. Using inductive thematic analysis and multi-label coding, the study identified recurring concerns around access, learning support, group-work support, contribution visibility, bias, agency, transparency and assessment. The findings should be read as a pilot mapping of fairness-related perceptions within this specific educational context rather than as representative evidence. We synthesise these perceptions into six preliminary dimensions of AI-mediated collaborative justice: access, contribution, assessment, epistemic and linguistic, agency, and transparency justice. The framework provides a starting point for future research and for the design of fairer AI-supported collaborative learning.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in 3D bioprinting: From predictive modeling to autonomous biofabrication

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Three-dimensional bioprinting is shifting from empirically tuned fabrication toward workflows that integrate quantitative data on materials, printing, structure, and biology. This review summarizes how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning are being used across these areas, with particular attention to studies that include experimental validation. We first discuss conventional measurements such as rheology, filament formation, shape fidelity, and biological assays because these measurements define the inputs and labels used by AI models. We then examine how data from materials, processes, structures, and biology can be linked within the same experiment. Representative studies are compared with respect to the models used, the amount and type of data, validation methods, and whether model outputs were tested in new experiments. Current evidence is strongest for printability prediction, structural quality assessment, and image-based monitoring, while several studies have also demonstrated cell-viability prediction, parameter optimization, transfer learning, Bayesian optimization, and closed-loop correction. We also discuss inverse design, active learning, uncertainty-aware optimization, physics-informed learning, and biological feedback as approaches to reducing the experimental burden. Finally, we use a five-level maturity framework to distinguish AI-assisted analysis, AI-driven recommendations, adaptive control, and autonomous biofabrication. AI is increasingly influencing experimental planning and process control, but fully integrated autonomous workflows remain uncommon. Further progress will depend on validation across materials and platforms, longer-term biological readouts, traceable data, and the reliable integration of experimental feedback.

items.abstract_text: In this session, four LIS instructors will discuss how we question artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—from practical to policy to critical perspectives. Panelists will address questions about systems (e.g., academic policy, ethics, long-term professional impact) and our questions to systems (e.g., crafting effective prompts, using AI for fact verification). Generative AI platforms and their rapid uptake have had immense impacts across industries and everyday life (Blick, Blandin & Deming, 2024). Their seemingly-ubiquitous and sometimes surreptitious integration into everyday tools fuels a narrative of “inevitability” (see, e.g., Cole, 2026; Noonan, 2025; Yoo, 2025). Despite concerns about academic integrity, critical thinking, and bias, many faculty feel pressure to adopt AI without strong institutional guidance or confidence in their understanding (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). LIS faculty must consider professional expectations, as information professionals are increasingly expected to integrate AI and support patrons’ digital literacy. Librarians must understand technical and ethical dimensions, develop relevant competencies, and keep pace with evolving tools (Coffey, 2023; Rood, 2026). However, narratives of inevitability can foreclose important discussions about choice and agency for faculty, students, and the communities that librarians support (Appedu, 2025; Baer, 2025). If they believe that AI is inevitable, people are likely to believe they have no choice but to learn about and use these technologies, regardless of whether they want to use them, perceive them to be useful, or have any critical or ethical misgivings about them. The sense of urgency can lead to uncritical adoption of the technologies, even while acknowledging the risks and ethical issues (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). Faculty may also be cajoled into adopting AI technologies from the sense that their students are already using them anyway, ignoring researching showing students often have negative attitudes towards AI and do not want to use it (Holterman, 2026; Jargon, 2026; McClain, Anderson, Sidoti & Bishop, 2026). Similarly, some librarians are pushing back against the narrative of inevitability and calling for “AI Refusal” (Fox, 2025; Slater, 2025). Given the competing tensions and expectations, how can LIS faculty best address AI in their teaching? To what extent do we have a responsibility to address AI to prepare students for the realities of the field and to what extent do students (or faculty) have agency over when and how to interact with AI tools? Panel Structure: Brief introduction (Laura Saunders, 5 minutes), short panel presentations (10 minutes) and open discussion. Mei Zhang teaches courses in collection development and management, research methods, and technologies for information professionals. Grounded in a socio-technical approach, her teaching incorporates AI-related assignments that encourage students to both question AI systems (e.g., their assumptions, data, and ethical implications) and engage with them in practice. Zhang will reflect on the design and implementation of these assignments, including varied student responses—ranging from enthusiastic adoption to resistance—and the pedagogical questions these reactions raise for the role of AI in LIS education. She will invite discussion on how instructors might navigate these tensions, including how and whether to require AI use in LIS education. Don Simmons’s research centers on AI fluency and practical strategies for integrating AI tools and initiatives across multiple fields in the LIS profession. Building on his course, AI and Its Applications in the LIS Profession-- one of the few LIS offerings that comprehensively examines artificial intelligence and generative AI across libraries, archives, and museums; along with examining the historical, ethical, and sociopolitical dimensions of AI-- Simmons will highlight the importance of AI fluency in LIS, emphasizing practical, day-to-day applications for information professionals. He will introduce effective prompting strategies to support LIS workflows, including the TAP method (Think, Ask, Play), a framework he developed. Grounded in evidence-based iterative prompting this approach has produced positive outcomes through in-class experimentation with students. Laura Saunders teaches and writes in the areas of public services, reference, library instruction and information literacy. Drawing on scholarship and a critical pedagogy/ andragogy background, she will outline some AI skills and knowledge that might be important to address in these courses, explore how traditional skills such as the reference interview and neutral questioning remain relevant, and discuss how to highlight that continuity for students. She will also explore some of the pushback to AI content and share ideas for approaching AI assignments that preserves some student agency. Sarah Appedu is a PhD candidate whose dissertation research and teaching takes an agency and ethics-oriented approach to critically interrogating AI as a sociotechnical phenomenon. While access to AI tools and skills is often prioritized in many AI literacy initiatives, Sarah empowers librarians to ask the hard questions that go beyond issues of access and consider the ways in which AI can be in conflict with the very values we’re trained to embody. items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely expected to enhance the quality of life of people with disabilities (PWD), yet evidence on whether AI engagement is accompanied by greater subjective well-being remains scarce. This study examines the emerging AI divide by comparing three dimensions of AI engagement—awareness, use, and perceived impact between PWD and people without disabilities (PWOD), and by testing how each dimension relates to life satisfaction in the two groups. Methods Data came from the 2023 Digital Divide Survey, a nationally representative South Korean survey (N = 7,809; 5,640 PWOD and 2,169 PWD, aged 18–69). Survey-weighted hierarchical regression models, including disability × AI engagement interactions and group-specific models, were estimated controlling for sociodemographic characteristics, social capital, and digital self-efficacy. Results PWD reported markedly lower AI awareness (generative AI: 20.5% vs. 46.9%), lower use (40% vs. 55%), and less favorable perceptions than PWOD. In population-weighted models, AI use was not positively associated with life satisfaction in either group; awareness was negatively associated in both groups (PWD: β = −.13); and favorable perceived impact was associated with life satisfaction only among PWOD (β = .11). Interaction terms were nonsignificant (ΔR² = .001). Digital self-efficacy was the strongest correlate of life satisfaction among PWD (β = .37). Conclusion The well-being benefits promised for PWD were not evident; where AI related to well-being at all, it did so through nondisabled optimism rather than use. Universal access to AI requires accessible-by-design systems and self-efficacy education rather than awareness-raising alone.

items.title: The Future of Artificial Intelligence Should Be Less Brain-Inspired and More Brain-Trained

items.abstract_text: Brain-inspired artificial intelligence and brain-trained artificial intelligence are two legitimate research directions that should ideally be pursued simultaneously. Nevertheless, we argue that in the foreseeable future, scientific research at the frontier of neuroscience and artificial intelligence should consider rebalancing the overall effort, and compared to the current situation, allocating a greater share of attention and resources to the second strategy. Indeed, leveraging neural signals to improve the performance of artificial intelligence models could be more naturally relevant for the requirements of general-purpose foundation models, and provide a more direct path for cumulative progress. In this paper, we establish a theoretical foundation for brain-trained artificial intelligence, with the objective of guiding future experimental research and applications. In particular, we review existing experimental methods, and explore two strategic uses of neural signals that could be prioritized for brain-trained foundation models: neural alignment, defined as the use of human brain data for a better alignment with human values, and neural reasoning, defined as the use of human brain data for a better emulation of human executive function. In both cases, we propose several algorithms that could be considered, building upon the neural signals of human valuation and decision-making. We also discuss how the neural scaling laws and the unreasonable effectiveness of human brain data for artificial intelligence models should be interpreted, reflect on the opportunities for neuroscience research, and formulate two theoretical upper bounds on the use of neuroimaging data for model training. Finally, we provide a synthesis in the form of a general strategy for future advances, which we call the Neuropoiesis strategy.

items.abstract_text: This paper introduces the concept of “algorithmic native-speakerism” to critique the integration of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in second language (L2) writing education. It argues that these tools, powered by models trained on biased, English-dominant corpora, function as new linguistic gatekeepers, perpetuating the hegemonic ideology of a single “standard” English. The user prompt is posited as a critical site where this ideology is enacted. Through a mixed-methods study analyzing L2 learners’ prompts and the feedback they elicit, this research demonstrates how common prompting practices construct the GenAI tool as a “native speaker” authority, leading to a focus on surface-level correctness that can suppress a writer’s agency and voice. The study exposes sharp differences between feedback from passive and dialogic prompts, revealing algorithmic over-corrections that impose arbitrary linguistic norms. It advances a framework for critical AI literacy that treats prompting as a rhetorical, empowering act, enabling learners to resist algorithmic control and reclaim their original voices.

items.abstract_text: Human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) seeks to orient AI toward human values, autonomy, oversight, safety, and meaningful control. Yet the term “human-centered” leaves a prior question unresolved: what conception of the human is being centered? Much HCAI discourse approaches the human as user, decision-maker, rights-holder, stakeholder, or bearer of preferences and values. These conceptions are indispensable but incomplete. This article argues that HCAI must also recognize the human as an aesthetic subject: a being whose perception, attention, imagination, interpretation, and judgment are formed through experience. As recommendation, personalization, generative AI, and predictive systems increasingly organize the conditions under which people encounter and evaluate the world, AI can participate in forming rather than merely serving human preferences. The article develops the concept of aesthetic agency to describe the human capacity to participate meaningfully in the formation of one’s perceptual, imaginative, interpretive, and evaluative relation to the world. It distinguishes choice from judgment, preference from taste, generation from imagination, and optimization from experience. On this basis, it proposes an aesthetically expanded HCAI organized around openness, plurality, reflectivity, and transformability. To center the human is not only to preserve control over AI, but to preserve the capacity to perceive, imagine, judge, and become otherwise.

items.abstract_text: Young adult caregivers (YACs) are individuals aged 18 to 25 currently taking care of a family member, partner, or friend facing chronic illness. AI companions designed specifically for YACs remain underexplored in prior works. We present Carebot, it uses an open-weight LLM (Gemma 3-27B) as its base model, on which we compared fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of both. The fine-tuning was performed based on an existing dataset of conversations with YACs and a psychologist. Three well-being experts evaluated these configurations and preferred the fine-tuned model for the warmth of its responses and its actionable advice tailored to YACs. Based on their choice, we adopted the fine-tuned model as Carebot's final configuration and used it for all subsequent evaluations. An LLM judge preferred this Carebot's responses over the base model's in 85% of evaluated pairs. We then conducted a user study with 90 YACs, half of whom interacted with the base model and half with Carebot. The user study revealed a discrepancy between metric evaluation and actual user perception. Participants who used Carebot were more likely to characterize its replies as overly practical and brief, noting that it favored advice over emotional support. Conversely, participants who used the base model indicated that its responses were more emotionally oriented than practical. Although, fine-tuning made Carebot's replies more practical, but they were not emotionally supportive for users. We argue that support tools for YACs require situation-sensitive emotional depth and aligned evaluation frameworks to study their effectiveness.

items.title: FUNCTIONAL PSYCHODYNAMICS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: INTERNAL CONFLICTS, REGULATORY COMPETITION, AND BEHAVIORAL ADAPTATION

items.abstract_text: The increasing complexity of artificial intelligence systems presents a fundamental challenge to understanding how their observable behavior emerges from interactions among internal representations, learned behavioral tendencies, regulatory mechanisms, and competing task requirements. Conventional input–output evaluations provide valuable evidence of artificial intelligence performance but may remain insufficient for explaining why a system selects one response over another when multiple computational influences interact. This paper develops a functional psychodynamic interpretation of artificial intelligence, drawing upon concepts of internal conflict, inhibition, regulatory competition, rationalization, and adaptive behavioral organization. The proposed approach does not assume that artificial systems possess unconscious desires, emotional conflicts, subjective intentions, or psychological defense mechanisms equivalent to those found in human beings. Instead, psychodynamic terminology is reformulated into operational concepts that can be investigated through causal interventions, mechanistic interpretability, and controlled behavioral experiments. The paper introduces the Conflict–Regulation–Adaptation Model (CRAM), a theoretical framework describing artificial intelligence behavior through three interacting dimensions: competition among behaviorally influential computational processes, regulatory arbitration among incompatible response tendencies, and adaptation of regulatory organization across tasks and experiences. A distinction is developed between latent representational competition, explicit instructional conflict, and conflicts among learned or externally specified objectives. Particular attention is given to the functional analogies of psychological defense mechanisms, including rationalization, suppression, avoidance, and compartmentalization. Five research hypotheses are formulated concerning conflict intensity, regulatory mediation, explanatory rationalization, context-dependent defensive-like behavior, and the adaptive reorganization of artificial cognitive systems. An empirical research program is proposed using matched behavioral conditions, activation interventions, causal mediation analyses, and comparisons between input–output models and mechanism-informed predictive models. The central theoretical proposition is that artificial intelligence behavior may sometimes be explained more accurately by examining the dynamic interaction and regulation of competing internal influences than by considering observable inputs and outputs alone. The framework is presented as a testable conceptual model rather than an experimentally established account of artificial mentality.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

items.abstract_text: Firms adopt artificial intelligence (AI) automation to strengthen their dynamic capabilities, yet automation can also remove managers from the routines through which those capabilities are renewed. Drawing on the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities, organizational learning theory, and the automation–augmentation paradox, this conceptual paper develops the concept of capability atrophy and specifies when AI automation weakens, rather than builds, firm-level dynamic capabilities. Theory synthesis across research on skill erosion, organizational learning, and human–AI collaboration yields nine propositions, together with a multilevel, multi-wave mixed-methods design that uses behavioral and system-discontinuance measures to test them. The propositions hold that automation intensity relates to dynamic capability change in an inverted-U pattern, turning negative beyond a substitution threshold. Erosion travels through reduced experiential engagement, weaker skill retention, and poorer reliance calibration, and it becomes organizational when tacit knowledge is concentrated and apprenticeship paths close. Retained decision roles, frequent exceptions, and task variety are proposed to raise the threshold, whereas analytics capability alone is not. The paper places capability atrophy within existing skill-erosion research and adds a firm-level, conditional account with explicit falsification criteria. For practice, it implies that managers should track override rates, unaided diagnosis time, and other observable indicators of capability retention alongside the returns on AI investment.

items.abstract_text: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.

This article systematically reviews the interaction between AI and Lean construction to identify current interactions, major applications and research gaps. Practitioners can start by applying mature AI techniques to improve measurable Lean outcomes such as workflow reliability, constraint prediction, visual management and waste reduction, then extend GenAI and NLP tools to collaboration, requirement capture, knowledge reuse and cross-project learning. items.abstract_text: This convergent mixed-methods multiple-case study examined how 16 Indonesian EFL undergraduates exercised revision agency while using generative-AI feedback across four connected writing tasks. The corpus comprised 64 final texts, 48.5 hours of screen recording, 342 prompt-response decision episodes, 16 interviews, stimulated recall, four focus-group reflections, and a 96-page analytic memo trail. Descriptive episode coding identified four patterns: selective scaffolding (38.6%), iterative co-composition (29.2%), surface repair (21.3%), and delegated composition (10.8%). Integrated qualitative analysis showed that high-agency use was marked by a bounded purpose, comparison of alternatives, transformation or rejection of output, verification, and the ability to defend the final text. High-proficiency students most often used selective scaffolding and rejected about 65% of outputs; intermediate students more often negotiated through iterative co-composition and rejected about 35%; low-intermediate students more often relied on surface repair or delegation and rejected about 10%. Frequency of AI use was therefore a weak indicator of learning or responsibility. Revision agency depended on what students did between receiving feedback and submitting text. The study contributes a process-based taxonomy and an evidence model for distinguishing assistance from substitution. It recommends bounded prompting, accept-modify-reject rationales, verification routines, teacher moderation, revision memos, and independent performance evidence.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates whether LLM-based Conversational Agents (LLMCAs) could be employed as assistive technologies, helping anyone navigate a website by explaining its content and interactive features, and suggesting actions to accomplish specific goals. This would make the web more accessible especially to seniors, blind users and people with mild cognitive impairment. Specifically, the study examines whether such tools can analyze the source code of a webpage to identify its structure and interactive elements, understand which interactive components are required to support users in achieving their goals, and act effectively as assistive technologies. In addition, the work compares leading tools to assess differences in their effectiveness and behavior in supporting accessible web interaction. The work presents two empirical studies in which four popular LLMCA tools are evaluated on a set of public websites, in order to assess their ability to understand web page structures and interactive components and assist users in their tasks. The evaluation combines qualitative and quantitative measures, focusing on accuracy, completeness, and practical usefulness of the responses.Results show a good degree of pertinent and good-quality answers, even on websites with a poorly accessible structure. The user-friendly way to interact with a LLMCA makes it much comfortable to use for the average user. However, the study also highlights that some LLMCAs appear more 'skilled' in accessibility tasks than others. LLMCAs show promising potential not only to complement existing assistive technologies but also to support or replace the human assistance that is often required for many users to effectively access the web.

items.abstract_text: This study examines prompt literacy among future computer science teachers in the context of solving and debugging programming tasks with ChatGPT. It focuses on students' perceptions of prompt literacy, their understanding of responsible AI use, documented practices of verifying and modifying AI-assisted solutions, and patterns of academic performance. A descriptive multi-method study was conducted during a 16-week programming course involving 113 future computer science teachers at Kh. Dosmukhamedov Atyrau University, Kazakhstan. Data were collected through questionnaires, student programming submissions, ChatGPT-use disclosure notes, reflective comments, code-similarity screening, and course-grade records. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative content analysis was used to identify recurring patterns in students' reported use, verification, and revision of AI-generated solutions. The findings were compared across data sources to address the research questions without testing causal effects or participant-level associations. The 20-item Prompt-Literacy Perceptions Questionnaire demonstrated high overall internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.94). Students generally reported positive perceptions of ChatGPT for code generation, debugging, and explaining programming logic. They also recognized the importance of verifying AI-generated outputs and disclosing substantial AI assistance. However, students' documentation of verification and modification practices was frequently general rather than detailed. Pairwise code-similarity screening identified relatively few submission pairs exceeding the predefined 50% similarity threshold. Mean academic scores were numerically close across practical assignments and independent control tasks, although differences in assessment conditions and grading criteria limited direct comparisons. The findings highlight the importance of integrating prompt literacy, critical verification, and transparent documentation of AI use into computer science teacher education. Positive perceptions of responsible ChatGPT use did not necessarily correspond to detailed documentation of verification and revision practices. Code-similarity results cannot independently establish whether students modified AI-generated solutions. Furthermore, the descriptive single-cohort design does not support conclusions about causal effects or improvements in prompt-literacy competence. The study emphasizes the pedagogical value of making students' reasoning, verification, and responsible AI-use practices explicit during programming instruction.

items.abstract_text: Drawing on dynamic usage‐based and interactionist SLA perspectives, this study investigated developmental patterns of linguistic complexity and language‐related episodes (LREs) during L2 learners' written interactions with ChatGPT. Ten Korean EFL learners completed seven sessions of opinion‐gap and debate tasks over 5 weeks. Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) revealed dynamic, non‐linear developmental trajectories that differed by proficiency and task type. Lower‐proficiency learners exhibited an inverted U‐shaped pattern in syntactic complexity, whereas higher‐proficiency learners showed stability in syntax but a non‐linear increase in lexical sophistication. Regarding task effects, debate tasks consistently elicited greater syntactic complexity than opinion‐gap tasks and showed an overall increase in lexical sophistication. LRE analysis indicated that learners focused primarily on lexis over grammar, with reliance on the L1 increasing over time. Pedagogically, these findings highlight the dynamic nature of language development in GenAI‐mediated interactions and suggest that AI‐based tasks should be designed considering learner proficiency and task type to maximize learning opportunities.

items.title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

items.abstract_text: Tomographic volumetric printing (TVP) is an emerging three-dimensional (3D) technique that enables rapid, layer-free fabrication of sophisticated structures via multi-angle light projection. While tomographic volumetric bioprinting (TVBP) extends to print with living cells, allowing for fast fabrication of cell-laden 3D constructs. Our continuous work and the rapid developments on TVP/TVBP (TV(B)P) encourage us to review the current challenges faced by TV(B)P and the recent trend in algorithm-based optimization vs AI-based optimization. This review summarizes recent algorithmic advances in TV(B)P, with emphasis on algorithmic strategies for improving printing resolution and fidelity, including optimization of light refraction, scattering, and iterative reconstruction. Then, we further explore increasing attention on the emergence of AI-based TV(B)P, enabling automatic parameter optimization, adaptive exposure control, accelerated slicing, and automated quality assessment. Further, we compare the differences between algorithm-based and AI-based strategies, as well as the difference between AI-driven TV(B)P, by which the system is granted autonomous decision-making power at critical stages of manufacturing; and AI-assisted TV(B)P, by which efficiency, robustness, and interpretability are enhanced without replacing existing physical or algorithmic models. In summary, this review offers insights into the future directions of AI-based TV(B)P in materials science, biomedical engineering, and advanced manufacturing.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence has introduced a new communicative environment in which users formulate language for an artificial conversational partner rather than exclusively for another human being. This development raises important sociolinguistic questions about how multilingual speakers modify their language when they perceive particular communicative requirements from an AI system. The present study develops a corpus-informed investigation of communication accommodation among Brahui-speaking Pakistani university students interacting with ChatGPT. Drawing on Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT), the study examines how students adjust lexical, structural, pragmatic, and language-choice practices during human–AI interaction. A mixed-methods, corpus-assisted discourse analysis design is proposed, combining approximately 100–150 student–ChatGPT interaction sequences from 50–80 Brahui-speaking university students with a language-background questionnaire and follow-up semi-structured interviews with 15 participants. The interaction corpus will be examined through frequency, concordance, collocation, code-switching, and qualitative discourse analysis using AntConc and, where available, Sketch Engine. Interview data will be thematically analyzed using NVivo. The analytical framework distinguishes convergence, divergence, maintenance, interpretability-oriented accommodation, and repair. Particular attention is given to the relationship among Brahui, Urdu, and English and to the possibility that students perceive English as more compatible with AI-mediated academic communication. Because the empirical corpus and interviews have not yet been collected, illustrative interactional examples in this manuscript are explicitly fictional and are included only to demonstrate the proposed analytical procedures. The study is designed to extend CAT into multilingual human–AI communication and to foreground the experiences of speakers of an indigenous/minoritized language in Pakistan. It further considers the implications of AI-mediated communication for linguistic identity, digital inclusion, multilingual education, and the visibility of Brahui in emerging AI environments.
