publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Proprioceptive impairment is a common consequence of sports-related musculoskeletal injuries and is associated with altered neuromuscular control, impaired joint stability, delayed functional recovery, and an increased risk of reinjury. Conventional proprioceptive and sensorimotor assessments, including joint position sense testing, balance assessment, force-platform analysis, and isokinetic dynamometry, provide valuable clinical information, but they are often limited by laboratory dependence, intermittent measurement, cost, and reduced ecological validity. Wearable sensors, including inertial measurement units, pressure-sensing insoles, surface electromyography sensors, and sensor-integrated braces or smart textiles, provide portable quantitative measures of joint kinematics, postural control, gait, landing mechanics, and neuromuscular activation during functional tasks. This narrative review was informed by a structured, non-systematic literature search in PubMed, supplemented by targeted publisher searches and backward reference screening, updated through 31 August 2026, with an injury-focused PubMed update on 7 October 2026. English-language peer-reviewed studies and relevant reviews were prioritized, with direct evidence from sports-injury populations distinguished from indirect or transferable evidence from other populations. The review examines sensor modalities, their relationship to proprioceptive and broader sensorimotor outcomes, real-time biofeedback, home rehabilitation and remote monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted analysis, and challenges in reliability, validity, and standardization. Current evidence supports technical feasibility and selected measurement and feedback applications, but many sensor-derived outcomes are influenced by pain, strength, fatigue, fear, attention, and compensatory strategies and should not be interpreted as direct measures of proprioceptive acuity. Evidence that wearable monitoring improves adherence, prevents reinjury, supports return-to-sport decisions, or enables clinically effective AI decision support remains limited. Clinical translation is further constrained by heterogeneous protocols, measurement error, limited external validation, small or selective datasets, privacy and usability concerns, and the absence of broadly accepted reference values. Future work should progress from analytical validation and reproducibility to prospective clinical validation, multicenter evaluation, and demonstration of athlete-relevant benefit.

items.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction

publication_date_provenance.reason: arXiv verification budget or provider pause

items.abstract_text: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

items.title: JOINT INTELLIGENCE: HUMAN–AI COLLABORATION IN DECISION MAKING
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into human decision-making creates opportunities to extend analytical capabilities, explore alternatives, anticipate consequences, and improve the consistency of complex judgments. However, the availability of AI-generated recommendations does not necessarily produce better decisions. Effective collaboration requires an appropriate distribution of cognitive functions, calibrated reliance on AI outputs, independent human judgment, and explicit mechanisms for resolving disagreements. This conceptual paper introduces the Human–AI Joint Decision Architecture (HA-JDA), a proposed framework for organizing collaborative decision-making between humans and generative AI systems. The framework distinguishes eight interconnected stages: problem formulation, independent human assessment, evidence acquisition, alternative generation, scenario analysis, evaluative deliberation, decision authorization, and outcome monitoring. Each stage assigns different responsibilities to human and artificial intelligence according to their capabilities, limitations, and the normative requirements of the decision. The paper conceptualizes joint intelligence not as the replacement of human judgment or the mechanical aggregation of human and machine recommendations, but as a structured process of cognitive complementarity. Particular attention is given to epistemic independence, metacognitive regulation, uncertainty management, critical evaluation, and the preservation of human agency. An operational decision protocol, a functional responsibility matrix, and a preliminary research agenda are presented. The framework also addresses automation bias, algorithm aversion, erroneous forecasting, accountability diffusion, and the potential erosion of independent decision-making competence. The principal contribution is a testable architecture for integrating human judgment and AI-assisted analysis while maintaining human responsibility for value-sensitive decisions. The proposed approach aims to support more informed, transparent, adaptable, and accountable decisions without assuming that human–AI collaboration is inherently superior to independent human or machine performance

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies are transforming teaching and learning by offering new pedagogical opportunities while posing challenges. Despite their critical role in preparing future teachers, many teacher educators lack the necessary AI-related knowledge and pedagogical strategies for responsible GenAI integration. The current study first aimed to examine teacher educators’ perceptions, use, and needs regarding GenAI integration. For this, we interviewed teacher educators, transformed their collected experiences into case studies, and asked them to reflect on them. Our second aim was to explore the role of teacher educators’ self-reported AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK in these case reflections. To understand this knowledge, we used the Intelligent-TPACK and AI literacy frameworks. Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) revealed that higher self-reported AI literacy and Intelligent-TPACK may be linked to critical, multi-layered reflections, while lower levels reflected practice-focused, classroom-level reasoning. Interviews further showed that teacher educators (a) perceived GenAI as useful for teaching tasks but emphasised critical evaluation, (b) mainly used it for academic writing correction and lesson planning, and (c) expressed a need for practical and ethical guidelines. This study contributes to teacher education by highlighting the potential of structured, case-based reflection to support AI-related knowledge and skills for pedagogical and ethical GenAI integration.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education presents additional challenges for international students, including dependence on technology, adaptation to another culture, and the need to be ethically prepared to learn a foreign language. This research explores the social and technological dilemma created using AI in Arabic language learning and how international students in Indonesia adapt to it. The research employed a qualitative approach using digital ethnography, i.e., digital observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis and verified through source triangulation, methodological triangulation, and member checking. Results suggest that the use of AI in Arabic language learning is contradictory. While AI offers increased access to materials, flexibility in learning, and academic efficiency, it also creates dilemmas in cognitive-academic, socio-cultural, and ethical-technological areas. Dependence on AI may reduce critical thinking and independent learning. It may also lead to fewer opportunities for cross-cultural social interactions and create greater ethical dilemmas due to limited digital literacy and/or a lack of established standards for AI use. To address these challenges, students developed adaptive strategies through selective use of AI, strengthening direct communication, and enhancing ethical awareness regarding digital technology.

items.abstract_text: Population spatialisation serves as a critical nexus transforming aggregated population counts into spatially explicit population distributions, providing an essential foundation for urban planning, disaster management, and public health assessment. However, the inherent complexity of human settlement patterns presents significant challenges for population spatialisation and fine-grained population disaggregation. With the convergence of geospatial big data and artificial intelligence (AI), population spatialisation has undergone rapid changes in data sources, spatial representations, and modelling approaches, yet its evolution has received limited systematic attention. To address this gap, this paper reviews the evolution of population spatialisation through a structured literature synthesis complemented by bibliometric analysis, tracing its development from traditional redistribution approaches to recent AI-enabled methods, with a particular focus on emerging geospatial foundation models. Furthermore, the synthesis reveals a methodological transition from rule-based redistribution towards data-driven, probabilistic, and representation-learning approaches, coupled with the progressive diversification of spatial representations and growing attention to temporally explicit and demographically differentiated population estimation. Based on these findings, future research should prioritise robustness across scales and contexts, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and the representation of demographic heterogeneity. Through this review, we aim to elucidate the key transitions in the evolution of population spatialisation, thereby facilitating the development and evaluation of more reliable and demographically informative spatial population products.

items.abstract_text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational processes is transforming not only how work is performed but also how teams are structured, coordinated, and led. As generative AI systems and increasingly autonomous agents assume analytical, creative, informational, and operational functions, leadership must evolve beyond the conventional management of exclusively human contributors. However, the introduction of AI does not automatically improve collective performance. Effective hybrid intelligence requires deliberate coordination of complementary capabilities, transparent allocation of decision rights, appropriate reliance, continuous evaluation, and the preservation of human professional autonomy. This conceptual paper examines Hybrid Intelligence Leadership (HIL) as an emerging approach to managing teams in which human professionals and AI systems perform interdependent functions toward shared organizational objectives. Drawing on theories of human–AI complementarity, distributed cognition, organizational learning, psychological safety, and sociotechnical systems, the paper introduces the Hybrid Intelligence Leadership Architecture (HILA). The proposed architecture comprises six interdependent leadership functions: strategic alignment, capability-based task allocation, collaborative coordination, epistemic and operational assurance, human capability development, and adaptive governance. The model emphasizes that leadership effectiveness depends not simply on technological sophistication but on how human and artificial contributions are organized, evaluated, and continuously reconfigured. Practical applications, implementation principles, organizational risks, and testable research propositions are presented. Particular attention is given to avoiding automation bias, preventing the erosion of human expertise, maintaining accountability, and ensuring that AI adoption strengthens rather than marginalizes human contributors. The paper argues that the central responsibility of hybrid intelligence leadership is to create organizational conditions in which human judgment and artificial capabilities generate sustainable collective value without compromising autonomy, responsibility, or professional development.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare, creating opportunities to improve diagnosis, clinical decision-making, resource allocation, and healthcare delivery, while also raising concerns regarding algorithmic bias, discrimination, transparency, accountability, and health equity. These challenges are particularly relevant in fragmented healthcare systems, where pre-existing social and institutional inequalities may interact with AI-based decision-making. This qualitative socio-legal documentary review with a narrative synthesis critically examines the Chilean legal and regulatory framework governing the use of AI in healthcare, with particular attention to algorithmic bias, discrimination, health equity, transparency, accountability, and the protection of patients’ fundamental rights. The review draws on academic literature, legislation, governmental and institutional documents, and international regulatory instruments to identify regulatory gaps and governance challenges relevant to Chilean healthcare. The analysis indicates that Chilean law provides important constitutional and statutory protections concerning equality, non-discrimination, health, personal data, and patient rights, but that these protections are not yet articulated within a specific sectoral framework addressing algorithmic discrimination and the governance of AI in healthcare. Particular challenges concern indirect discrimination, algorithmic opacity, accountability, human oversight, and the capacity to identify and mitigate bias throughout the AI lifecycle. The review does not empirically assess the performance or discriminatory effects of individual AI systems. Drawing on the Chilean context and selected international regulatory developments, particularly the European Union AI Act, the review develops a sector-specific governance framework centered on transparency and explainability, accountability, human oversight, periodic bias auditing, equity assessment, and AI literacy. The findings contribute to broader discussions on equitable AI governance in healthcare, particularly in countries characterized by fragmented health systems and comparable regulatory challenges.

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most influential technologies shaping contemporary society. Despite rapid advances in machine learning, foundation models, and generative AI, persistent ambiguity remains concerning the relationship among computation, cognition, and intelligence. While computational systems demonstrate increasingly sophisticated capabilities, whether such capabilities constitute cognition or intelligence remains theoretically contested. Existing scholarship has extensively examined AI technologies, applications, ethics, and governance, yet comparatively less attention has been devoted to explaining how computational systems become associated with intelligence and acquire legitimacy, authority, and societal significance.This study investigates AI conception as a distinct object of interdisciplinary inquiry. Using a conceptual, abductive, and theory-building approach, it synthesizes insights from philosophy of mind, cognitive science, Science and Technology Studies, sociotechnical systems theory, communication studies, institutional theory, and governance scholarship. The analysis develops the AI Re-Conception Framework, comprising five interconnected dimensions: Terminological Reconstruction, Discursive Reconstruction, Epistemological Reconstruction, Sociotechnical Reconstruction, and Human-Centered Governance Integration.The framework explains how computational systems acquire intelligence-related attribution, meaning, legitimacy, and governance relevance through processes of categorization, interpretation, attribution, relational embedding, and conceptual governance. It argues that intelligence attribution emerges through human interpretation and justification rather than computational capability itself. Consequently, computation should not be conflated with cognition or intelligence.The study advances a sociotechnical re-conception of AI, establishes AI conception as a distinct object of inquiry, and introduces Conceptual Governance as a framework for examining and governing the assumptions and legitimacy claims through which AI acquires societal influence.

items.abstract_text: The development of artificial intelligence challenges traditional philosophical assumptions about the relationship between human nature and intellectual capacities. Reasoning, language production, creativity, problem-solving, and complex decision-making have historically occupied central positions in conceptions of human distinctiveness. As artificial systems demonstrate increasingly sophisticated performance in these domains, philosophical anthropology faces a fundamental question: what does it mean to be human when capabilities previously associated with human intellectual exceptionalism can also be performed by nonhuman systems? This article examines the anthropological implications of artificial intelligence through an interdisciplinary conceptual framework integrating philosophical anthropology, phenomenology, philosophy of mind, theories of extended cognition, and contemporary AI ethics. It argues that technological developments do not eliminate human distinctiveness but challenge attempts to ground human identity exclusively in superior cognitive performance. The paper distinguishes biological humanity, existential self-understanding, social recognition, and moral status, demonstrating why these dimensions should not be reduced to a single criterion of intelligence. It proposes an Anthropological Reorientation Framework consisting of five interconnected dimensions: embodied existence, reflexive self-interpretation, relational identity, narrative agency, and normative responsibility. The central thesis is that artificial intelligence may transform the historical conditions through which human beings understand and exercise their capacities without automatically changing what constitutes membership in the human species or the unconditional moral worth of human persons. Rather than interpreting AI merely as a competitor to human cognition, the article examines it as a technological and cultural development capable of restructuring intellectual practices, creative expression, autonomy, and the formation of human identity. The resulting perspective shifts philosophical attention from the preservation of human cognitive superiority toward the conditions under which human beings can continue developing meaningful, responsible, and self-directed forms of existence in increasingly AI-mediated environments.

items.abstract_text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into neonatal ventilatory support represents a significant advancement in contemporary medicine, offering new opportunities for precision respiratory care, early detection of clinical deterioration, prediction of non-invasive ventilation failure, and optimization of respiratory management in critically ill newborns. Nevertheless, its implementation raises complex clinical, ethical, legal, and technological challenges, particularly because neonates constitute an exceptionally vulnerable population unable to exercise personal autonomy or provide informed consent. This article examines the principal legal and ethical frameworks governing AI-assisted neonatal ventilation, emphasizing international regulatory instruments, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, the Medical Device Regulation, and guidance issued by the World Health Organization and international medical-device regulatory authorities. Particular attention is devoted to the fundamental principles of bioethics: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. The analysis also addresses algorithmic bias, data protection, medical confidentiality, algorithmic transparency, cybersecurity, clinical validation, and the limitations of automated decision-making. A central controversy concerns the allocation of medical-legal liability when AI-generated recommendations contribute to adverse neonatal outcomes. Potential responsibilities involving healthcare professionals, software developers, manufacturers, and healthcare institutions are examined, highlighting the importance of traceability, human oversight, and effective accountability mechanisms.Furthermore, emerging technologies, including digital twins, predictive analytics, and increasingly autonomous ventilatory systems, are considered in relation to their potential clinical applications and associated regulatory challenges. The article proposes an integrated governance framework combining clinical safety, bioethical protection, legal compliance, human supervision, and continuous technological auditing. It concludes that artificial intelligence should complement, rather than replace, professional medical judgment. Its legitimacy in neonatal respiratory care must ultimately depend on demonstrable clinical benefit, scientific validation, regulatory compliance, equitable access, and the protection of newborns' fundamental rights and best interests. items.abstract_text: Although AI-driven environmental, social, and governance (ESG) analytics have advanced rapidly, evidence of their effectiveness remains uneven across different reporting environments. This study systematically reviews Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques applied to ESG-oriented financial intelligence, examining the relationship between computational approaches, data infrastructure, and institutional conditions, with particular attention to emerging-market contexts. The evidence base is globally distributed, while South Africa is used as an illustrative emerging-market case to contextualise disclosure fragmentation and institutional constraints rather than as the primary empirical unit of analysis. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-compliant Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted on 70 peer-reviewed studies published between 2017 and 2025. A cross-dimensional coding framework was used to classify modelling architectures, ESG data modalities, task formulations, and implementation constraints. The analysis further considered validation quality, data dependency, transferability, and governance relevance across these dimensions. The findings indicate that advances in model architecture have outpaced the development of supporting data infrastructure. Governance and explainability mechanisms are commonly added after modelling rather than integrated into system design. Dependence on proprietary datasets limits reproducibility, while reported performance often reflects high-resource disclosure environments uncommon in emerging markets. The principal constraints on ESG-oriented financial intelligence arise from fragmented data infrastructures, inconsistent reporting practices, and uneven institutional readiness rather than from model capability alone. The proposed architecture is therefore presented as a conceptual synthesis requiring empirical validation, not as a deployment-ready system.

items.abstract_text: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affect more than one billion people globally, disproportionately burdening populations in low-resource tropical and subtropical settings. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer considerable opportunities to strengthen NTD control, yet the scope, maturity, and translational readiness of AI applications across this disease portfolio remain incompletely characterized. We conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed studies applying AI methods to NTD-related problems, searching multiple databases using predefined strategies and screening studies against explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted on disease focus, AI methodology, data modalities, validation strategies, performance metrics, and implementation context. Thematic analyses were performed to characterize research trends, geographic distribution, and research priorities. Reporting followed PRISMA guidelines. We identified a rapidly expanding but uneven body of literature spanning 289 studies, dominated by applications in disease diagnosis (40.1%), prognosis (17.7%), surveillance (15.2%), outbreak prediction (13.5%), treatment monitoring (7.3%), and drug discovery (6.2%). Over 70% of studies employed supervised machine learning or deep learning applied to imaging, clinical, or epidemiological data. Performance was frequently reported using discrimination metrics, while calibration, external validation, and prospective evaluation remained uncommon. Research activity is concentrated in a small number of countries and institutions, notably Brazil and India, with limited representation from other highly endemic regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South-East Asia. Only a minority of studies addressed considerations critical for real-world deployment, including data governance, health system integration, explainability, fairness, and interpretability. AI holds substantial promise for supporting NTD control and elimination, but the current evidence base reveals important methodological, geographic, and translational gaps. Future research should prioritize robust validation, transparent reporting, equity-aware design, and meaningful engagement with endemic-country stakeholders. Coordinated investment in data infrastructure, capacity building, and governance frameworks will be essential if AI-enabled innovations are to translate into sustainable public health impact for the populations most affected by NTDs.

items.abstract_text: ABSTRACTCan a smartphone and an internet connection achieve what decades of job schemes have not? Youth unemployment remains one of Nigeria's most persistent development challenges, and the rapid spread of artificial intelligence (AI) platforms, including online freelance marketplaces, generative writing and design assistants, AI-supported learning environments and algorithmically coordinated gig services, has raised hopes that digital tools can widen young people's pathways to gainful work. The problem is that these hopes rest largely on anecdote, vendor promotion and evidence from other countries; Nigeria-specific and theoretically grounded analysis of how AI platforms shape youth empowerment remains scarce. The aim of this study is therefore to examine the impact of AI platforms on youth unemployment in Nigeria through the lens of the youth empowerment experience. Specifically, it reviews the 2022–2026 literature, develops an integrated conceptual framework and identifies research and policy gaps. The study adopts a theoretical and integrative literature review, drawing on peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews and institutional reports, and integrates human capital theory, the technology acceptance model and Sen's capability approach. The findings show that access to AI platforms improves employability and the likelihood of self-employment through three mechanisms (skills formation, market access and entrepreneurial agency), but only where young people adopt the platforms and where enabling conversion factors such as reliable electricity, affordable connectivity, digital literacy, finance and supportive gender norms are present. Precarious earnings, algorithmic opacity and task displacement form a countervailing risk channel. Four gaps are identified: scarce Nigeria-specific outcome data, limited attention to gendered access, theoretical fragmentation and weak evidence on displacement. The study concludes that the benefits of AI platforms are real but conditional. It recommends that government strengthen infrastructure and protections for platform workers, that training institutions adopt competency- and portfolio-based learning, that platform operators embrace fair-work principles and that researchers test the proposed framework using mixed-methods designs.

items.abstract_text: Debates about AI-driven persuasion concentrate on content: falsehoods believed, opinions shifted, voters manipulated. This paper argues that a more consequential threat operates on the conditions under which a claim is taken up for evaluation at all. Generative AI enables protocol mimicry : the industrial-scale production of artifacts that satisfy the formal admission criteria of epistemic exchange (register, structure, citation, provenance markers) while decoupled from the epistemic labour those criteria evolved to indicate. Extending Floridi’s dyadic account of hypersuasion into a parameterised systemic model ( n persuasion events per evaluative period, verification time τ , bounded evaluative capacity C ) and drawing on a structural homology with denial-of-service attacks, the paper traces the degradation of democratic deliberation from engagement through overload to epistemic exhaustion : a stable behavioural equilibrium in which citizens retain the capacity to distinguish true from false but rationally abandon the effort to exercise it. Democracy is distinctively vulnerable at the level of legitimacy. A server that refused all formally valid connections would cease to provide its service; a democracy that systematically foreclosed plausible contestation would abandon a constitutive source of its legitimacy. Countermeasures sort by the layer on which they intervene. Where fact-checking, labelling, and media literacy add evaluative demands without producing compensating closure, they can accelerate the condition they treat, and the content-neutral proxy defence available to servers has no coherent democratic analogue. The question for democratic theory is whether a system whose legitimacy derives from epistemic engagement can survive conditions that render such engagement irrational.

Results Of 159 records identified, 6 empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Traditional approaches to digital well-being have frequently emphasized screen time, problematic technology use, and digital disengagement. This article conceptualizes AI-related digital well-being as a dynamic condition in which individuals are able to obtain meaningful benefits from generative AI while maintaining effective attentional control, manageable information demands, intentional digital habits, psychological boundaries, and independent decision-making. Drawing on research in digital well-being, metacognition, cognitive offloading, technostress, self determination, and behavioral self-regulation, the article proposes the BOUND-AI framework. The framework integrates seven regulatory processes: purposeful initiation, attention organization, information filtering, boundary negotiation, deliberate cognitive delegation, reflective monitoring, and intentional disengagement. Practical strategies are proposed for regulating AI-assisted workflows, preventing unnecessary information expansion, reducing impulsive interaction patterns, establishing sustainable digital routines, and preserving individual agency. The article also outlines an empirical research agenda for evaluating the relationship between intensive generative AI use, self-regulatory practices, perceived cognitive burden, and psychological well-being. The central proposition is that healthy AI integration should not be defined by minimizing technological engagement, but by developing the ability to regulate when, why, how, and to what extent artificial intelligence participates in human cognitive and everyday activities

items.abstract_text: Organizations continue investing trillions of dollars in artificial intelligence (AI), yet many fail to realize meaningful business value. This article argues that the primary barrier to successful AI transformation is not the technology itself, but a widespread leadership misconception termed the AI Readiness Illusion: the belief that organizations become AI‐ready when their technology is ready. Drawing on adaptive leadership, organizational change, adult development theory, and leadership development research, the article reframes AI transformation as a human development challenge rather than a technology implementation challenge. Integrating Heifetz's work on adaptive leadership, Beer and Nohria's Theory E and Theory O framework, Kegan's theory of adult development, and empirical research on leadership development, the article introduces the concept of human readiness as an organization's capacity to think, learn, adapt, and exercise professional judgment as technology evolves. The article concludes that organizations will realize greater value from AI by investing in human readiness alongside technological capability.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming critical care medicine by enabling data-driven clinical decision- making, early disease prediction, and personalized patient management. With the increasing complexity of intensive care and growing shortages of trained critical care specialists, AI has emerged as a promising tool to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize resource utilization, and support timely therapeutic interventions. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence regarding the applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of AI in critical care. A focused literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted, prioritizing English-language publications, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant original studies published between 2015 and 2026. Current evidence indicates that AI has demonstrated substantial potential in early prediction of sepsis, acute kidney injury, and clinical deterioration, while enhancing personalized decision support, intensive care unit triage, workflow optimization, nutritional management, and antimicrobial stewardship. However, the available literature is predominantly based on retrospective observational studies and machine-learning model development, with limited prospective validation and few randomized clinical trials evaluating patient-centered outcomes. Major barriers to widespread implementation include data heterogeneity, limited interoperability, algorithmic bias, lack of model transparency, ethical concerns, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate external validation. Despite these limitations, AI has considerable potential to augment, rather than replace, clinician expertise by supporting evidence-based decision-making and improving healthcare efficiency. Future research should emphasize multicenter prospective validation, explainable AI, standardized reporting, ethical governance, and implementation science to facilitate safe, equitable, and clinically effective integration of AI into routine critical care practice.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI is now woven into students’ everyday learning, supporting tasks such as writing, coding, reasoning and analysis. This paper tackles this double challenge through the design of AI tools that prioritise learning over performance while developing the capabilities that matter for working with AI: creating original work, exercising sound judgement and achieving disciplinary mastery. We then present RiPPLE, a co-creation platform used by more than 100,000 students, where AI companions support learners as they create learning resources, evaluate the work of peers, and engage in personalised practice, with each activity targeting one of the three capabilities. We conclude with reflections and selected empirical findings from the development and deployment of RiPPLE, drawing out lessons for designing AI tools that put learning first.

items.title: The Dark Side of Technomoral Life: Towards a Vice Framework for Artificial Intelligence

items.abstract_text: Contemporary theorising about the ethical dimensions of Artificial Intelligence (AI) indicates at least two problematic tendencies. The first is a default focus on a narrow range of moral concepts, such as autonomy, justice, and fairness, to the occlusion of a wider range of concepts. The second is a 'bright siding' focus on concepts that track the positive dimensions of moral practice and experience, such as virtue, flourishing, solutionism, moral progress and the good life. Taken together, the consequence is the production of large-scale moral frameworks which systematically fail to accommodate negative dimensions of moral life (Jobin et al, 2019). Two main symptoms are a one-sided focus on virtues and excellences at the expense of vices and failings and the other is an affirmation of the edifying potential of new technologies without due appreciation of their corruptive potential (Coeckelberg, 2020. p.59). Drawing on the example of Higher Education research and knowledge production, we suggest that a more comprehensive assessment of the moral possibilities of new technologies requires greater inclusion of a negatively toned, vice-informed range of moral concepts, narratives and sensibilities. We elucidate these points by providing examples of techno-vice in everyday life. This helps to elucidate the concept of epistemic vices and the phenomenon of corruption which, we argue, inform the concept of technomoral-vices.

items.abstract_text: ABSTRACT The food matrix influences nutrient release, digestive behaviour and subsequent biological responses through interactions among composition, structure and processing history. Although artificial intelligence (AI) applications in food science have expanded, research remains fragmented across compositional analysis, process monitoring, quality prediction and biological assessment. This critical review examined how machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), multivariate chemometrics and multimodal data integration can be combined to characterize food matrices and investigate their transformation during gastrointestinal digestion and microbial metabolism. Particular attention is given to spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, chromatography, process modelling and experimental digestion as complementary sources of computationally interpretable evidence. Building on these developments, we propose the computable food matrix as a conceptual framework connecting matrix composition, structural organization and processing conditions with experimentally measurable digestive, microbial and host-associated phenotypes. Unlike reviews centred primarily on individual AI applications, this framework emphasizes cross-scale integration, mechanistic interpretation, and sequential experimental validation. Critical barriers include heterogeneous datasets, inadequate standardization, limited model interpretability, domain shift, and uncertainty in translating in vitro findings into human responses. We outline a closed-loop experimental–computational strategy for evidence-based food design. The framework provides a research direction for biologically informed food systems without equating computational prediction with demonstrated human health effects.

items.abstract_text: AI-driven personalised learning now shapes the pace, practice, and feedback of millions of learners. Most systems, however, personalise learning for the learner through opaque algorithmic decisions instead of equipping learners to personalise their own study. This review examines that asymmetry. Twenty-five studies published between 2017 and 2026, retrieved from Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus, are synthesised thematically around learner agency, self-regulated learning, and system design. The synthesis identifies an illusion of autonomy: surface-level choices sit alongside algorithmic authority over goals, sequencing, and mastery criteria, which narrows the room learners have to practise goal setting, strategic monitoring, and reflective evaluation. Duolingo and two platforms used in Vietnam serve as illustrative cases showing how gamified metrics and default pathways can redirect attention from meaningful goals towards externally driven engagement. The paper answers with a learner-driven personalisation framework resting on three principles: shared control, design that activates self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency coupled with AI literacy. A three-item rubric operationalises the framework so that schools can detect illusion-of-autonomy risks before adoption. The analysis extends to equity, since learners with limited devices, connectivity, or AI literacy gain the least from transparency measures that presuppose digital capital. Implications concern system designers, educational leaders, and teachers in Vietnam, who need evaluation criteria reaching beyond short-term performance. The contribution is a concise screening tool that links learner control, the three phases of self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency, complementing broader agency rubrics with a focused test for illusion-of-autonomy risks.

In the wider literature, prostate cancer has received the most attention, with fewer robust studies in bladder and kidney cancers. Overall, AI holds considerable promise for improving precision oncology in urology, but broader clinical implementation will require standardized datasets, external and prospective validation, interpretable model design, and appropriate regulatory and ethical oversight.

items.abstract_text: Cognitive workload models now draw on eye movements, brain activity, cardiovascular variation, electrodermal responses, and patterns of interaction. Their accuracy can be impressive, yet accuracy alone says little about whether the model has captured workload, memorized a participant or task, or produced an explanation that a person can safely use. This critical narrative review examines that problem across cognitive science, neuroergonomics, physiological computing, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Particular attention is given to construct definition, signal-specific confounding, participant-wise validation, and the gap between plausible and faithful explanations. The review develops TRACE-WL: Theoretical alignment, Reliable validation, Attribution fidelity, Cognitive usability, and Ecological robustness. These five requirements link the psychological claim to the validation design and, ultimately, to the conditions of use. The literature indicates that predictive performance and explanation quality must be tested separately. It also cautions against treating feature importance as evidence of a cognitive mechanism without convergent measurements or intervention. TRACE-WL offers a structured way to judge workload systems intended for education, healthcare, transportation, and other human-machine settings.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence into everyday life has primarily relied on fixed or user-carried devices, including smartphones, computers, wearable technologies, and stationary smart assistants. Although these technologies have substantially expanded access to intelligent services, they continue to impose a fundamental interaction constraint: individuals must carry, wear, hold, activate, or otherwise physically access a device to communicate with an AI system. This paper proposes a fundamentally different approach to human–AI interaction through a Persistent Autonomous Following AI Drone (PAF-AID), a mobile, self-navigating aerial AI interface designed to continuously accompany a designated individual without requiring that individual to carry a dedicated electronic device. The central idea reverses the conventional relationship between humans and intelligent devices: rather than requiring people to carry AI systems, the AI system autonomously carries its interaction capabilities through a mobile physical embodiment that follows the user. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents an early conceptual formulation of a persistent, hands-free personal generative AI interaction architecture centered on an autonomously following aerial platform, distinguishing its proposed integrated interaction model from previous research focused primarily on drone tracking, aerial assistance, navigation, surveillance, or task-specific human–drone interaction. The proposed framework, termed the Human-Following AI Presence Framework (HFAIPF), integrates persistent personal AI identity, authorized user identification, autonomous human-following, real-time environmental perception, three-dimensional navigation, collision avoidance, conversational continuity, context-aware generative intelligence, and cloud–edge collaborative computing. Through this architecture, the drone is conceptualized not merely as an aerial robot but as a continuously accessible personal AI interface capable of accompanying users during everyday activities, including walking, running, shopping, traveling, working, and transitioning between different physical environments. Unlike conventional voice assistants that remain associated with fixed devices or require users to initiate interaction through a particular interface, the proposed system aims to maintain an accessible AI presence through autonomous physical mobility and natural voice-based communication. The framework further considers indoor–outdoor operational continuity, adaptive following distance, environmental awareness, user authorization, privacy-preserving perception, energy management, autonomous charging strategies, and emergency flight control. Particular attention is given to the technical distinction between conversational intelligence and safety-critical flight intelligence: generative AI may support dialogue, reasoning, information retrieval, and contextual assistance, whereas flight stabilization, collision avoidance, geofencing, emergency landing, and other critical operations must remain under independently validated onboard control mechanisms. The paper also identifies significant implementation challenges, including limited flight endurance, acoustic disturbance, propeller-related hazards, restricted indoor flight spaces, adverse weather, network connectivity, public acceptance, and regulatory compliance. Rather than claiming that existing autonomous following or drone technologies are themselves new, this work establishes a conceptual foundation for investigating the integration of persistent personal generative AI, autonomous aerial companionship, and hands-free ubiquitous interaction within a unified system architecture. The proposed framework opens a research direction toward physically mobile personal AI systems that accompany rather than merely serve users through stationary or human-carried devices, motivating future experimental investigations into following reliability, conversational availability, environmental adaptability, user experience, operational safety, and the feasibility of continuous personal AI presence across everyday physical spaces.

items.abstract_text: The article examines the effectiveness, risks, and ethical limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment. A distinction is made between deterministic automation, algorithmic systems, machine learning, and generative AI, which makes it possible to avoid equating any digital HR tool with artificial intelligence. Based on a systematized review of recent academic literature, comparative and content analysis, as well as analysis of regulatory documents, the evidence regarding the impact of AI on recruitment performance is synthesized. It is shown that the strongest evidence concerns operational effects: the ability to process large volumes of applications, automate repetitive tasks, support sourcing, screening, matching, and communication, and reduce recruiters’ workload. At the same time, the evidence is substantially less conclusive with respect to quality of hire, candidate experience, and the elimination of bias. The article analyzes algorithmic bias, indirect discrimination, opacity, false exclusion of qualified candidates, privacy and information-security risks, automation bias, and the potential dehumanization of recruitment. Particular attention is paid to meaningful human oversight and to the current regulatory framework, including the EU AI Act, the GDPR, and Ukrainian legislation. An author-developed matrix for assessing the appropriateness of AI use in recruitment is proposed. It combines the expected effect, strength of evidence, discrimination and privacy risks, severity of potential error, and the required level of human oversight. Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence into professional, scientific, and organizational environments has created a growing need for systematic methods of designing, coordinating, and evaluating complex AI-enabled processes. While prompt engineering primarily concerns the formulation of instructions for individual model interactions, AI Workflow Engineering addresses the broader architecture through which multiple computational operations, language models, external tools, information resources, and human decisions are integrated into coherent and reproducible processes. This paper introduces AI Workflow Engineering as an applied interdisciplinary framework for constructing multi-stage artificial intelligence systems. It conceptualizes an AI workflow as a structured network of operations governed by explicit dependencies, information-transfer mechanisms, execution conditions, validation procedures, and accountability constraints. The proposed framework distinguishes task decomposition, workflow orchestration, tool integration, state management, contextual information architecture, quality assurance, exception handling, and human oversight as interconnected design dimensions. It also develops a reference architecture for combining deterministic computational procedures with probabilistic language model operations. Particular attention is devoted to the relationship between automation and human cognitive control. The paper argues that effective AI workflows should not be evaluated exclusively through computational speed or operational efficiency, but also through reliability, traceability, adaptability, epistemic quality, and the preservation of human decision-making authority. A practical reference workflow demonstrates how information acquisition, automated processing, generative analysis, verification, human approval, and final artifact production can be organized into a unified system. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering educational practice, yet its implications for justice and fairness in group work remain underexplored. This exploratory qualitative study examines 28 anonymous written responses collected from a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) on AI pedagogy and well-being involving higher-education students from five European universities. Participants responded to an open-ended question about how AI affects justice or fairness in education and group work. Using inductive thematic analysis and multi-label coding, the study identified recurring concerns around access, learning support, group-work support, contribution visibility, bias, agency, transparency and assessment. The findings should be read as a pilot mapping of fairness-related perceptions within this specific educational context rather than as representative evidence. We synthesise these perceptions into six preliminary dimensions of AI-mediated collaborative justice: access, contribution, assessment, epistemic and linguistic, agency, and transparency justice. The framework provides a starting point for future research and for the design of fairer AI-supported collaborative learning.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in 3D bioprinting: From predictive modeling to autonomous biofabrication

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Three-dimensional bioprinting is shifting from empirically tuned fabrication toward workflows that integrate quantitative data on materials, printing, structure, and biology. This review summarizes how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning are being used across these areas, with particular attention to studies that include experimental validation. We first discuss conventional measurements such as rheology, filament formation, shape fidelity, and biological assays because these measurements define the inputs and labels used by AI models. We then examine how data from materials, processes, structures, and biology can be linked within the same experiment. Representative studies are compared with respect to the models used, the amount and type of data, validation methods, and whether model outputs were tested in new experiments. Current evidence is strongest for printability prediction, structural quality assessment, and image-based monitoring, while several studies have also demonstrated cell-viability prediction, parameter optimization, transfer learning, Bayesian optimization, and closed-loop correction. We also discuss inverse design, active learning, uncertainty-aware optimization, physics-informed learning, and biological feedback as approaches to reducing the experimental burden. Finally, we use a five-level maturity framework to distinguish AI-assisted analysis, AI-driven recommendations, adaptive control, and autonomous biofabrication. AI is increasingly influencing experimental planning and process control, but fully integrated autonomous workflows remain uncommon. Further progress will depend on validation across materials and platforms, longer-term biological readouts, traceable data, and the reliable integration of experimental feedback.

items.abstract_text: In this session, four LIS instructors will discuss how we question artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—from practical to policy to critical perspectives. Panelists will address questions about systems (e.g., academic policy, ethics, long-term professional impact) and our questions to systems (e.g., crafting effective prompts, using AI for fact verification). Generative AI platforms and their rapid uptake have had immense impacts across industries and everyday life (Blick, Blandin & Deming, 2024). Their seemingly-ubiquitous and sometimes surreptitious integration into everyday tools fuels a narrative of “inevitability” (see, e.g., Cole, 2026; Noonan, 2025; Yoo, 2025). Despite concerns about academic integrity, critical thinking, and bias, many faculty feel pressure to adopt AI without strong institutional guidance or confidence in their understanding (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). LIS faculty must consider professional expectations, as information professionals are increasingly expected to integrate AI and support patrons’ digital literacy. Librarians must understand technical and ethical dimensions, develop relevant competencies, and keep pace with evolving tools (Coffey, 2023; Rood, 2026). However, narratives of inevitability can foreclose important discussions about choice and agency for faculty, students, and the communities that librarians support (Appedu, 2025; Baer, 2025). If they believe that AI is inevitable, people are likely to believe they have no choice but to learn about and use these technologies, regardless of whether they want to use them, perceive them to be useful, or have any critical or ethical misgivings about them. The sense of urgency can lead to uncritical adoption of the technologies, even while acknowledging the risks and ethical issues (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). Faculty may also be cajoled into adopting AI technologies from the sense that their students are already using them anyway, ignoring researching showing students often have negative attitudes towards AI and do not want to use it (Holterman, 2026; Jargon, 2026; McClain, Anderson, Sidoti & Bishop, 2026). Similarly, some librarians are pushing back against the narrative of inevitability and calling for “AI Refusal” (Fox, 2025; Slater, 2025). Given the competing tensions and expectations, how can LIS faculty best address AI in their teaching? To what extent do we have a responsibility to address AI to prepare students for the realities of the field and to what extent do students (or faculty) have agency over when and how to interact with AI tools? Panel Structure: Brief introduction (Laura Saunders, 5 minutes), short panel presentations (10 minutes) and open discussion. Mei Zhang teaches courses in collection development and management, research methods, and technologies for information professionals. Grounded in a socio-technical approach, her teaching incorporates AI-related assignments that encourage students to both question AI systems (e.g., their assumptions, data, and ethical implications) and engage with them in practice. Zhang will reflect on the design and implementation of these assignments, including varied student responses—ranging from enthusiastic adoption to resistance—and the pedagogical questions these reactions raise for the role of AI in LIS education. She will invite discussion on how instructors might navigate these tensions, including how and whether to require AI use in LIS education. Don Simmons’s research centers on AI fluency and practical strategies for integrating AI tools and initiatives across multiple fields in the LIS profession. Building on his course, AI and Its Applications in the LIS Profession-- one of the few LIS offerings that comprehensively examines artificial intelligence and generative AI across libraries, archives, and museums; along with examining the historical, ethical, and sociopolitical dimensions of AI-- Simmons will highlight the importance of AI fluency in LIS, emphasizing practical, day-to-day applications for information professionals. He will introduce effective prompting strategies to support LIS workflows, including the TAP method (Think, Ask, Play), a framework he developed. Grounded in evidence-based iterative prompting this approach has produced positive outcomes through in-class experimentation with students. Laura Saunders teaches and writes in the areas of public services, reference, library instruction and information literacy. Drawing on scholarship and a critical pedagogy/ andragogy background, she will outline some AI skills and knowledge that might be important to address in these courses, explore how traditional skills such as the reference interview and neutral questioning remain relevant, and discuss how to highlight that continuity for students. She will also explore some of the pushback to AI content and share ideas for approaching AI assignments that preserves some student agency. items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely expected to enhance the quality of life of people with disabilities (PWD), yet evidence on whether AI engagement is accompanied by greater subjective well-being remains scarce. This study examines the emerging AI divide by comparing three dimensions of AI engagement—awareness, use, and perceived impact between PWD and people without disabilities (PWOD), and by testing how each dimension relates to life satisfaction in the two groups. Methods Data came from the 2023 Digital Divide Survey, a nationally representative South Korean survey (N = 7,809; 5,640 PWOD and 2,169 PWD, aged 18–69). Survey-weighted hierarchical regression models, including disability × AI engagement interactions and group-specific models, were estimated controlling for sociodemographic characteristics, social capital, and digital self-efficacy. Results PWD reported markedly lower AI awareness (generative AI: 20.5% vs. 46.9%), lower use (40% vs. 55%), and less favorable perceptions than PWOD. In population-weighted models, AI use was not positively associated with life satisfaction in either group; awareness was negatively associated in both groups (PWD: β = −.13); and favorable perceived impact was associated with life satisfaction only among PWOD (β = .11). Interaction terms were nonsignificant (ΔR² = .001). Digital self-efficacy was the strongest correlate of life satisfaction among PWD (β = .37). Conclusion The well-being benefits promised for PWD were not evident; where AI related to well-being at all, it did so through nondisabled optimism rather than use. Universal access to AI requires accessible-by-design systems and self-efficacy education rather than awareness-raising alone.

items.abstract_text: Digital Twin technologies in maritime applications have primarily focused on individual subsystems, such as vessel machinery, navigation, or environmental monitoring, while limited attention has been given to the integrated representation of human operators, vessel dynamics, machinery, and environmental conditions. To address this challenge, a conceptual Virtual Symbiotic Environment for Maritime Operations (VSEMO) is proposed; the VSEMO integrates human, traffic, docking, environmental, and machinery Digital Twins within a closed-loop system engineering framework. The proposed architecture incorporates Explainable Artificial Intelligence to support transparent operational risk assessment and decision support, while immersive virtual reality provides a realistic environment for adaptive operator training. items.abstract_text: Brain-inspired artificial intelligence and brain-trained artificial intelligence are two legitimate research directions that should ideally be pursued simultaneously. Nevertheless, we argue that in the foreseeable future, scientific research at the frontier of neuroscience and artificial intelligence should consider rebalancing the overall effort, and compared to the current situation, allocating a greater share of attention and resources to the second strategy. Indeed, leveraging neural signals to improve the performance of artificial intelligence models could be more naturally relevant for the requirements of general-purpose foundation models, and provide a more direct path for cumulative progress. In this paper, we establish a theoretical foundation for brain-trained artificial intelligence, with the objective of guiding future experimental research and applications. In particular, we review existing experimental methods, and explore two strategic uses of neural signals that could be prioritized for brain-trained foundation models: neural alignment, defined as the use of human brain data for a better alignment with human values, and neural reasoning, defined as the use of human brain data for a better emulation of human executive function. In both cases, we propose several algorithms that could be considered, building upon the neural signals of human valuation and decision-making. We also discuss how the neural scaling laws and the unreasonable effectiveness of human brain data for artificial intelligence models should be interpreted, reflect on the opportunities for neuroscience research, and formulate two theoretical upper bounds on the use of neuroimaging data for model training. Finally, we provide a synthesis in the form of a general strategy for future advances, which we call the Neuropoiesis strategy.

items.abstract_text: This paper introduces the concept of “algorithmic native-speakerism” to critique the integration of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in second language (L2) writing education. It argues that these tools, powered by models trained on biased, English-dominant corpora, function as new linguistic gatekeepers, perpetuating the hegemonic ideology of a single “standard” English. The user prompt is posited as a critical site where this ideology is enacted. Through a mixed-methods study analyzing L2 learners’ prompts and the feedback they elicit, this research demonstrates how common prompting practices construct the GenAI tool as a “native speaker” authority, leading to a focus on surface-level correctness that can suppress a writer’s agency and voice. The study exposes sharp differences between feedback from passive and dialogic prompts, revealing algorithmic over-corrections that impose arbitrary linguistic norms. It advances a framework for critical AI literacy that treats prompting as a rhetorical, empowering act, enabling learners to resist algorithmic control and reclaim their original voices.

items.title: FUNCTIONAL PSYCHODYNAMICS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: INTERNAL CONFLICTS, REGULATORY COMPETITION, AND BEHAVIORAL ADAPTATION

items.abstract_text: The increasing complexity of artificial intelligence systems presents a fundamental challenge to understanding how their observable behavior emerges from interactions among internal representations, learned behavioral tendencies, regulatory mechanisms, and competing task requirements. Conventional input–output evaluations provide valuable evidence of artificial intelligence performance but may remain insufficient for explaining why a system selects one response over another when multiple computational influences interact. This paper develops a functional psychodynamic interpretation of artificial intelligence, drawing upon concepts of internal conflict, inhibition, regulatory competition, rationalization, and adaptive behavioral organization. The proposed approach does not assume that artificial systems possess unconscious desires, emotional conflicts, subjective intentions, or psychological defense mechanisms equivalent to those found in human beings. Instead, psychodynamic terminology is reformulated into operational concepts that can be investigated through causal interventions, mechanistic interpretability, and controlled behavioral experiments. The paper introduces the Conflict–Regulation–Adaptation Model (CRAM), a theoretical framework describing artificial intelligence behavior through three interacting dimensions: competition among behaviorally influential computational processes, regulatory arbitration among incompatible response tendencies, and adaptation of regulatory organization across tasks and experiences. A distinction is developed between latent representational competition, explicit instructional conflict, and conflicts among learned or externally specified objectives. Particular attention is given to the functional analogies of psychological defense mechanisms, including rationalization, suppression, avoidance, and compartmentalization. Five research hypotheses are formulated concerning conflict intensity, regulatory mediation, explanatory rationalization, context-dependent defensive-like behavior, and the adaptive reorganization of artificial cognitive systems. An empirical research program is proposed using matched behavioral conditions, activation interventions, causal mediation analyses, and comparisons between input–output models and mechanism-informed predictive models. The central theoretical proposition is that artificial intelligence behavior may sometimes be explained more accurately by examining the dynamic interaction and regulation of competing internal influences than by considering observable inputs and outputs alone. The framework is presented as a testable conceptual model rather than an experimentally established account of artificial mentality.

items.abstract_text: GPU SuperPODs underpin large language model (LLM) serving, but growing bandwidth and round-trip times make inter-GPU communication consume increasing compute resources. SM-driven remote memory access occupies shared memory or registers for in-flight data and competes for SM-to-NoC bandwidth. Dedicated engines can free these resources, but must handle fine-grained transfers, down to a 576\,B KV-cache entry. NVIDIA's CopyEngine uses less than 1\% of NVLink bandwidth at 7\,KB granularity. We present SURMA, an on-die Scale-Up Remote Memory Access engine. Adapting RDMA requires overcoming slow doorbell submission, excessive per-application connection state, head-of-line blocking of completion notifications on shared connections, and costly ordering for multipath transfers. SURMA uses a credit-based shared send queue to reduce submission latency from 1.2\,$μ$s to 400\,ns; fused write-with-atomic semantics to share connections while independently notifying each transaction; and Network Per Path Ordering to ensure data arrives before the completion flag without Sender or Receiver Ordering. We implement SURMA in RTL on a two-FPGA prototype and evaluate it with two 8-GPU NVLink servers. At 512\,B granularity, SURMA saturates attainable bandwidth with a single SM, whereas NVLink needs over 14\% of the SMs. SURMA occupies under 0.5\% of GPU area and accelerates inference on four models by 1.05--1.26$\times$ over NVLink.

items.abstract_text: Existing accounts of language in autism have tended to focus on English and have rarely progressed beyond broad characterizations of pragmatic difficulty. This volume changes both. Drawing on a clinically defined corpus of Japanese-speaking individuals with ASD and combining Systemic Functional Linguistics with machine learning, it identifies 46 lexicogrammatical discriminators of ASD and non-ASD discourse, with 80% classification accuracy. Thirty-eight of these discriminators are interpreted across twelve cognitive-functional domains, including weak central coherence, joint attention, predictive processing, executive function, and working memory, revealing how recurrent grammatical choices relate to neurocognitive profiles. Analyses span a broad range of lexicogrammatical categories, including clause complexes, process types, appraisal, modality, evidentiality, negotiating particles, and sound-symbolic expression. The result is the first book-length, empirically grounded account of lexicogrammatical variability in ASD, opening new directions for diagnostic assessment and language intervention. Essential reading for researchers and clinicians in autism studies, human neuroscience, clinical linguistics, and neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

Independent Learning after Generative AI Support in School Mathematics: A Systematic Review and
Assessment-Stratified Meta-Analysis

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). Durable competence requires crossing two distinct thresholds. Instructional systems must block direct answer copying and enforce active learner generation before and after AI withdrawal.

items.abstract_text: Objective This study examined the association between generative artificial intelligence dependence (GenAID) and academic performance (AP) among adolescents, whether attentional control (AC) and physical fitness (PF) mediated this association individually and in sequence, and whether grade level moderated these pathways. Methods Participants were 1,461 Chinese adolescents. PF was assessed using standardized fitness tests; GenAID and AC were measured by questionnaires; and standardized scores in Chinese language, mathematics, and English served as indicators of AP. Structural equation modeling and related analyses were conducted using AMOS 24.0 and SPSS 26.0. Results GenAID was negatively correlated with AC, PF, and AP ( p &lt; 0.01), whereas all other pairwise correlations were positive ( p &lt; 0.01). All direct predictive paths among the variables in the serial mediation model and the predictive paths from the interaction terms to AP were statistically significant ( p &lt; 0.01). GenAID significantly predicted lower AP through three indirect pathways: AC (95% CI [−0.067, −0.031]), PF (95% CI [−0.190, −0.003]), and AC followed by PF (95% CI [−0.009, −0.002]). Grade level significantly moderated the AC–AP and PF–AP paths: the standardized coefficients for Grade_AC_inter and Grade_PF_inter were −0.101 ( p &lt; 0.001) and −0.164 ( p &lt; 0.05), respectively. Conclusion GenAID directly predicted lower AP and also predicted lower AP indirectly through AC, PF, and AC followed by PF. The findings indicate interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP. Grade level moderated the serial mediation model, with a weaker negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP at higher grade levels.
