items.abstract_text: Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p &lt; 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. items.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.abstract_text: Secondary school students increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), and evidence shows it can either support or weaken their self-regulated learning (SRL). PCO was positively related to SRL (β = 0.291), whereas SCO was negatively related to it (β = −0.266). Both forms of offloading partially mediated the relationships of TMS and AIL with SRL. PCAU strengthened the TMS–PCO path (β = 0.257), and scaffolding was not significantly related to productive offloading when peer collaboration was low. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

items.abstract_text: Conversational Agents (CAs) is rapidly transforming higher education by providing personalised learning support, adaptive feedback, and interactive educational experiences. However, most research has focused on learning performance rather than students psychological wellbeing. This scoping review examines how Self-Determination Theory (SDT) has been applied in the design of conversational AI to promote digital wellbeing and compassionate educational technology. Guided by the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), a systematic search of four major databases identified 28 eligible studies published between 2018 and 2026. Thematic analysis revealed that conversational AI predominantly supports students competence through intelligent tutoring, adaptive scaffolding, and personalised feedback, while explicit support for autonomy and relatedness remains limited. Digital wellbeing is rarely considered an intended design outcome. Based on these findings, the review proposes a preliminary SDT informed conversational AI design framework comprising four interconnected principles which are supporting learner autonomy, strengthening competence, fostering relatedness through compassionate interactions, and promoting responsible AI use to enhance digital wellbeing. Integrating motivational psychology with human-centred AI design, this review provides practical guidance for developing AI systems that support learner agency, psychological wellbeing, and sustainable engagement, contributing to the design of compassionate educational technologies for the future of higher education.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make learning feel easier, but whether this ease helps students accurately judge what they have learned remains unclear. Drawing on the cue-utilization framework, this research examines processing fluency as a metacognitive mechanism linking GenAI-assisted learning to judgments of learning (JOLs) and calibration. Across three experiments with university students, we tested how AI assistance, explanation fluency, and unaided retrieval shape subjective learning judgments relative to subsequent independent test performance. Study 1 ( N = 264) showed that GenAI-assisted learning increased processing fluency and JOLs, with a significant indirect association linking AI assistance to JOLs through processing fluency. Study 2 ( N = 360) manipulated fluency in scripted AI explanations delivered through a simulated GenAI interface and compared them with conventional-text learning. High-fluency explanations elicited higher JOLs and greater positive calibration bias than low-fluency explanations and conventional-text learning, although the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in objective test performance. Absolute calibration error did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 3 ( N = 386) showed that a brief no-AI retrieval attempt substantially weakened the relationship between processing fluency and JOL and reduced overall positive calibration bias. However, the retrieval-related reduction in calibration bias did not differ significantly between the high and low-fluency conditions. Together, the findings suggest that GenAI can shape metacognitive judgments by changing how fluent learning feels, while the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in immediate independent test performance. Providing learners with opportunities for unaided retrieval may help shift judgments from AI-generated processing ease toward more diagnostic evidence of what they can independently retrieve.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into higher education has intensified debate over how AI-assisted learning may be associated with students’ cognitive development. Although prior studies have examined the benefits and risks of AI use, less attention has been paid to the distinction between frequent AI usage as a learning behavior and large language model dependence (LLMD) as a habitual reliance on LLMs for cognitive and academic tasks. This study therefore distinguishes frequent AI usage as a learning behavior from LLMD as a habitual reliance on LLMs when completing cognitive and academic tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined how AI usage is associated with university students’ critical thinking through LLMD, metacognitive awareness, and AI literacy. Survey data were collected from 878 Chinese university students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with LLMD, which represented the strongest direct association in the model, while LLMD was negatively associated with metacognitive awareness, AI literacy, and critical thinking. The mediation analysis further indicated a significant negative total indirect association between AI usage and critical thinking through LLMD and lower levels of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying the distinction between AI usage and LLMD and by identifying metacognitive awareness and AI literacy as cognitive resources associated with critical thinking in AI-assisted learning contexts. Practically, the study suggests that universities should move beyond simple restriction-oriented responses and pay greater attention to the quality of students’ AI engagement, including metacognitive monitoring, AI literacy, and awareness of dependence-related patterns.

items.abstract_text: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

items.abstract_text: Introduction: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can minimise large language model hallucinations while supporting self-regulated learning. We evaluated the impact of student engagement with a grounded RAG-AI tool (Google NotebookLM) on formative and internal assessment scores in undergraduate pathology, validated a 3-item AI Disclosure Form, and explored cognitive adoption barriers. Methods In a 12-week longitudinal study using an interrupted time series design, Phase II medical students (N = 211) received curated NotebookLM modules alongside core lectures. Students completed weekly quizzes, a 3-item disclosure form assessing the frequency, application mode, and trust in the AI resources, and end-of-study mixed-method questionnaires. Longitudinal cohorts were classified into High, Low, Inconsistent, and non-usage groups, with differences evaluated via ANOVA. Results The 3-item disclosure form demonstrated high reliability. The average scores of formative quizzes (p = 0.656) and summative internal exams (p = 0.961) did not differ significantly between the engagement groups. However, there were notable differences in performance during some of the dense, complex sections (Lung, p < 0.001; Renal, p < 0.001). Frequent users used active Socratic chat and self-quizzing to handle high cognitive demands. In contrast, inconsistent users showed "cognitive flight" under stress, and non-respondents scored significantly lower (24.83 ± 13.76). Conclusion A standalone RAG-AI tool does not automatically improve the overall performance of a group. Instead, it helps manage cognitive load during demanding modules for learners who are good at self-regulated learning. Future use needs structured workflows within a Learning Management System and training for prompt verification.

items.abstract_text: This study examined the effects of Generative AI (GenAI)-assisted learning on the critical thinking skills of higher secondary school students. A quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test design with a non-equivalent control group was used. The sample consisted of 59 Grade XII students of Garrison Academy Kharian Cantt (Army Public School and College), Punjab, Pakistan: 28 girls in the experimental group and 31 boys in the control group. For one month, the experimental group was taught with GenAI tools (Claude and DeepSeek) and the control group was taught with traditional methods. Critical thinking was measured before and after the teaching period with a 30-item Critical Thinking Questionnaire based on Facione's (1990) six skills: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, and self-regulation. The data were analysed with paired-samples t-tests, independent-samples t-tests on gain scores, and analysis of covariance. The total critical thinking score of the experimental group rose from M = 72.71 (SD = 5.11) to M = 121.25 (SD = 7.79), t(27) = 29.02, p < .001, d = 7.37, and that of the control group rose from M = 68.68 (SD = 7.75) to M = 77.58 (SD = 8.03), t(30) = 8.15, p < .001, d = 1.13. The mean gain of the experimental group (48.54 points) was significantly larger than that of the control group (8.90 points), t(57) = 20.21, p < .001, d = 5.27, and the analysis of covariance, which adjusted for the pre-test score, gave the same result, F(1, 56) = 466.24, p < .001, partial η² = .893. All six skills improved more in the experimental group. For classroom practice, the result suggests that guided GenAI activities, in which students compare AI answers, check them against the textbook, and give their own reasons, are worth adding to regular teaching under the teacher's supervision. The effect sizes were unusually large, the experimental group also started higher than the control group (p = .023), and the pre-test reliability of the questionnaire was low (α = .29). The findings should be read with care because the groups were intact classes that also differed in gender. items.abstract_text: Generative AI could improve physicians' clinical performance, yet its use in medical training raises questions about whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use AI effectively and independently. We conducted a longitudinal randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students (389 analysed). Students completed clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were randomised to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the AI assistant, the AI assistant followed by scaffolding, or both simultaneously. AI scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their reasoning without providing direct answers; the assistant provided requested information and answers. The study comprised an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn. Frontier large language models (LLMs) completed the same tasks as an additional benchmark. Students initially performed below LLMs but later exceeded them following the interventions. Students who began with AI scaffolding achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than those given access to the AI assistant from the outset both during the subsequent intervention phase (75.2% vs 66.0%; OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12–2.68]) and after withdrawal (24.6% vs 14.4%; OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15–4.14]). After withdrawal, scaffold-first groups were the only groups to outperform both unsupported students (24.5–24.7% vs 9.0%; ORs 3.77–3.87, 95% CIs [1.25–12.00]) and LLMs (24.5–24.7% vs 8.6%; ORs 3.48–3.50, 95% CIs [1.22–9.89]). Introducing the AI assistant after scaffolding decreased intrinsic cognitive load ( t (50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and increased metacognitive evaluation ( t (50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). These findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding precedes answer-providing assistance to strengthen diagnostic performance both during AI-supported learning and after AI support is withdrawn.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.

While tomographic volumetric bioprinting (TVBP) extends to print with living cells, allowing for fast fabrication of cell-laden 3D constructs. items.abstract_text: Introduction Generative AI chatbots now give students instant commentary on their writing, yet little is known about how engaging with that commentary relates to the self-regulatory capacities on which writing development depends. This study examined a chain mediation model in which generative AI feedback use is associated with writing self-regulation through feedback literacy and, in turn, second language writing anxiety. Wave 1 assessed generative AI feedback use and feedback literacy; wave 2 assessed writing anxiety and writing self-regulation. Serial mediation analysis used 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples, with item-level validity checks and re-estimations without item parcels added as sensitivity analyses. Results Generative AI feedback use was positively associated with later writing self-regulation [ c = 0.265, 95% CI (0.190, 0.339)]. The total indirect effect was 0.128 [0.094, 0.167], or 48.3% of the total association: 0.086 [0.053, 0.122] via feedback literacy, 0.024 [0.008, 0.049] via writing anxiety, and 0.018 [0.009, 0.031] for the serial route. The direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137). Focal paths kept their signs and significance when item parcels were removed and when only feedback-seeking items defined the predictor. Discussion These estimates describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. The pattern is consistent with a theoretically proposed ordering; the pedagogical suggestions are recommendations only, not demonstrated outcomes. items.abstract_text: University students, particularly those who also work or hold organizational roles, frequently experience academic overload, stress, and burnout. Existing digital tools tend to address either task management or well-being, rarely both, and many lose users within days. This study reports the evidence-informed design of StudyFlow, a mobile-first platform that helps students turn unstructured academic demands into a prioritized, actionable plan, and examines how its design aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A design science research approach was followed. A targeted narrative review of literature published from 2021 to 2026 on student stress, working students, digital well-being interventions, engagement, and gamification informed a proto-persona, eight use cases, and nine functional requirements. A high-fidelity interactive prototype was generated through a five-stage natural-language prompt sequence in Google Stitch and refined in Google AI Studio. The intended feature set was compared with four widely used productivity and well-being applications, and each feature group was mapped to SDG targets with measurable evaluation indicators. The review yielded seven design implications, each traced to specific requirements and interface decisions. The prototype implements a four-stage workflow (set up, capture, organize and act, reflect) across dashboard, brain dump, task, focus, insights, and settings screens. None of the four comparator applications supported academic assignment breakdown, and none combined task capture, prioritization, focus support, reflection, and progress feedback in a single workflow. Streaks and usage metrics were deliberately framed as optional, non-punitive cues. StudyFlow shows how evidence on student stress and app engagement can be translated into a coherent, low-friction design that targets student well-being (SDG Target 3.4), persistence in tertiary education (Target 4.3), and the inclusion of working students (Target 10.2). Because no user testing has yet been conducted, no effectiveness claims are made; a staged usability and pilot evaluation protocol is proposed.

items.abstract_text: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has led universities and other higher education institutions to rethink the ways in which knowledge is conveyed, learning is facilitated, and academic performance is evaluated. While such technologies present possibilities for tailored explanations, feedback that supports learning as it unfolds, and joint inquiry, they also give rise to concerns regarding inaccurate information, reliance on machines for thinking, academic integrity, and inequities in access. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of selected literature and institutional guidance, this conceptual paper explores the pedagogical ramifications of LLMs. The paper contends that integrating them effectively demands learning and research environments that bring together subject-specific knowledge, critical questioning, openness about bounded AI use, and demonstrable competence. Constructive alignment, self-regulated learning, cognitive load theory, and cognitive engagement supply the conceptual bases for linking intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment. A cyclical process is put forward, comprising independent engagement, AI-assisted interaction under guidance, verification, application, and reflection. The paper goes on to elaborate dimensions of institutional policy, encompassing governance, curriculum, assessment, research integrity, privacy, intellectual property, equity, procurement, and quality assurance. Specific consideration is devoted to contexts with constrained ICT resources. The paper's conclusion is that the educational value of LLMs rests on purposeful design of specific institutional AI policy that is clear, transparent and progressive.

items.title: The Cognitive Offloading Dilemma: Exploring How Generative AI Dependency Shapes Students’ Independent Thinking, Cognitive Confidence, and Intellectual Autonomy

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: A polished assignment can conceal who chose the method, weighed the evidence and reached the conclusion, which makes a student’s independent reasoning difficult to assess. Drawing on the metacognitive account of cognitive offloading and Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined how reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) relates to independent thinking, cognitive confidence and intellectual autonomy. Semi-structured online interviews were conducted with 22 undergraduate and postgraduate students, aged 20 to 29, from universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, each describing a recent academic episode involving GenAI. Thematic analysis traced when students sought assistance, which decisions they delegated and how they later justified their choices, and produced six themes. Delegating study planning preserved autonomy when students kept control over content, whereas removing a familiar AI prompt exposed difficulty in selecting a method despite earlier success with calculations. Confidence also diverged from accuracy: one student withheld a sound answer without AI confirmation, while another trusted a diagnosis because AI agreed with it, although both had missed the same error. Comparing drafts, checking sources and answering peers’ questions helped students identify assumptions and give reasons for revision. The findings support assessment practices that distinguish producing an answer with assistance from being able to explain or defend it without assistance.

items.abstract_text: Connectivity programmes often assume that a young person who gets online will be able to find a way to earn. Evidence provides partial support: faster internet has increased employment in a number of African countries [17]. However, many young Africans with internet access continue to work in informal, low-paid and insecure jobs. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) raises a further question: who is able to benefit from these technologies, and under what conditions might they widen existing disparities? This paper asks what needs to connect digital access to sustainable livelihoods for young people in Kenya and, by implication, in other African contexts. It develops the Capability-to-Livelihood Pathway Framework, comprising five interrelated components: access conditions; a four-level capability stack connecting foundational digital literacy, functional AI literacy, critical AI literacy and occupational application; conversion factors that shape whether capabilities can generate income; livelihood pathways; and outcome measures focused on security and progression rather than income at a single point in time. The framework is developed through an integrative conceptual synthesis of scholarship on digital inequality, AI and employment, youth employment programmes, and relevant policy and labour-market evidence, using Kenya as the principal contextual case. Four propositions are advanced for empirical testing. The paper’s central contribution is to shift the measure of programme success from skills delivered to livelihoods sustained.

items.abstract_text: Chronic diseases are a major global public health concern and place a substantial burden on individuals, healthcare systems, and society. Their prevention and management depend not only on effective medical treatment but also on sustained engagement in health-promoting behaviors. These behaviors include regular physical activity, healthy dietary practices, medication adherence, self-monitoring, smoking cessation, and other disease-related self-management activities. However, initiating and maintaining such behaviors can be challenging, particularly because individuals differ in their health conditions, risk profiles, knowledge, motivation, behavioral readiness, and support needs. Therefore, accessible, personalized, and continuous interventions are needed to support health behavior change in both individuals at increased risk of chronic diseases and those already living with chronic conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents have emerged as promising tools for supporting health behavior change. Through natural language interaction and other interactive functions, these agents may provide personalized health information, motivational support, goal setting, action planning, self-monitoring, feedback, reminders, and ongoing behavioral guidance. Advances in natural language processing, machine learning, and large language models have further expanded the potential capabilities of AI agents, enabling more flexible, context-sensitive, and personalized interactions. Nevertheless, the application of AI agents in chronic disease prevention and management is developing rapidly, and the available evidence remains diverse in terms of target populations, technological approaches, intervention strategies, theoretical foundations, and evaluated outcomes. A comprehensive mapping of this evidence is needed to understand the current state of the field and identify priorities for future research and development. This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on the application of AI agents for health behavior change in chronic disease prevention and management. Specifically, it will examine the characteristics of the populations and chronic diseases addressed, the types and technological features of AI agents, the health behaviors targeted, the design and delivery of interventions, the behavioral theories and behavior change techniques employed, and the outcomes reported. Particular attention will be paid to how AI agents support behavior change through interactive communication, personalization, behavioral monitoring, feedback, motivational strategies, and other intervention components. The review will be guided by the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. The population will include individuals living with chronic diseases and those at increased risk of developing chronic diseases. The concept will focus on AI agents that provide interactive communication and behavioral support, including AI-powered chatbots, large language model-based agents, virtual health assistants, virtual coaches, dialogue systems, and other relevant interactive AI systems. The context will encompass chronic disease prevention and management across healthcare, community, home-based, and digital health settings. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in nine electronic databases: China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data Knowledge Service Platform, China Science and Technology Journal Database (VIP), Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (SinoMed), PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, ProQuest, and Embase. The search strategy will combine terms related to artificial intelligence agents, chronic diseases, and health behavior change. Studies published in English or Chinese will be considered, with no restrictions on publication year. publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

items.abstract_text: This study compares how mediators and potential clients perceive and accept the use of AI in mediation, drawing on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). Using data from 109 mediators and 152 potential clients, this study found that clients are more receptive to AI than mediators, as indicated by significantly higher performance expectancy on 8 tasks and behavioral intentions across all tasks. To map these similarities and differences, this study proposes the Dual Concern Task Model, a theoretical framework mapping AI acceptance in mediation between mediators and clients. This study also found that professional acceptability—mediators' overall judgment that AI is acceptable for use in mediation practice—plays an important role in shaping mediators' performance expectancy, which in turn influences their behavioral intention. This suggests that mediators' evaluations of AI may be grounded in professional accountability and their obligations to clients. This study offers a focused extension of UTAUT by introducing professional acceptability as a construct influencing performance expectancy in mediation. This study also provides practical insights for mediators, training programs, and governing agencies to make informed decisions about AI in mediation, grounded in empirical findings.

items.abstract_text: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

items.abstract_text: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. items.abstract_text: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of large language models (LLMs) into intellectual activities requires a reconsideration of prompt engineering as more than the technical optimization of instructions. Although conventional prompting techniques primarily seek to improve the relevance, accuracy, and structure of artificial intelligence outputs, they often provide insufficient attention to the cognitive processes through which users formulate requests, evaluate generated information, regulate reliance on automation, and maintain independent judgment. This paper introduces Metacognitive Prompt Engineering (MPE) as a proposed human-centered framework for designing, monitoring, and regulating interactions with generative artificial intelligence. Drawing on theories of metacognition, self-regulated learning, cognitive monitoring, automation reliance, and human–AI collaboration, MPE conceptualizes prompting as an iterative process involving goal clarification, cognitive task allocation, epistemic monitoring, evidence-based verification, and adaptive strategy regulation. The paper distinguishes metacognitive prompt engineering from conventional prompt optimization and model-centered metacognitive prompting. It proposes a five-phase regulatory framework, identifies practical design principles, introduces reusable prompting protocols, and develops a research agenda for evaluating the framework's potential effects on cognitive autonomy, confidence calibration, decision quality, and independent learning. Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between model-generated expressions of uncertainty and independently justified confidence, as well as the limitations of self-correction without external feedback. The central argument is that effective human–AI interaction should be assessed not exclusively through the quality of generated outputs but also through the quality of the cognitive regulation exercised by the human user. MPE is presented as a theoretical and methodological proposal rather than an empirically validated intervention. Its effectiveness, boundary conditions, and possible unintended consequences require systematic investigation

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in educational practice, transforming lesson planning, instructional delivery, assessment, learning analytics, and teacher professional development. Although research on AI in education has expanded rapidly, the psychological consequences of AI adoption for teachers remain theoretically fragmented. Existing studies have examined technology acceptance, AI literacy, technology self-efficacy, instructional confidence, and professional identity, yet these constructs have rarely been integrated into a coherent account of how AI reshapes teachers’ beliefs about their own professional capabilities. This narrative review synthesizes the emerging literature through a theory-building perspective grounded primarily in social cognitive theory and informed by technology acceptance, cognitive load, professional identity, social comparison, and human–AI interaction perspectives. We propose a framework of AI-Mediated Efficacy Reconstruction, conceptualizing AI not as a direct determinant of teacher self-efficacy but as a socio-technical factor that changes the availability, interpretation, and attribution of efficacy-relevant experiences. AI can facilitate mastery experiences, provide vicarious learning opportunities, offer timely feedback, reduce routine cognitive demands, and expand access to professional learning. However, the same technologies may generate cognitive overload, technical anxiety, professional comparison, identity threat, reduced autonomy, and technological dependence. We identify Efficacy Attribution as a potentially central mechanism determining whether AI-supported performance is internalized as evidence of teachers’ own professional capability or attributed primarily to the technological system. On this basis, we distinguish Augmented Efficacy, in which AI extends teachers’ capabilities while preserving professional agency, from Dependent Efficacy, in which perceived competence becomes increasingly contingent upon AI assistance. The framework further proposes that these processes are moderated by teacher characteristics, AI-system characteristics, teaching tasks, organizational context, and time. We conclude by outlining implications for measurement, teacher professional development, AI design, organizational policy, and future longitudinal and experimental research.

items.abstract_text: Disruptions in the supply chain (SC) are occurring more often and becoming more complex, posing significant challenges for engineering management and operational resilience. Current prediction methods do not adequately reflect the relationships and uncertainty among variables, as well as the causal factors of disruption events. In this study, we present a novel uncertainty-aware hybrid framework, namely, the University of Queensland Creative Arts/Creativity Network (UQ-CRGATNet), which introduces Dynamic Graph Attention Networks (DGAT), a tab transformer network for contextual feature learning, resilience-aware representation, Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, and an ensemble meta-learner of Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost). Moreover, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Non-combinatorial Optimization via Trace Exponential and Augmented lagRangian for Structure learning (NOTEARS) enable feature attribution and causal disruption analytics that are human-understandable and support trustworthy decisions. The proposed framework is a joint model that models graph-structured relationships, heterogeneous tabular information, predictive uncertainty, and resilience indicators within a unified learning architecture. The extensive experiments performed on a real-world supply chain dataset show that they significantly outperform conventional machine learning, ensemble learning, and transformer baselines. UQ-CRGATNet achieves excellent Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) and Precision-Recall characteristics, with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 99.87, 99.87, 99.89, 99.88, and 99.73%, respectively. The uncertainty-guided ensemble will increase prediction accuracy, while causal analytics will provide actionable managerial insights into the drivers of disruptions. The results show that the proposed framework provides a strong, interpretable, and scalable solution for proactively predicting supply chain disruptions and supporting resilient engineering management.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. items.abstract_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune condition associated with markedly elevated cardiovascular disease (CVD) morbidity and mortality. Black, Hispanic, and Latin American individuals experience disproportionate CVD burden due to intersecting structural, social, and clinical barriers. Modifiable lifestyle factors, including physical inactivity, tobacco use, and suboptimal dietary patterns, further exacerbate risk. Emerging ML-based studies suggest improved individualized CVD risk stratification in SLE compared with traditional general-population risk calculators, highlighting the potential for precision-focused approaches. AI-enabled tools offer promising avenues for personalized risk prediction and resource optimization; however, rigorous attention to algorithmic fairness, transparency, and health equity is essential to ensure responsible implementation. items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a promising resource for supporting students with dyslexia. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature examines AI primarily as an assistive technology, with limited attention to the cognitive mechanisms through which it may enhance reading development. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework that integrates Baddeley’s multicomponent model of working memory with contemporary AI-supported educational tools. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, special education, cognitive load theory, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and self-determination theory, the paper argues that AI should be understood not merely as an instructional aid but as an external cognitive support system that complements and extends the functional capacity of working memory during reading. Specifically, the framework illustrates how AI technologies—including text-to-speech systems, speech recognition, adaptive learning environments, and generative AI applications—may reduce cognitive load while supporting the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, and episodic buffer. Through this cognitive alignment, AI has the potential to facilitate decoding, comprehension, learner engagement, and reading autonomy among students with dyslexia. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded perspective that connects cognitive theory with emerging educational technologies. Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of a specific intervention, the paper provides an integrative model to guide future empirical research, instructional design, and the development of AI-supported reading interventions for learners with dyslexia.

items.title: Manipulation without Lies: AI Hyperpersuasion and the Limits of the Deception Paradigm

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Large language models can now outperform human persuaders in controlled settings, and they do so in whichever direction they are instructed to persuade. Regulatory and ethical responses to this development nevertheless remain anchored in what this article calls the deception paradigm: the assumption that communicative influence becomes wrongful when, and because, it involves false assertion. The article argues that this paradigm systematically fails to capture AI hyperpersuasion. Drawing on the philosophical literature on manipulation, it shows that hyperpersuasion characteristically operates through true but selectively curated content, adaptive framing, simulated intimacy, and the exploitation of individually diagnosed cognitive dispositions – techniques that bypass rather than deceive rational agency. It then examines Article 5(1)(a)–(b) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Although the prohibition is conceptually open to manipulation without deception, its operative test – material distortion, appreciable impairment of informed decision-making, counterfactual decision change, and significant harm – is inherited from unfair commercial practices law and reproduces the architecture of fraud, leaving paradigmatic cases of hyperpersuasion untouched. Extending the analysis from individual autonomy to democratic epistemology, the article contends that hyperpersuasion threatens democracy not primarily by aggregating individual harms but by degrading the epistemic conditions – independence of judgment formation, a shared space of reasons, and the contestability of public claims – on which collective self-government depends. Regulating hyperpersuasion therefore requires a shift from content-based tests of falsity and harm to process- and relationship-based criteria that target asymmetric epistemic power.

items.abstract_text: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into mental health support settings, understanding how individuals engage with AI‐based tools for psychological support is increasingly important. This study introduces the nine‐item AI‐Assisted Psychological Support Use Scale (AAPSU), a behavioural measure of how people use conversational or generative AI for emotional regulation, self‐reflection, well‐being‐related decision‐making and support‐seeking. The scale development process included item generation, expert review, pilot testing, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and reliability testing. EFA identified two theoretically coherent subscales: self‐regulatory and reflective use (six items) and substitutive use (three items). CFA provided internal confirmation of this structure, with satisfactory model fit and strong factor loadings. Internal consistency was high for self‐regulatory and reflective use (Cronbach's α = 0.903), substitutive use (Cronbach's α = 0.888) and the total scale ( α = 0.919). Convergent‐validity analyses showed meaningful associations with attachment to AI systems, attitudes towards AI in mental health contexts and AI mindset. These findings support the AAPSU as a brief, reliable and theoretically grounded measure of AI‐assisted psychological support use while indicating the need for replication in more diverse samples.

items.abstract_text: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

items.abstract_text: Nigeria’s mental health system serves less than 10% of those in need, with severe provider shortages and deep-seated stigma. Generative AI chatbots offer scalable support, yet how Nigerian adults experience attachment to non-human therapeutic agents remains unexplored. To examine lived experiences of AI therapeutic relationships among Nigerian adults, focusing on attachment formation, cultural acceptability, and perceived authenticity within contexts of care scarcity. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis with 37 adults (18–45 years) who engaged AI mental health chatbots for ≥ 4 weeks. Semi-structured interviews explored relational experiences, trust development, privacy concerns, and comparisons with human/traditional healing. Four superordinate themes emerged: (1) Relational Ambivalence ; participants valued 24/7 availability and non-judgmental space yet struggled with perceived lack of genuine human reciprocity; (2) Cultural Navigation ; users actively adapted Western therapeutic frameworks to local idioms of distress, blending AI interactions with family counsel and spiritual practices; (3) Stigma Sanctuary ; chatbots provided confidential entry points circumventing community visibility and professional hierarchy; and (4) Fragile Dependency ; prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways. Most participants maintained “instrumental intimacy”; emotional reliance tempered by awareness of algorithmic artifice. Nigerian adults develop pragmatic, contextually mediated attachments to AI therapeutic agents that reflect both global digital therapeutic trends and local specificities of care scarcity, stigma, and pluralistic healing. AI chatbots function not as human substitutes but as bridging objects temporary relational anchors in systems of profound unmet need. Findings suggest ethical deployment in LMICs requires culturally adaptive design, transparent algorithmic boundaries, and mandatory human handoff protocols to prevent dependency in unsupported contexts. items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND: In recent years, there has been a notable surge in the ability of machines to perform complex and intelligent human-centered tasks, particularly within the domain of cardiovascular health. Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms reflect the considerable potential for such analyses to meaningfully extend into translational device development and clinical usage of medical devices, especially mechanical circulatory support (MCS) therapies. Here, we investigate and report the applications, limitations, and strategies in which AI is currently being employed in MCS and the potential opportunities of AI approaches to advance the field of MCS. METHODS: To effectively assess the scope and impact of AI in MCS, we conducted a systematic literature review. A comprehensive search of 4 recognized research databases (PubMed, Google Scholar, Ovid MEDLINE, and ProQuest) was performed using this Boolean string: "(Artificial Intelligence) AND (AI) AND (Mechanical Circulatory Support) AND (MCS) NOT (Heart Transplant) NOT (Cardiogenic Shock) NOT (Critical Care)." This strategy was designed to identify the application of AI in MCS only. Database search results were then screened by titles and abstracts, followed by full-text eligibility assessment and duplicate removal. Following these screening and eligibility steps, 30 of the 328 identified articles remained for inclusion. RESULTS: Most relevant publications covered two main subjects: the prediction and management of postoperative outcomes, and the development of personalized device-patient matching and timing. Across the reviewed studies, AI/ML models demonstrated promising performance in study-specific predictions of complications, recovery-related outcomes, and survival and were investigated as tools to support clinical decision-making. Barriers to broad implementation of AI include the necessity for sizable, high-quality datasets to achieve algorithm training benchmarks, the lack of organized and complete databases, such as INTERMACS, and limited computational resources. Emerging frontiers of MCS recognize the potential for AI and ML techniques to refine image recognition capabilities, diagnostic assessment, device placement, and post-implantation monitoring approaches in the future. CONCLUSIONS: AI-driven approaches demonstrate a promising convergence of computational power and clinical expertise, with the potential to support more personalized, efficient, and informed management of MCS patients. However, the current evidence remains largely exploratory, and broad implementation will require robust clinical validation together with attention to data integrity, model accuracy, resource access, and clinical acceptance.

items.abstract_text: The article examines the effectiveness, risks, and ethical limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment. A distinction is made between deterministic automation, algorithmic systems, machine learning, and generative AI, which makes it possible to avoid equating any digital HR tool with artificial intelligence. Based on a systematized review of recent academic literature, comparative and content analysis, as well as analysis of regulatory documents, the evidence regarding the impact of AI on recruitment performance is synthesized. It is shown that the strongest evidence concerns operational effects: the ability to process large volumes of applications, automate repetitive tasks, support sourcing, screening, matching, and communication, and reduce recruiters’ workload. At the same time, the evidence is substantially less conclusive with respect to quality of hire, candidate experience, and the elimination of bias. The article analyzes algorithmic bias, indirect discrimination, opacity, false exclusion of qualified candidates, privacy and information-security risks, automation bias, and the potential dehumanization of recruitment. Particular attention is paid to meaningful human oversight and to the current regulatory framework, including the EU AI Act, the GDPR, and Ukrainian legislation. An author-developed matrix for assessing the appropriateness of AI use in recruitment is proposed. It combines the expected effect, strength of evidence, discrimination and privacy risks, severity of potential error, and the required level of human oversight. Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.

items.abstract_text: Existing accounts of language in autism have tended to focus on English and have rarely progressed beyond broad characterizations of pragmatic difficulty. This volume changes both. Drawing on a clinically defined corpus of Japanese-speaking individuals with ASD and combining Systemic Functional Linguistics with machine learning, it identifies 46 lexicogrammatical discriminators of ASD and non-ASD discourse, with 80% classification accuracy. items.abstract_text: Literature reviews on the ethics of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) have multiplied quickly, and the result is an evidence base that is abundant but scattered. Practitioners seeking guidance grounded in evidence have nowhere consolidated to turn. This study addresses that problem through an umbrella review, conducted under Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. A structured Scopus search produced a final corpus of thirteen peer-reviewed systematic and scoping reviews, published between 2020 and 2026. We analysed the corpus in two stages: a quantitative, descriptive mapping, then a six-phase qualitative thematic analysis. The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. Fairness is the concern the reviews examine most fully. Well-being is the one they examine least. The thematic analysis organised the evidence into three macro-themes, trust dynamics in AI-enabled HRM, algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation, and employee well-being and vulnerability, and showed that the literature has treated these as isolated questions. Our main contribution is the Integrated Ethical AI-HRM Framework, which orders the three pillars into a single structure: fairness and transparency condition employee trust, trust in turn shapes well-being, and the long-term durability of workplace AI depends on mitigating algorithmic bias and keeping algorithmic reasoning explainable.

items.abstract_text: Drug prescription review is a key link in ensuring patient medication safety and improving the quality of medicine. This article is a narrative review of the development history, core technical architecture, main application models, implementation benefits, and the challenges and future trends of information-based drug prescription review. Rule engines, clinical decision support, machine learning and generative artificial intelligence have extended review from static rule checking towards risk prediction and text understanding, but these technologies differ substantially in validation, interpretability and maturity. Information-based review achieves real-time, standardised interception and alerting of prescription risks at scale and reduces the rate at which recognised prescribing errors reach the patient; the evidence for reductions in preventable adverse drug events and in patient outcomes such as admissions and mortality is, however, weaker, heterogeneous and dominated by single-centre or before-and-after designs. System limitations, clinical adaptability, data quality, alert fatigue, interoperability, equity and law still require attention, and future value will depend less on algorithmic sophistication than on validation in real settings, interoperable data and human oversight.

items.abstract_text: Combinatorial decision making is a fundamental area in computer science, and significant attention has been devoted to designing effective algorithms for such problems. Given the power of machine learning, data-driven methods have been shown to be effective in designing algorithms for combinatorial decision making problems. However, combinatorial decision making problems over graphs still remain challenging when important information about the graph is missing in real-world applications. One specific problem in this domain is the query-decision regression task, where the goal is to find a high-quality solution, also referred to as a decision, for an unseen input, referred to as a query, by leveraging historical query-decision pairs on graphs with missing edge information. The current state-of-the-art method addresses this problem by generating multiple groups of edge weights randomly and learning a weighted combination of these groups to estimate the missing information. However, the performance of this method is limited by the quality of the generated edge weight groups. To overcome this challenge, we first propose SocialLearner, a specialized framework for the query-decision regression formulation on social network problems, such as misinformation prevention, source detection, and community protection. This novel framework incorporates the merits of ensemble models and importance sampling for better edge weight generation and more accurate weight approximation. We evaluate the performance of SocialLearner by comparing it with existing methods. The results show significant improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency, demonstrating that SocialLearner is a scalable and effective framework for solving social network problems. Building upon SocialLearner, we further introduce QDR-Soup, an extended framework aimed at solving the query-decision regression formulation of general combinatorial decision making problems over graphs. Experimental evidence shows that QDR-Soup is an effective and reliable approach for query-decision regression tasks. Compared to the state-of-the-art method, our approach improves the ratio to the optimal solution across various datasets and problems, e.g., from 0.54 to 0.82 on a Steiner tree problem dataset. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers a new paradigm for solving complex combinatorial decision making problems. To bridge the gap between traditional algorithms and LLM-driven decision making, we aim to explore their potential to assist in algorithm design for combinatorial decision-making problems. Despite this promise, applying LLMs directly to such problems remains difficult due to their inherent complexity and structural constraints. As an initial step, we focus on developing powerful multi-agent systems to address simpler reasoning problems. While large language model-based multi-agent systems demonstrate strong capabilities across different reasoning tasks, current methods often rely on static or task-specific designs. These instance-agnostic methods overlook varying instance complexities, leading to redundant communication in simple scenarios and insufficient coordination in demanding ones. Consequently, they fail to achieve effective and efficient collaborative reasoning among agents. To overcome these limitations, we propose Difficulty-Aware Graph Pruning (\textbf{DAGP}), an adaptive framework that configures communication structures based on instance-specific difficulty. DAGP integrates a difficulty estimation module and a sparsity control mechanism to selectively activate communication edges based on each instance, promoting efficient and targeted collaboration. Empirical evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DAGP consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other baselines while reducing average token usage by 45%. Parallel to the architectural efficiency of multi-agent systems, efficient deployment of these complex decision-making agents is equally important. Driven by the real-world demand for self-hosted deployment, we further propose a novel perspective for measuring parameter importance by treating quantization as a form of noise injection for mixed-precision quantization. Rather than using indirect metrics such as Hessian matrices, our approach directly injects Gaussian noise into pre-trained models to observe performance degradation, providing a more direct measure of parameter sensitivity for mixed-precision quantization of large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that our method recovers 83.24% of full-precision performance on LLaMA3.2-3B at an average precision of 3.2 bits, outperforming AutoRound by 74.06% and HAWQ by 2.77%. On Qwen3-4B, our approach retains 80.66% of full-precision performance at 3.1 bits. This work explores a shifting paradigm in combinatorial decision making, spanning the transition from traditional data-driven optimization to adaptive reasoning with large language models. By bridging the gap between classical algorithms and LLM-driven agents, these contributions offer solutions that enhance both collective intelligence and deployment efficiency in real-world applications.
