This need is particularly relevant in projects funded through national and European programs, where the project timeline guides the achievement of milestones and targets, procedural monitoring, and reporting. Planning, however, cannot be reduced to a mere technical formality: within educational organizations—understood as complex and adaptive systems—it constitutes a process of negotiating meanings, distributing responsibilities, and reflectively regulating action (Sibilio, 2014). From this perspective, the Gantt chart can become an authentic and engaging task through which stakeholders translate general objectives into observable actions, discuss priorities and constraints, make reasoned decisions, and progressively assess the project’s sustainability. The introduction of AI can reinforce this function, but it also carries the risk of deeming outputs plausible and effective simply because they are produced quickly or presented in an orderly manner. The scientific problem that underpins this study therefore concerns the conditions under which AI can support motivation, agency, and authenticity in design without undermining professional judgment, human responsibility, and adherence to contextual needs. The choice of the diagram draws on the function originally attributed by Gantt to the temporal representation of work: to make the sequence of activities, progress, and organizational responsibilities clear (Gantt, 1919). The objective is to compare general-purpose generative AI tools with specific project management applications capable of generating or supporting Gantt charts, evaluating their potential, limitations, and pedagogical and organizational implications. The focus is not only on the technical quality of the schedule but also on its ability to encourage participation, make decisions transparent, foster accountability, and support planning that is authentically connected to real-world professional situations. The research adopts a “ ” design for an exploratory-comparative study and uses a single simulated case scenario related to the planning of an educational or training intervention. The same scenario—including objectives, target audience, duration, available resources, organizational constraints, expected outcomes, and professional roles—is subjected to the various tools through a standardized sequence of requests. A first prompt calls for the production of the general plan; a second prompt asks users to specify activities, sub-activities, durations, dependencies, responsibilities, milestones, and potential critical issues; a third prompt requires users to revise the schedule in the event of an unforeseen circumstance, in order to assess the tool’s ability to adapt the plan without losing consistency. To reduce variability attributable to the wording of the instructions, the content, order, and level of detail of the prompts are kept constant, while also recording the steps necessary to obtain a usable output. The outputs are compiled into a document corpus comprising tables, time-based representations, textual explanations, and revision proposals. The unit of analysis consists of both the entire design artifact and the individual elements that comprise it. The evaluation is structured into two complementary levels. The first considers accuracy, completeness, temporal consistency, clarity of phases, correctness of dependencies, clarity of responsibilities, usability, accessibility, customization options, and economic sustainability. The second examines pedagogical relevance: alignment between activities and learning objectives, the ability to make decisions understandable, support for collaboration, promotion of learner agency, and the presence of risks related to delegation or automated decision-making. The findings are organized using a common matrix and interpreted through SWOT analysis, which is employed to identify the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of the various tools (Helms & Nixon, 2010). A human review of the outputs is also conducted to identify omissions, inconsistencies, impossible dependencies, or unjustified assumptions. The comparison does not aim to produce an absolute ranking but rather to verify the suitability of the solutions with respect to the specific educational task and the competencies required to manage them. The expected results indicate a functional differentiation among the categories of tools. General-purpose solutions should offer greater speed in initial design, in breaking down activities, and in reformulating the plan, proving particularly useful during the start-up and exploration phases. Dedicated applications, on the other hand, should ensure a more stable representation of dependencies, more controllable updates to deadlines, and better traceability of responsibilities. In both categories, the quality of the output should depend significantly on the accuracy of the initial information, the user’s ability to formulate relevant requests, and the critical review of the product. items.title: Information Overload and Disutility in Generative AI Systems as Cognitive Extension: A Bounded Rationality Perspective

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

items.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.title: Too good to resist? Affective engagement and a competence–regulation gap predict self-reported over-reliance on generative AI among vocational foreign-language learners

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

items.abstract_text: Conversational Agents (CAs) is rapidly transforming higher education by providing personalised learning support, adaptive feedback, and interactive educational experiences. However, most research has focused on learning performance rather than students psychological wellbeing. This scoping review examines how Self-Determination Theory (SDT) has been applied in the design of conversational AI to promote digital wellbeing and compassionate educational technology. Guided by the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), a systematic search of four major databases identified 28 eligible studies published between 2018 and 2026. Thematic analysis revealed that conversational AI predominantly supports students competence through intelligent tutoring, adaptive scaffolding, and personalised feedback, while explicit support for autonomy and relatedness remains limited. Digital wellbeing is rarely considered an intended design outcome. Based on these findings, the review proposes a preliminary SDT informed conversational AI design framework comprising four interconnected principles which are supporting learner autonomy, strengthening competence, fostering relatedness through compassionate interactions, and promoting responsible AI use to enhance digital wellbeing. Integrating motivational psychology with human-centred AI design, this review provides practical guidance for developing AI systems that support learner agency, psychological wellbeing, and sustainable engagement, contributing to the design of compassionate educational technologies for the future of higher education.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.abstract_text: Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming ubiquitous in consumers' lives and search activities. AI applications that can create content, have conversations, respond to emotions, recognize images and objects, and construct real‐world experiences (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Google Lens, Apple Vision Pro) are transforming consumer search by functioning as psychological surrogates that assume key cognitive, evaluative, perceptual, and relational processes on consumers' behalf. Yet limited research has examined how these technologies transform the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer search. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic narrative review of 75 articles on the psychological foundations of consumer search and introduces the concept of AI psychological surrogacy, which happens when advanced‐AI technologies assume key psychological processes traditionally performed by humans. We develop a conceptual framework that theorizes AI psychological surrogacy across three higher‐order systems (affective‐relational delegation, cognitive‐evaluative substitution, and sensory‐perceptual construction) and six mechanisms: affective transference, relational surrogacy, cognitive delegation, evaluative surrogacy, perceptual offloading, and sensory augmentation. We advance six research propositions and a research agenda for investigating how reliance on AI as a psychological surrogate may alter consumer cognition, evaluation, perception, and relational dynamics.

items.title: Generative AI Use and Student Well-Being in Higher Education: A Literature Review
items.venue: Academic journal of management and social sciences

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.

items.abstract_text: Drawing on dynamic usage‐based and interactionist SLA perspectives, this study investigated developmental patterns of linguistic complexity and language‐related episodes (LREs) during L2 learners' written interactions with ChatGPT. Ten Korean EFL learners completed seven sessions of opinion‐gap and debate tasks over 5 weeks. Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) revealed dynamic, non‐linear developmental trajectories that differed by proficiency and task type. Lower‐proficiency learners exhibited an inverted U‐shaped pattern in syntactic complexity, whereas higher‐proficiency learners showed stability in syntax but a non‐linear increase in lexical sophistication. Regarding task effects, debate tasks consistently elicited greater syntactic complexity than opinion‐gap tasks and showed an overall increase in lexical sophistication. LRE analysis indicated that learners focused primarily on lexis over grammar, with reliance on the L1 increasing over time. Pedagogically, these findings highlight the dynamic nature of language development in GenAI‐mediated interactions and suggest that AI‐based tasks should be designed considering learner proficiency and task type to maximize learning opportunities.

items.venue: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development
items.abstract_text: Abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

items.abstract_text: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

This conceptual article argues that CTE should be reconceptualized from an educational pathway to workforce infrastructure that continuously connects education, industry, technology, policy, and lifelong learning. items.abstract_text: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. items.abstract_text: The study uses a Christian-anthropological approach to evaluate the educational application of generative artificial intelligence. Its central question is: what gives the teacher a human, irreplaceable essence, and which tasks can be delegated to artificial intelligence in ways that preserve the goals of Christian education while making learning more effective? The argument connects theological anthropology, personalist thinking, and educational research. As a conceptual-normative synthesis rather than an empirical intervention, it draws on the doctrine of Imago Dei, Buber’s I–Thou relation, and Simone Weil’s notion of attention to mark the ontological difference between the person and machine simulation. The article argues that artificial intelligence can significantly strengthen technical and informational pedagogical work, but it cannot replace the relational, moral, spiritual, and vocational dimensions of education. Functional similarity, on this reading, does not amount to substantial identity: a language model has no conscious self that could answer for its outputs. Learning understood as formatio also demands effort, waiting, and uncertainty, which the promise of frictionless learning tends to erase. Five dimensions of the teaching role – presence, moral responsibility, authority, vocational guidance, and community – are shown to resist automation. The study proposes a three-zone delegation matrix: delegable tasks, co-pilot tasks under teacher supervision, and non-delegable, person-specific pedagogical moments. Each zone is paired with its main risk and a pedagogical condition: factual error calls for teacher control and source criticism, deskilling for the teacher’s final decision, and depersonalization for a personal, accountable human judgment. The article concludes that the role of artificial intelligence in Christian education lies in multiplying human capabilities rather than replacing the human teacher.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping English-language learning and digitally mediated work, yet research on AI-supported language development, psychological conditions, AI literacy, and graduate employability has largely developed in separate literatures. This focused narrative review integrates these domains to examine how AI-supported English learning may relate to graduate employability among university students and recent graduates, particularly in EFL and other non-native-English-speaking higher-education contexts. The final evidence base comprises 46 unique sources, including 19 published between 2018 and 2026 and 27 earlier foundational or contextual sources, drawn from empirical studies, reviews, theoretical literature, competence frameworks, and selected authoritative reports. The review examines how specific AI affordances support or constrain language-learning processes and differentiated English outcomes; how functional English communication relates to employability capabilities; how motivation, language anxiety, linguistic and digital self-efficacy, and career confidence operate as distinct antecedents, conditioning factors, or outcomes; and how critical AI literacy intersects with language and professional competence. Its distinctive contribution is a mechanism-based framework linking AI affordances, language-learning processes, English communicative outcomes, employability capabilities, perceived employability, opportunity access, and labor-market outcomes while explicitly distinguishing comparatively well-supported proximal relationships from tentative downstream transitions. The synthesis indicates that AI-supported learning can support feedback uptake, revision, repeated practice, interaction, and selected linguistic and psychological outcomes, but evidence for durable independent proficiency is more heterogeneous and direct evidence for employment, earnings, retention, or career progression remains limited. Benefits are conditional on pedagogical design, independent practice, human interaction, equitable access, and responsible AI use. Accordingly, the framework should be interpreted as a set of mechanism-based propositions rather than a validated causal model linking AI use directly to employability or employment. Because source identification and selection were purposive rather than exhaustive, the conclusions remain subject to selection and publication bias, geographical imbalance, methodological heterogeneity, reviewer judgment, and the rapid evolution of AI technologies. Of the 46 sources, 15 are classified as primary empirical publications, and four provide RQ1-specific direct evidence on AI-supported English-language learning. Two primary empirical publications examine graduate employability-related competencies or perceptions; one additional publication synthesizes earlier empirical assessments. Although some evidence concerns graduates’ employment experiences, no included study directly tests the effect of AI-supported English learning on job attainment or other labor-market outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in educational practice, transforming lesson planning, instructional delivery, assessment, learning analytics, and teacher professional development. Although research on AI in education has expanded rapidly, the psychological consequences of AI adoption for teachers remain theoretically fragmented. Existing studies have examined technology acceptance, AI literacy, technology self-efficacy, instructional confidence, and professional identity, yet these constructs have rarely been integrated into a coherent account of how AI reshapes teachers’ beliefs about their own professional capabilities. This narrative review synthesizes the emerging literature through a theory-building perspective grounded primarily in social cognitive theory and informed by technology acceptance, cognitive load, professional identity, social comparison, and human–AI interaction perspectives. We propose a framework of AI-Mediated Efficacy Reconstruction, conceptualizing AI not as a direct determinant of teacher self-efficacy but as a socio-technical factor that changes the availability, interpretation, and attribution of efficacy-relevant experiences. AI can facilitate mastery experiences, provide vicarious learning opportunities, offer timely feedback, reduce routine cognitive demands, and expand access to professional learning. However, the same technologies may generate cognitive overload, technical anxiety, professional comparison, identity threat, reduced autonomy, and technological dependence. We identify Efficacy Attribution as a potentially central mechanism determining whether AI-supported performance is internalized as evidence of teachers’ own professional capability or attributed primarily to the technological system. On this basis, we distinguish Augmented Efficacy, in which AI extends teachers’ capabilities while preserving professional agency, from Dependent Efficacy, in which perceived competence becomes increasingly contingent upon AI assistance. The framework further proposes that these processes are moderated by teacher characteristics, AI-system characteristics, teaching tasks, organizational context, and time. We conclude by outlining implications for measurement, teacher professional development, AI design, organizational policy, and future longitudinal and experimental research.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. Drawing comparative insights from the EU AI Act, it examines gaps in Bangladesh’s digital legislation and institutional practice and identifies best practices. It also compares practice in the neighbouring countries of India and Pakistan to assess Bangladesh’s position within South Asia’s regional AI governance framework. Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

items.abstract_text: Large language models can now outperform human persuaders in controlled settings, and they do so in whichever direction they are instructed to persuade. Regulatory and ethical responses to this development nevertheless remain anchored in what this article calls the deception paradigm: the assumption that communicative influence becomes wrongful when, and because, it involves false assertion. The article argues that this paradigm systematically fails to capture AI hyperpersuasion. Drawing on the philosophical literature on manipulation, it shows that hyperpersuasion characteristically operates through true but selectively curated content, adaptive framing, simulated intimacy, and the exploitation of individually diagnosed cognitive dispositions – techniques that bypass rather than deceive rational agency. It then examines Article 5(1)(a)–(b) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Although the prohibition is conceptually open to manipulation without deception, its operative test – material distortion, appreciable impairment of informed decision-making, counterfactual decision change, and significant harm – is inherited from unfair commercial practices law and reproduces the architecture of fraud, leaving paradigmatic cases of hyperpersuasion untouched. Extending the analysis from individual autonomy to democratic epistemology, the article contends that hyperpersuasion threatens democracy not primarily by aggregating individual harms but by degrading the epistemic conditions – independence of judgment formation, a shared space of reasons, and the contestability of public claims – on which collective self-government depends. Regulating hyperpersuasion therefore requires a shift from content-based tests of falsity and harm to process- and relationship-based criteria that target asymmetric epistemic power.

items.title: Human-LLM Cognitive Extension: A Framework for Studying Coupled Cognition

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare, creating opportunities to improve diagnosis, clinical decision-making, resource allocation, and healthcare delivery, while also raising concerns regarding algorithmic bias, discrimination, transparency, accountability, and health equity. These challenges are particularly relevant in fragmented healthcare systems, where pre-existing social and institutional inequalities may interact with AI-based decision-making. This qualitative socio-legal documentary review with a narrative synthesis critically examines the Chilean legal and regulatory framework governing the use of AI in healthcare, with particular attention to algorithmic bias, discrimination, health equity, transparency, accountability, and the protection of patients’ fundamental rights. The review draws on academic literature, legislation, governmental and institutional documents, and international regulatory instruments to identify regulatory gaps and governance challenges relevant to Chilean healthcare. The analysis indicates that Chilean law provides important constitutional and statutory protections concerning equality, non-discrimination, health, personal data, and patient rights, but that these protections are not yet articulated within a specific sectoral framework addressing algorithmic discrimination and the governance of AI in healthcare. Particular challenges concern indirect discrimination, algorithmic opacity, accountability, human oversight, and the capacity to identify and mitigate bias throughout the AI lifecycle. The review does not empirically assess the performance or discriminatory effects of individual AI systems. Drawing on the Chilean context and selected international regulatory developments, particularly the European Union AI Act, the review develops a sector-specific governance framework centered on transparency and explainability, accountability, human oversight, periodic bias auditing, equity assessment, and AI literacy. The findings contribute to broader discussions on equitable AI governance in healthcare, particularly in countries characterized by fragmented health systems and comparable regulatory challenges.

items.abstract_text: Although AI-driven environmental, social, and governance (ESG) analytics have advanced rapidly, evidence of their effectiveness remains uneven across different reporting environments. This study systematically reviews Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques applied to ESG-oriented financial intelligence, examining the relationship between computational approaches, data infrastructure, and institutional conditions, with particular attention to emerging-market contexts. The evidence base is globally distributed, while South Africa is used as an illustrative emerging-market case to contextualise disclosure fragmentation and institutional constraints rather than as the primary empirical unit of analysis. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-compliant Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted on 70 peer-reviewed studies published between 2017 and 2025. A cross-dimensional coding framework was used to classify modelling architectures, ESG data modalities, task formulations, and implementation constraints. The analysis further considered validation quality, data dependency, transferability, and governance relevance across these dimensions. The findings indicate that advances in model architecture have outpaced the development of supporting data infrastructure. Governance and explainability mechanisms are commonly added after modelling rather than integrated into system design. Dependence on proprietary datasets limits reproducibility, while reported performance often reflects high-resource disclosure environments uncommon in emerging markets. The principal constraints on ESG-oriented financial intelligence arise from fragmented data infrastructures, inconsistent reporting practices, and uneven institutional readiness rather than from model capability alone. The proposed architecture is therefore presented as a conceptual synthesis requiring empirical validation, not as a deployment-ready system.

items.abstract_text: AI-driven personalised learning now shapes the pace, practice, and feedback of millions of learners. Most systems, however, personalise learning for the learner through opaque algorithmic decisions instead of equipping learners to personalise their own study. This review examines that asymmetry. Twenty-five studies published between 2017 and 2026, retrieved from Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus, are synthesised thematically around learner agency, self-regulated learning, and system design. The synthesis identifies an illusion of autonomy: surface-level choices sit alongside algorithmic authority over goals, sequencing, and mastery criteria, which narrows the room learners have to practise goal setting, strategic monitoring, and reflective evaluation. Duolingo and two platforms used in Vietnam serve as illustrative cases showing how gamified metrics and default pathways can redirect attention from meaningful goals towards externally driven engagement. The paper answers with a learner-driven personalisation framework resting on three principles: shared control, design that activates self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency coupled with AI literacy. A three-item rubric operationalises the framework so that schools can detect illusion-of-autonomy risks before adoption. The analysis extends to equity, since learners with limited devices, connectivity, or AI literacy gain the least from transparency measures that presuppose digital capital. Implications concern system designers, educational leaders, and teachers in Vietnam, who need evaluation criteria reaching beyond short-term performance. The contribution is a concise screening tool that links learner control, the three phases of self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency, complementing broader agency rubrics with a focused test for illusion-of-autonomy risks.

It argues that these tools, powered by models trained on biased, English-dominant corpora, function as new linguistic gatekeepers, perpetuating the hegemonic ideology of a single “standard” English. The user prompt is posited as a critical site where this ideology is enacted. Through a mixed-methods study analyzing L2 learners’ prompts and the feedback they elicit, this research demonstrates how common prompting practices construct the GenAI tool as a “native speaker” authority, leading to a focus on surface-level correctness that can suppress a writer’s agency and voice. It advances a framework for critical AI literacy that treats prompting as a rhetorical, empowering act, enabling learners to resist algorithmic control and reclaim their original voices.

items.abstract_text: Existing accounts of language in autism have tended to focus on English and have rarely progressed beyond broad characterizations of pragmatic difficulty. This volume changes both. Drawing on a clinically defined corpus of Japanese-speaking individuals with ASD and combining Systemic Functional Linguistics with machine learning, it identifies 46 lexicogrammatical discriminators of ASD and non-ASD discourse, with 80% classification accuracy. Thirty-eight of these discriminators are interpreted across twelve cognitive-functional domains, including weak central coherence, joint attention, predictive processing, executive function, and working memory, revealing how recurrent grammatical choices relate to neurocognitive profiles. Analyses span a broad range of lexicogrammatical categories, including clause complexes, process types, appraisal, modality, evidentiality, negotiating particles, and sound-symbolic expression. The result is the first book-length, empirically grounded account of lexicogrammatical variability in ASD, opening new directions for diagnostic assessment and language intervention. Essential reading for researchers and clinicians in autism studies, human neuroscience, clinical linguistics, and neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.abstract_text: Literature reviews on the ethics of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) have multiplied quickly, and the result is an evidence base that is abundant but scattered. Practitioners seeking guidance grounded in evidence have nowhere consolidated to turn. This study addresses that problem through an umbrella review, conducted under Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. A structured Scopus search produced a final corpus of thirteen peer-reviewed systematic and scoping reviews, published between 2020 and 2026. We analysed the corpus in two stages: a quantitative, descriptive mapping, then a six-phase qualitative thematic analysis. The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. Fairness is the concern the reviews examine most fully. Well-being is the one they examine least. The thematic analysis organised the evidence into three macro-themes, trust dynamics in AI-enabled HRM, algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation, and employee well-being and vulnerability, and showed that the literature has treated these as isolated questions. Our main contribution is the Integrated Ethical AI-HRM Framework, which orders the three pillars into a single structure: fairness and transparency condition employee trust, trust in turn shapes well-being, and the long-term durability of workplace AI depends on mitigating algorithmic bias and keeping algorithmic reasoning explainable.

items.abstract_text: This systematic review identified ethical risks associated with medical AI agents and developed a governance framework adapted to China's healthcare context. PubMed, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang Data were searched for records published or publicly released between January 1, 2020 and 30 June 2025. Of 1239 records identified, 837 underwent title and abstract screening, 68 were assessed in full, and 58 were included in the synthesis. The evidence base comprised 12 core agentic sources, 24 agent-focused boundary sources, and 22 governance, policy, legal, or normative sources. Eight non-exclusive ethical-risk themes were identified, led by safety, reliability, and hallucination; accountability and liability; bias and fairness; and privacy and security. Core agentic evidence indicated that multi-step execution, external tool use, persistent memory, and multi-agent coordination may amplify error propagation, provenance, privacy, and responsibility-allocation risks. Six representative cases and governance events were analyzed separately using the Four Principles of Biomedical Ethics to examine how similar risks arise across different technologies, jurisdictions, and institutional settings. The synthesis informed a four-component governance framework linking ethical and legal challenges, biomedical ethical principles, operational governance mechanisms, and expected outcomes. The proposed mechanisms include lifecycle risk monitoring, human oversight and escalation, responsibility allocation, privacy and data governance, documentation and auditability, fairness and equitable-access safeguards, and multistakeholder ethics review. The framework is intended as a policy-oriented and institutionally adaptable proposal rather than a validated intervention and requires prospective evaluation in specific cases of healthcare organizations and governance events.

items.abstract_text: Drug prescription review is a key link in ensuring patient medication safety and improving the quality of medicine. The traditional manual review model is limited by human resources, the speed of information updates and individual experience differences, making it difficult to cope with the increasingly complex environment of medication review. This article is a narrative review of the development history, core technical architecture, main application models, implementation benefits, and the challenges and future trends of information-based drug prescription review. Rule engines, clinical decision support, machine learning and generative artificial intelligence have extended review from static rule checking towards risk prediction and text understanding, but these technologies differ substantially in validation, interpretability and maturity. Information-based review achieves real-time, standardised interception and alerting of prescription risks at scale and reduces the rate at which recognised prescribing errors reach the patient; the evidence for reductions in preventable adverse drug events and in patient outcomes such as admissions and mortality is, however, weaker, heterogeneous and dominated by single-centre or before-and-after designs. System limitations, clinical adaptability, data quality, alert fatigue, interoperability, equity and law still require attention, and future value will depend less on algorithmic sophistication than on validation in real settings, interoperable data and human oversight.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming part of the everyday preparation of academic and professional presentations. Generative AI systems and AI-enabled presentation platforms can support brainstorming, content organisation, slide design, visual selection, language refinement and rehearsal. Yet the convenience of these systems creates a pedagogical tension: a technically polished presentation may not necessarily indicate that the student understands the content or can communicate it confidently in real time. This study examines the relationship between AI-assisted preparation and undergraduate students’ presentation performance, with particular attention to content ownership, confidence, creativity, audience engagement and spontaneous communication. A descriptive qualitative design was used with 40 first-year engineering students. Data were gathered through a structured Google Form survey and classroom video observations. The study focused on students’ use of tools such as ChatGPT, Canva and PowerPoint Designer, their degree of personalisation of AI-generated material, and their self-perceived confidence during live presentation. The findings indicate widespread use of AI during preparation, but also a noticeable gap between efficient slide production and effective oral delivery. Students who relied heavily on AI-generated material often found it difficult to explain ideas fluently, sustain audience engagement and respond spontaneously to questions. Students who revised AI-assisted content, added their own examples and rehearsed their presentations demonstrated stronger signs of confidence, eye contact and clarity. The study therefore argues for a human-centred, balanced model in which AI functions as a scaffold rather than a substitute for thinking and speaking. The paper proposes a practical AI–Presentation Balance Framework that integrates topic understanding, responsible prompting, personalisation, visual design, rehearsal and human delivery. The framework has implications for English language teaching, engineering education and employability-oriented communication training.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Smoking remains a leading cause of preventable mortality worldwide, yet conventional treatments–including psychotherapy–face persistent challenges related to accessibility and consistent efficacy. Digital therapies, including e-Health, m-Health, and AI-driven approaches, offer promising avenues to personalize and scale behavioral interventions. Methods This systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of app-based mindfulness interventions (MBIs) for smoking cessation in people who smoke, compared with a control condition, and was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Comprehensive searches were conducted across four databases in November 2024. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, results were synthesized narratively, and the certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE. Eight eligible reports, describing six independent studies, were identified, encompassing a total of 810 participants. Results Some studies reported reductions in cigarettes per day and craving, particularly among users who actively engaged with the interventions. However, only one small pilot trial, in which the app was combined with contingency management, found higher abstinence rates than the comparator, and the largest trial found no difference in biochemically verified abstinence at 6 months. Moreover, considerable heterogeneity in study populations, intervention designs, and outcome measures – alongside limited statistical power – hinders definitive conclusions, and the certainty of the evidence was very low for all outcomes. Discussion Digital mindfulness therapies are a scalable approach that could complement smoking cessation support, but current evidence does not show that they increase abstinence. Their integration into public health strategies warrants further investigation, with emphasis on adequately powered trials with biochemically verified long-term abstinence, standardizing protocols, and enhancing user engagement to optimize outcomes.

items.abstract_text: A growing body of research has focused on the potential of Robot‐Assisted Language Learning (RALL) over the past decades. However, how such an approach affects English as a foreign language (EFL) learners' psycho‐emotional states is left under‐researched. To address this gap, this study adopted an exploratory longitudinal design to investigate changes in Chinese EFL students' achievement emotions and well‐being following a two‐semester RALL intervention. A sample of 87 students participated in a course in which AI‐driven conversational agents were integrated into language learning activities. Two questionnaires measuring achievement emotions and well‐being were administered before and after the intervention. The results of paired‐samples t ‐tests indicated significant changes in both achievement emotions and well‐being. Specifically, positive achievement emotions increased, negative achievement emotions decreased and all dimensions of well‐being showed significant improvement after the intervention. The study offers practical implications for adopting RALL in EFL contexts more with special attention to its psycho‐affective consequences for teachers and learners.

items.title: LEARNING-DRIVEN OPTIMIZATION AND EFFICIENT LLM-BASED REASONING FOR COMBINATORIAL DECISION MAKING
items.venue: Library, Museums and Press - UDSpace (University of Delaware)

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Combinatorial decision making is a fundamental area in computer science, and significant attention has been devoted to designing effective algorithms for such problems. Given the power of machine learning, data-driven methods have been shown to be effective in designing algorithms for combinatorial decision making problems. However, combinatorial decision making problems over graphs still remain challenging when important information about the graph is missing in real-world applications. One specific problem in this domain is the query-decision regression task, where the goal is to find a high-quality solution, also referred to as a decision, for an unseen input, referred to as a query, by leveraging historical query-decision pairs on graphs with missing edge information. The current state-of-the-art method addresses this problem by generating multiple groups of edge weights randomly and learning a weighted combination of these groups to estimate the missing information. However, the performance of this method is limited by the quality of the generated edge weight groups. To overcome this challenge, we first propose SocialLearner, a specialized framework for the query-decision regression formulation on social network problems, such as misinformation prevention, source detection, and community protection. This novel framework incorporates the merits of ensemble models and importance sampling for better edge weight generation and more accurate weight approximation. We evaluate the performance of SocialLearner by comparing it with existing methods. The results show significant improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency, demonstrating that SocialLearner is a scalable and effective framework for solving social network problems. Building upon SocialLearner, we further introduce QDR-Soup, an extended framework aimed at solving the query-decision regression formulation of general combinatorial decision making problems over graphs. Experimental evidence shows that QDR-Soup is an effective and reliable approach for query-decision regression tasks. Compared to the state-of-the-art method, our approach improves the ratio to the optimal solution across various datasets and problems, e.g., from 0.54 to 0.82 on a Steiner tree problem dataset. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers a new paradigm for solving complex combinatorial decision making problems. To bridge the gap between traditional algorithms and LLM-driven decision making, we aim to explore their potential to assist in algorithm design for combinatorial decision-making problems. Despite this promise, applying LLMs directly to such problems remains difficult due to their inherent complexity and structural constraints. As an initial step, we focus on developing powerful multi-agent systems to address simpler reasoning problems. While large language model-based multi-agent systems demonstrate strong capabilities across different reasoning tasks, current methods often rely on static or task-specific designs. These instance-agnostic methods overlook varying instance complexities, leading to redundant communication in simple scenarios and insufficient coordination in demanding ones. Consequently, they fail to achieve effective and efficient collaborative reasoning among agents. To overcome these limitations, we propose Difficulty-Aware Graph Pruning (\textbf{DAGP}), an adaptive framework that configures communication structures based on instance-specific difficulty. DAGP integrates a difficulty estimation module and a sparsity control mechanism to selectively activate communication edges based on each instance, promoting efficient and targeted collaboration. Empirical evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DAGP consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other baselines while reducing average token usage by 45%. Parallel to the architectural efficiency of multi-agent systems, efficient deployment of these complex decision-making agents is equally important. Driven by the real-world demand for self-hosted deployment, we further propose a novel perspective for measuring parameter importance by treating quantization as a form of noise injection for mixed-precision quantization. Rather than using indirect metrics such as Hessian matrices, our approach directly injects Gaussian noise into pre-trained models to observe performance degradation, providing a more direct measure of parameter sensitivity for mixed-precision quantization of large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that our method recovers 83.24% of full-precision performance on LLaMA3.2-3B at an average precision of 3.2 bits, outperforming AutoRound by 74.06% and HAWQ by 2.77%. On Qwen3-4B, our approach retains 80.66% of full-precision performance at 3.1 bits. This work explores a shifting paradigm in combinatorial decision making, spanning the transition from traditional data-driven optimization to adaptive reasoning with large language models. By bridging the gap between classical algorithms and LLM-driven agents, these contributions offer solutions that enhance both collective intelligence and deployment efficiency in real-world applications.

items.title: Designing with Artificial Intelligence: Gantt Chart Tools, Educational Leadership, and Process Management
items.venue: Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching

publication_date_provenance.reason: OpenAlex publication_date alone does not verify the original publication event

items.abstract_text: This paper addresses the use of generative artificial intelligence and digital tools designed for creating Gantt charts to support educational planning, leadership, and shared process management. In school, university, and socio-educational contexts, the growing complexity of projects requires skills in planning, coordination, monitoring, and evaluation, along with tools capable of visualizing operational phases, timelines, responsibilities, milestones, and dependencies between activities. This need is particularly relevant in projects funded through national and European programs, where the project timeline guides the achievement of milestones and targets, procedural monitoring, and reporting. Planning, however, cannot be reduced to a mere technical formality: within educational organizations—understood as complex and adaptive systems—it constitutes a process of negotiating meanings, distributing responsibilities, and reflectively regulating action (Sibilio, 2014). From this perspective, the Gantt chart can become an authentic and engaging task through which stakeholders translate general objectives into observable actions, discuss priorities and constraints, make reasoned decisions, and progressively assess the project’s sustainability. The introduction of AI can reinforce this function, but it also carries the risk of deeming outputs plausible and effective simply because they are produced quickly or presented in an orderly manner. The scientific problem that underpins this study therefore concerns the conditions under which AI can support motivation, agency, and authenticity in design without undermining professional judgment, human responsibility, and adherence to contextual needs. The choice of the diagram draws on the function originally attributed by Gantt to the temporal representation of work: to make the sequence of activities, progress, and organizational responsibilities clear (Gantt, 1919). The objective is to compare general-purpose generative AI tools with specific project management applications capable of generating or supporting Gantt charts, evaluating their potential, limitations, and pedagogical and organizational implications. The focus is not only on the technical quality of the schedule but also on its ability to encourage participation, make decisions transparent, foster accountability, and support planning that is authentically connected to real-world professional situations. The research adopts a “ ” design for an exploratory-comparative study and uses a single simulated case scenario related to the planning of an educational or training intervention. The same scenario—including objectives, target audience, duration, available resources, organizational constraints, expected outcomes, and professional roles—is subjected to the various tools through a standardized sequence of requests. A first prompt calls for the production of the general plan; a second prompt asks users to specify activities, sub-activities, durations, dependencies, responsibilities, milestones, and potential critical issues; a third prompt requires users to revise the schedule in the event of an unforeseen circumstance, in order to assess the tool’s ability to adapt the plan without losing consistency. To reduce variability attributable to the wording of the instructions, the content, order, and level of detail of the prompts are kept constant, while also recording the steps necessary to obtain a usable output. The outputs are compiled into a document corpus comprising tables, time-based representations, textual explanations, and revision proposals. The unit of analysis consists of both the entire design artifact and the individual elements that comprise it. The evaluation is structured into two complementary levels. The first considers accuracy, completeness, temporal consistency, clarity of phases, correctness of dependencies, clarity of responsibilities, usability, accessibility, customization options, and economic sustainability. The second examines pedagogical relevance: alignment between activities and learning objectives, the ability to make decisions understandable, support for collaboration, promotion of learner agency, and the presence of risks related to delegation or automated decision-making. The findings are organized using a common matrix and interpreted through SWOT analysis, which is employed to identify the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of the various tools (Helms & Nixon, 2010). A human review of the outputs is also conducted to identify omissions, inconsistencies, impossible dependencies, or unjustified assumptions. The comparison does not aim to produce an absolute ranking but rather to verify the suitability of the solutions with respect to the specific educational task and the competencies required to manage them. The expected results indicate a functional differentiation among the categories of tools. General-purpose solutions should offer greater speed in initial design, in breaking down activities, and in reformulating the plan, proving particularly useful during the start-up and exploration phases. Dedicated applications, on the other hand, should ensure a more stable representation of dependencies, more controllable updates to deadlines, and better traceability of responsibilities. In both categories, the quality of the output should depend significantly on the accuracy of the initial information, the user’s ability to formulate relevant requests, and the critical review of the product. It is also expected that seemingly complete outputs may contain simplifications, missing activities, unrealistic timelines, or attributions of responsibility that are inconsistent with the context. items.title: What is the Role of Small Models in the LLM Era: A Survey

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in various reasoning tasks, which leads to the development of increasingly large models. However, scaling up model sizes results in significantly higher computational costs and energy consumption, which makes these models impractical for academic researchers and businesses with limited resources. At the same time, Small Models (SMs) are frequently used in practical settings, although their significance is currently underestimated. This raises important questions about the role of SMs in the era of LLMs, a topic that has received limited attention in prior surveys. In this work, we systematically examine the relationship between LLMs and SMs from two key perspectives: Collaboration and Competition ( or Complementarity ). We hope this survey provides valuable insights for practitioners, fostering a deeper understanding of the contribution of small models and promoting more efficient use of computational resources. Code and additional resources for this survey are available at: https://github.com/tigerchen52/awesome_role_of_small_models.

items.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Academic Writing: Linguistic Accuracy and Ethical Concerns

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: This study examines the use of artificial intelligence tools in academic writing, with particular attention to linguistic accuracy, writing quality, and ethical concerns in higher education. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, writing process theory, Computer-Assisted Language Learning, applied linguistics, and academic integrity frameworks, the study investigates AI-supported revision as a situated writing practice rather than as a general substitute for scholarly work. A mixed-methods empirical design was organized around 240 short paired academic writing samples, 426 questionnaire responses from students, postgraduate researchers, and academic staff, 38 semi-structured interviews, expert evaluation of writing quality, and analysis of institutional academic-integrity guidelines. Quantitative findings indicate that AI-assisted revision was associated with higher expert ratings for grammar accuracy, sentence clarity, cohesion, vocabulary precision, and academic register within controlled short writing tasks, but it did not produce equivalent gains in originality, disciplinary argumentation, or critical stance. Regression results show that critical AI literacy, institutional guidance, and ethical concern predicted responsible-use behavior more strongly than tool-use frequency alone. Qualitative findings show that participants valued AI tools as accessible language-support systems, yet remained concerned about authorship ambiguity, dependency, privacy, plagiarism risk, citation reliability, and loss of writer voice. The study contributes a Responsible AI-Supported Academic Writing Model that connects linguistic revision with writer agency, disclosure, human verification, and ethical authorship. The findings suggest that AI-assisted writing is most defensible when used as accountable revision support, not as a replacement for critical thinking, disciplinary knowledge, or original scholarly contribution.

items.title: From the fluency fallacy to the micro-to-macro validity gap: opportunities and pitfalls of LLMs in social simulation

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into social simulation has generated considerable enthusiasm, but also raises substantial methodological and epistemological challenges. This critical review examines the use of LLMs as cognitive or decision-making components of simulated agents from a computational social science perspective. Rather than treating the psychological evaluation of LLMs as separate from simulation mechanics, we argue that their behavioral and epistemic limitations can become systemic vulnerabilities when scaled to multi-agent societies. We first map the rapidly evolving landscape of LLM-driven platforms, ranging from small narrative sandboxes to population-scale and spatially structured simulations. We then develop a unified critical framework for analyzing the Micro-to-Macro Validity Gap: the propagation, nonlinear amplification, or convergent contraction of micro-level limitations—including hallucinations, stochastic inconsistency, representational biases, and alignment effects—into agent-level distortions (such as average persona convergence) and macro-level risks (such as artificial consensus and behavioral homogenization), while exposing evaluators to epistemic vulnerabilities such as the Fluency Fallacy and automation bias. We identify contexts in which LLM-based agents offer genuine operational value, including serious games, participatory environments, and exploratory modeling, while distinguishing these uses from confirmatory research with unconstrained models and precise social forecasting. Finally, we examine theory-driven hybrid architectures that embed LLMs within explicit, mechanistic, and reproducible Agent-Based modeling (ABM) frameworks. We argue that such architectures offer a promising but not sufficient path toward improving epistemic control: their validity depends on multi-level evaluation of environmental dynamics, individual behavior, cross-level interactions, and aggregate outcomes, and they remain vulnerable to the risk of physics washing.

items.abstract_text: Human oversight is widely required for autonomous and artificial-intelligence systems, yet assigning a human role does not establish that the person can influence a hazardous trajectory. This study develops a bounded Safety-Control Governance Framework for assessing whether documentary human-control claims are operationally inspectable. Drawing on systems-theoretic safety, supervisory control, situation awareness, resilience engineering, meaningful human control, and AI governance, the framework distinguishes seven operational functions—authority allocation, feedback and observability, situational comprehension, intervention timing, safe-state objective, escalation, and recovery—and two cross-cutting governance functions: accountability assignment and documentation or assurance. The framework was applied to a purposive corpus of 24 public documents spanning autonomous mobility, maritime autonomy, drones and emergency operations, and high-risk AI or command support, producing 216 document–function observations. Authority and accountability were Explicit in 20 of 24 documents and documentation or assurance in 23 of 24. Explicit specification was less frequent for intervention timing (8 of 22 known cases), safe-state objectives (7 of 23), escalation (10 of 24), and recovery (6 of 24). Documentary families supplied complementary evidence, while configuration analysis located distinct discontinuities, including explicit authority while feedback and comprehension were not both Explicit in ten documents. Most degradation-pattern evidence was anticipatory or prescriptive rather than event-based. These numerical profiles are conditional on the final coding rules and source selection. The framework provides an evidence-linked protocol for tracing documentary control gaps; it does not assess operational performance.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers South African manufacturing small, medium and micro enterprises (SMMEs) opportunities to strengthen production efficiency, quality control, predictive maintenance, supply-chain coordination and innovation. Yet responsible adoption remains constrained by limited finance, infrastructure, skills, data capability and governance capacity. This article examines how entrepreneurial leadership and organisational readiness shape responsible AI adoption and how AI-enabled manufacturing innovation may support sustainable business performance under appropriate readiness and governance conditions.This article presents a structured conceptual review of individually cited literature on AI adoption, responsible-AI governance and manufacturing SMMEs. The review is selective rather than exhaustive and does not claim compliance with PRISMA 2020; a prospective protocol specifies how a subsequent systematic review could be conducted, but the conceptual claims rest only on sources fully identified in the reference list and discussed individually in the manuscript.The review develops the Responsible Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework for South African Manufacturing SMMEs (RAIA–MSMME) as a parsimonious organising model. International AI-adoption evidence is situated within South Africa’s regulatory and institutional environment, including POPIA, Information Regulator requirements, manufacturing-support programmes and local 4IR capability-development platforms, with attention to township and rural manufacturers. The resulting relationships require empirical testing.
